https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Synthesis of Novel Two-Dimensional Graphene-like Nanomaterials for Catalysis and Energy Applications
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Modern catalytic technologies are costly and inefficient at targeting the harmful byproducts of refining processes. However, recent studies show that contemporary catalysts stand to improve through doping and colloidal synthetic methods to produce low-cost, highly active hybrid materials. The key to unlocking the full potential of these hybrid materials lies in maximizing the available active surface area to influence hydrodenitrogenation, hydrodeoxygenation and hydrodesulfurization. Here, our work shows promise in working at the nanoscale to tune the properties of these catalysts and to produce them at a fraction of the cost of comparable, high-efficacy catalysts. This project targets the synthetic study of single nanosheets of Molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ), a highly investigated catalyst for electrochemical studies and energy applications, produced via colloidal synthesis using Cobalt and Nickel dopants. Our results demonstrated an increased catalytic activity for the hydrogen evolution reaction – signaling an expectation of promising results for hydrodesulfurization, which has a similar chemical pathway - when utilizing Cobalt as a dopant in conjunction with specific synthetic parameters including nucleation time, reaction temperature, dopant concentration, and the Sulfur precursor. After determining viable candidates for further reaction-based studies through Linear Sweep Voltammetry, we confirmed the structure of our materials through X-Ray Diffraction and examined the incorporated dopant percentage through Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry. Thus, by assurance of our characterizations, we have developed a method of improving the catalytic activity of Molybdenum disulfide by producing Cobalt-doped MoS 2 nanosheets with the goal of innovating cost-effective, consistent, and alternative catalysts that can optimize current processing methods in chemical manufacturing.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Enhancing Electrolytic Ozone Selectivity and Activity with SnO2- Sb-Ni-Gd Electrocatalysts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Electrolytic synthesis of ozone is unique from other synthesis techniques due to its ability to generate ozone directly in water with generally lower equipment costs relative to competing methods. The selectivity and stability of the catalyst material used in electrolytic synthesis is, however, a major disadvantage when compared to long term operation of other methods. Many investigators have contributed to finding new, highly selective, and minimally hazardous catalysts for ozone synthesis, such as Ni and Sb doped SnO2, but as of yet none have proven adequately energy efficient nor stable. In this investigation, we perform electrochemical testing and ozone quantification on a new material combination: Gd, Ni, and Sb doped SnO2 films. SnO2-Sb-Ni-Gd films exhibit substantially higher electrochemical activity and selectivity for electrolytic ozone generation than films doped with just Sb and Ni or just Sb and Gd. Faradaic efficiencies exceeding 60% were exhibited by this catalyst, giving an optimistic nod towards the viability of this material and meriting further testing into its stability.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Characterization of Carbon Based Catalyst Supports Using Cyclic Voltammetry and Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy for Carbon Dioxide Reduction Applications
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Catalysts are instrumental in making otherwise expensive chemical processes time and cost efficient, and their effectiveness can be maximized by increasing their active surface area. By depositing catalytic material onto a support with maximized surface area, catalyst activity can be increased without a substantial volume of catalytic material. For electrochemical processes, certain carbon materials are ideal for this purpose because they exhibit high surface areas, electrical conductivity, and resistance to thermal and chemical degradation. The determination of the electrochemically active surface area within any given carbon support is therefore of great interest for material selection and as a baseline for performance characterization. The electroactive surface area can be determined on a conductive material by exploiting the effect of the electrochemical double layer, which can be modeled as a capacitor. A capacitance from this double layer can be calculated by measuring the charge transferred when a given potential is applied. This capacitance is proportional to, and therefore can be used to calculate, the electrochemically active surface area of a conductive material. By using cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and specific capacitance values for carbon from literature, specific electrochemically active surface areas and resistances of various carbon based supports were calculated. From these, candidates were chosen for catalyst deposition for the reduction of supercritical carbon dioxide into chemical fuels.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: High Temperature Alkene Oligomerization on Single Site Cobalt Catalyst
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Nonrenewable resources make up 80% of worldwide energy consumption and are being depleted faster than they can regenerate themselves. It is vital that new energy resources are discovered to provide for society’s current and future needs. Shale gas, which contains short-length alkanes (methane, ethane, propane), has steadily become a more prominent resource over the past decade because of advancements in drilling technology. Ethane and propane can be catalytically converted into longer chains through a two-step process of dehydrogenation, to convert alkanes to olefins, followed by oligomerization, to convert olefins to higher molecular weight hydrocarbons that can be used in fuels and petrochemicals. While these processes are traditionally performed under different conditions, they share common intermediates. A stable single-site cobalt catalyst (Co 2+ /SiO 2 ) was synthesized to perform high-temperature ethylene oligomerization. The Co 2+ single site structure was confirmed using X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) at the Advanced Photon Source (APS), Argonne National Laboratory. The C-H bond activation capability of Co 2+ /SiO 2 was benchmarked against literature using propane dehydrogenation at 550°C and propylene hydrogenation at 200°C with conversions up to 25% and selectivities up to 99%. Ethylene oligomerization performed at atmospheric pressure and temperatures greater than 350°C resulted in a large selectivity (>50%) towards butenes as well as the formation of hexenes (>30% selectivity) and trace amounts of other higher molecular weight hydrocarbons. At higher pressures, these reactions are predicted to condense to liquid fuel products that are more compatible with the United States transportation methods.

Oxidative damage by ROS numerous diseases and conditions such as diabetes and aging. On the other hand, ROS are essential for metabolic processes such as homeostasis, and selectiv e and site-specific ROS generation can be used in chemotherapeutics . Thus, understanding ROS production and monitoring the amount of ROS in the human body is of great importance, which makes understanding the interaction between iron ions and GSSG beneficial. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Selective Cleavage of Lignin β-O-4 Ether Linkage By Pd/CeO 2 Catalyst with Unique Metal-Support Interaction
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The catalytic activity of heterogeneous catalysts based on noble metals is investigated for the conversion of lignin to precursors of various commodity chemicals. Here we use a model compound containing a β-O-4 ether linkage to understand its cleavage mechanism and kinetics as analogous to that in lignin. Various parameters including temperature, pressure, solvent, and choice of metals and supports have been optimized to obtain the most practical and efficient conditions for industrial applications. It has been found that Pd is the most capable noble metal catalyst tested for β-O-4 cleavage compared to Pt and Ru. The support CeO 2 gives the highest selectivity towards acetophenone (rather than hydrogenated products) when compared to other supports including both ‘‘reducible’’ (TiO 2 ) and ‘‘irreducible’’ (Al 2 O 3 and SiO 2 ) metal oxides. The unique support effects of CeO 2 when paired with Pd make it the most effective support. To optimize process temperatures, conversion of the model compound, 2-phenoxy-1-phenylethan-1-ol (PPE) was investigated at 50, 70, 90, and 110 °C under 5 bar H 2 . While the conversion of PPE was found to increase with temperature, we have found that increasing the pressure does not follow the same trend. When varying the hydrogen pressure between 5 and 50 bar at a constant 80 °C, the highest conversion (59%) after 4 hours is achieved at only 10 bar. Here, we propose a pressure (H 2 ) dependent mechanism that involves balancing hydride and PPE on the catalyst surface to cleave the β-O-4 linkage in PPE to selectively form acetophenone, phenol, cyclohexanol, and cyclohexanone. Our results show interesting insights into the various interactions hydrogen has with aromatic substrates on the surface of metal nanoparticles and lead to the design and optimization of a catalytic reaction that can selectively produce commodity chemical precursors from renewable feedstock, such as polystyrene and Nylon-6.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Mesoporous Silica Supported Perovskite Oxide for Low Temperature Thermochemical CO 2 Conversion
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Today, carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emission levels are higher than at any other point in human history, and chemical reactions can be used to establish a synthetic carbon cycle, which would reduce emissions and produce liquid fuel. The reverse water-gas shift chemical looping process (RWGS-CL) is a reaction of interest because it is effective for converting large amounts of CO 2 and the resulting carbon monoxide (CO) can be used to produce hydrocarbons that are liquid fuel or chemical intermediates. Perovskite oxides are an effective catalyst for the RWGS-CL based on converting CO 2 to CO at efficient conversion temperatures, ability to form oxygen vacancies, and structural stability. The perovskite oxide used is La 0.75 Sr 0.25 FeO 3 (LSF). Recent studies have shown silica (SiO 2 ) as the most efficient support material for the perovskite oxide catalyst used in RWGS-CL. The form of SiO 2 that has been experimented with to provide support for LSF is SBA-15, because of its large pore volume and surface area, coupled with potential to support smaller particles of the perovskite increasing the number of active sites available, which would enhance conversion. Here we have analyzed adaptations to the synthesis procedure of perovskite oxides and SBA-15 to develop a single synthesis procedure for a composite material. These materials are characterized by X-ray Diffraction, N 2 -physisorption, CO 2 -Chemisoprtion, and temperature-programmed reduction, oxidation, and RWGS-CL experiments.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Understanding Cation Effects in the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction on Cu(100) Surfaces
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a half-cell electrochemical process in which H 2 evolves from water electrolysis. This reaction competes with the electroreduction of CO 2 into hydrocarbon fuels, decreasing electrocatalyst selectivity towards desirable hydrocarbon products. In the present theoretical work, we studied cation effects in the HER on Cu (100) surfaces. Copper is the only metal electrocatalyst that can convert CO 2 through electroreduction into hydrocarbon fuels. Being able to prevent the competing HER reaction could help make CO 2 electroreduction into a practical process. We seek to elucidate the mechanism through which alkali metal cations hinder the HER from a fundamental-molecular perspective. Although several researchers have reported that the HER is not significantly affected by the presence of alkali cations relative to other products, preliminary experimental results from collaborators suggested that there is a cation-size dependence effect on the HER. Our hypothesis is that an electric field results from cation presence near the electrode surface, affecting energy barriers for the H* adsorption Volmer step by interacting with the partially charged transition state. To test our hypothesis, computational techniques based on the Density Functional Theory (DFT) were used to model the Volmer step reaction mechanism. The cation effects were implicitly taken into account by applying electric fields to our model. Our results are in qualitative agreement with experiments that show that increasing the cation size increases the HER rate for same charge cations. The cation effect mechanism still to be elucidated from further calculations and experimentation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Molybdenum Disulfide Thin Films As a Catalyst for Hydrogen Evolution
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In the search for alternative energy sources, hydrogen fuel cells have appeared as a promising clean source of energy, particularly in automobiles. The fuel cell requires hydrogen gas, which is produced through the hydrogen evolution reaction. Researchers have searched for a cheap, efficient catalyst for this reduction reaction, which may make implementation of this technology on an industrial scale more realistic. Molybdenum disulfide thin films are relatively inexpensive and easy to make through electrodeposition, so they make promising candidates for catalysts. Doping the films with nickel has been shown to change the properties of the film, so may improve its catalytic activity. Catalysis testing for the hydrogen evolution reaction demonstrates that while hydrogen begins to reduce on a non-catalytic indium tin oxide (ITO) film at -0.6V, the reduction will occur at around -0.4 and -0.3V for MoS 2 and Ni-doped MoS 2 , respectively. This indicates that less power will be required to start the hydrogen evolution reaction when Ni-doped MoS 2 is used as a catalyst. Cyclic voltammetry of a ferrocyanide/ferricyanide redox reaction using Ni-doped MoS 2 demonstrates that the shifted hydrogen reduction peak is not due to an increase in surface area or an increase in electrical conductivity. Thus, doping the MoS 2 thin films with Ni significantly increases their efficiency in this critical reaction.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Electrochemical Synthesis of Urea Derivatives Via Ionic Liquid Electrolytes, Primary Amines, and Carbon Dioxide.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Urea is the most synthesized organic compound by mass in the world and 80% of urea available is used to make fertilizer. Since the need for fertilizer is growing every year, the need for urea is increasing as a consequence. Current industry methods for synthesizing urea are expensive, not energy efficient, and have low yields. We are developing an electrochemical reaction which can be performed assisted with ionic liquid as a catalyst to synthesize urea in higher efficiency and at a lower cost. The reaction was delivered successfully in various primary amines in an attempt to synthesize the ureal derivatives. Different potentials and reaction times were tested on all of the amines used in the reaction but had no effect. The reaction was then improved by purging CO2 into the ionic liquid before addition of the primary amine. This gave significantly higher yields with all amines and a 50% reduction in reaction time. Reactions were then performed with ionic liquid and without ionic liquid and the reactions containing ionic liquid were formed product while the reactions without ionic liquid formed only salt. As a result of future findings, the use of Urea in current industries and laboratories could be significantly enhanced in regard to the amount of time, cost, and resources needed.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Mixed Metal Oxides for Thermochemical Energy Storage
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: As more non-dispatchable renewable generation resources are integrated to the power grid, pressure is exerted on the existing fossil fleet to provide flexible power output to accommodate their intermittent nature. This will lead to fossil plants operating at lower efficiencies and capacity factors due to rapid cycling. Bulk energy storage has the potential to relieve the strain on these plants by allowing fossil plants to fire during periods of low power prices or demand. Although electricity storage technologies can be used to collect the electric power generated by a fossil plant, alternatively, thermal energy can potentially be captured from ultra-supercritical steam (580-620°C) via thermochemical energy storage. This study sought to evaluate different mixed-metal oxide (MMO) compounds with a pyrochlore crystal structure (A 2 B 2 O 7 ) to be used as thermochemical energy storage media. Specifically, both Fe-based lanthanum zirconate pyrochlores (La 2 Fe x Zr 2-x O 7-δ ) and manganese oxides (Mn 1-x Fe x O 3-δ ) were synthesized and characterized at various temperatures and red-ox cycling experiments. The impact of transition metal substitution (3, 6, and 9 wt.% Fe) into the B-site of the pyrochlore on the heats of reduction and oxidation was measured using microreactors. Fundamental material characterization such as BET surface area and XRD powder diffraction was conducted to supplement the reaction experiments. Temperature programmed reduction (TPR) experiments revealed that the pyrochlore reduction temperature was lowered with an increase in Fe weight loading. The lanthanum zirconate pyrochlore with 6 wt.% Fe loading displayed more consistent stability over 10 red-ox cycles as compared to the manganese oxide with 12 wt.% Fe loading. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) showed that the energy storage capacity of manganese oxide was found to be significantly more than lanthanum zirconate. Future work involves additional red-ox cycling experiments (e.g. 100+ cycles, varying temperatures, and cycle times) to discern the long-term stability of future TCES materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Oxygen Reduction Reaction on Gold Electrode Surfaces in Acidic Medium
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) attains a major role in energy conversion complexes given it is catalyzed by fuel cells for the efficient and sustainable production of electricity. In acidic medium, the reduction of oxygen is favored in a two-electron transfer pathway which involves two reduction products: hydrogen peroxide and water. The reduction performance of three different gold electrodes with varying surface areas was tested as a sustainable and more earth-abundant alternative to the reduction of molecular oxygen on platinum polycrystalline electrodes. Such comparison would lead to the maximization of hydrogen peroxide production in acidic medium. For this study, the electrochemical reduction of oxygen was examined in a 0.1M HClO 4 solution by identifying the reduction potentials of oxygen in the distinct gold electrodes utilized as electrocatalysts. With each individual potential, electric current present in solution was measured as a function of time via amperometry. 1 H NMR spectroscopy was performed in order to characterize the product and determine the efficiency of the production of hydrogen peroxide in each gold electrode. The theoretical yield of hydrogen peroxide when compared within the three gold electrodes presented no direct proportion to surface area as expected. Such incongruence could be due to difference in crystalline structure within the electrodes. The sufficient production of hydrogen peroxide would give way to oxidation of compounds of interest such as ethylene glycol in order to further explore their performance as fuel alternatives.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Towards Efficient and Stable Nifeox Alkaline Oxygen Evolution Electrocatalysts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Alkaline anion exchange membrane electrolyzers have high potential to support renewable energy systems through energy storage in the form of hydrogen. However, the efficiency of these electrolyzers is significantly hindered by the sluggish kinetics of the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). High overpotentials are needed to overcome this kinetic hinderance, which translates to higher energy requirements for water electrolysis. Effective electrocatalysts can lower the overpotential for OER and water electrolysis, but these catalysts need to be highly active, stable, and inexpensive. The most active catalysts for OER are IrO x and RuO x ; however, these catalysts contain precious transition metals that are prohibitively costly to deploy on a large scale. Nickel-Iron oxide catalysts (NiFeO x ) are non-precious alternatives for OER catalysis, which have shown higher activity than IrO x in alkaline conditions. However, the long-term stability of these NiFeO x has not been adequately demonstrated to date. We have synthesized carbon-supported NiFeO x nanoparticles using a straightforward wet impregnation method. This catalyst can achieve 10 mA/cm 2 at 300 mV overpotential at room temperature and at 240 mV at 70°C in alkaline aqueous solution. The stability of this catalyst, however, is poor in concentrated alkaline electrolytes. Thus, we are working to determine the cause of instability in this catalyst. Our working hypothesis is that the poor stability results primarily from oxidative degradation of the carbon support. We have evaluated this hypothesis by integrating accelerated degradation electrochemistry experiments with detailed materials analysis techniques, including SEM, XRD, and Raman Microscopy.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Advanced Reactor Design for Carbon-Free Ammonia SOFCs: An Automated Profiling Approach
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: There is a growing need for alternative low emission energy sources. Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFCs) are a high efficiency, relatively durable, fuel flexible and low emission alternative to common energy sources. Ammonia is an attractive fuel for SOFCs because it contains no carbon, is easy to store, and is highly efficient due to endothermic cracking. This coupled with the hydrogen oxidation reaction allows for efficient heat utilization. In this study, a method for automated temperature control of the SOFC is developed in conjunction with axial temperature and concentration profiles of tubular SOFCs ( t -SOFCs) in order to investigate the coupled ammonia decomposition and hydrogen oxidation reactions. Automated control of the t -SOFC provides for easy mass data recording allowing for hours of temperature and current data to be stored. Fast ammonia decomposition over the Ni catalyst is evident at the inlet of t -SOFC and complete ammonia conversion is confirmed above 600ºC. It is found that direct ammonia-fueled t -SOFC and an equivalent hydrogen-nitrogen fueled t -SOFC provide identical performances. The temperature and concentration profiles validate that the efficient heat integration inside ammonia-fueled t -SOFC is feasible if operated at 700ºC and below. The results confirm that the overall reactions proceed in a two-step process: the endothermic decomposition of ammonia followed by the exothermic oxidation of hydrogen. These results support foundational background for the development of autothermal ammonia SOFCs.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Sustainable Plastic Precursors from Hydrothermal Catalytic Cracking of Palmitic Acid: A Reaction Pathway Study
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Petroleum-derived naphtha cracking is currently used to produce important plastics precursors such as xylene and toluene. Due to growing concerns of climate change and efforts to produce clean energy, a sustainable, petroleum-free method of producing these important chemical process precursors is necessary. Research has found promise in the hydrothermal catalytic cracking of naturally occurring fatty acids, specifically palmitic acid found in palm oil, to form aromatics. A variety of catalysts have been used for this process, the most notable being HZSM-5 which has been proven to be effective at selectively producing aromatics and converting biomass [1]. While prior work shows promise, more work is necessary to investigate palmitic acid cracking due to the lack of focus on reaction pathway and less-than-desirable aromatic yields. We hypothesized that decreasing water and catalyst loading as well as using nano-HZSM-5 could increase the yield of aromatics, specifically xylene and toluene, compared to prior work. Batch reactions of palmitic acid catalytic cracking were conducted in supercritical conditions (400⁰C and 3200 psi) with water and nano-HZSM-5 catalyst, and products were characterized using gas chromatography with mass spectrometry (GC/MS), with flame ionization detection (GC/FID), and with thermal conductivity detection (GC/TCD). It was found that water loading of 15 weight percent produced higher yields of xylene and toluene than reported literature values. We also set out to understand the reaction pathway by varying the length of the reaction time (0 to 45 minutes) and the temperature (350, 400) as well as running hydrothermal cracking of the fatty acid without catalyst. From our results, we speculate that the reaction occurs through intermediates at the catalyst surface and is preceded primarily by non-limiting decarboxylation and chain-cracking of the palmitic acid. It has been found that palmitic acid catalytic cracking can produce promising yields of aromatics, and our investigation of the reaction pathway can aid in potential scale-up design decisions for the process. Work on this project is being continued to thoroughly investigate the reaction pathway of intermediates and the stability of products during the reaction. References: [1] Na Mo and Phillip E. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Industrial wastewater containing phenolic compounds represents a serious discharge problem due to its low biodegradability, high toxicity and ecological aspects, as well as causing considerable damage to ecosystems and human health. Advanced oxidation processes have proven highly effective and the coupling of these systems as a pretreatment to conventional biological processes is positioned as an economically viable alternative for the elimination of toxic and persistent pollutants, such as petroleum derivatives. One of the advanced oxidation processes under study is the Fenton process with ultraviolet light, this allows mineralization and not only the removal of contaminants. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Metal Mixing of Copper Oxide Sorbents for Sulfur Contaminant Removal from Hydrocarbon Streams
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Sulfur contaminants in natural gas and hydrocarbons at even trace amounts (1-1000 ppm-mol) poison catalysts, corrode pipelines and are hazardous to the environment due their conversion to sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) during combustion, which contributes to acid rain. In industry, sulfur contaminants, such as hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S), are commonly removed through metal-oxide based chemisorption, where H 2 S reacts over a metal oxide solid surface at elevated process temperatures (473-1073K). These processes are attractive because of their high removal capacity and highly pure effluent streams. Recently, there has been an interest in low-temperature H 2 S metal-oxide based chemisorption due to safety and economic reasons. Thus, copper oxide (CuO) is an attractive sorbent because of the highly favorable thermodynamics of the reaction that not only allow for low-temperature removal, but also allow for the decrease of H 2 S concentrations from several thousand ppm to sub-ppm levels. The mixing and doping of oxides have been shown to increase the reactivity of sorbents with contaminants. Little work however has been conducted to understand the effects of the structural and chemical changes resulting from the introduction metals to CuO sorbents on the sorption capacity. In this work, CuO sorbents were mixed with various metals (Ba, Mn, Bi, Mg, Al, Zn, Ni, Co and La) to investigate the effect of introducing these metals on the sorbent removal capacity. The doped CuO spherical nanoparticles were synthesized via co-precipitation. The synthesized nanomaterials were then characterized using a variety of techniques and tested for low-temperature H 2 S removal by running packed bed sulfidation experiments at 1000 ppm-vol inlet H 2 S concentration, temperature of 323K and pressure of 1 atm. The experiments showed that doped CuO-sorbents with crystallite sizes larger than 12 nm perform poorly. It was found that all metal dopants with the exception of La and Zn resulted in decreased capacities compared to those expected from pure CuO samples with similar crystallite sizes. La doped CuO sorbents resulted in about a 75% increase in sorption capacity compared to pure CuO samples with similar crystallite sizes.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: A Flow Cell-Based Approach to Characterizing the Kinetics of Redox Flow Battery Electrolytes
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Wind and solar energy installations will be deployed at an increasing rate in the coming decades due to increasing demand for carbon-free electricity. However, energy from these sources is intermittent and peak production fails to coincide with peak demand. In order for the grid to become completely reliant on renewable energy, energy storage systems must be adjacently deployed to support the grid during low production periods. The redox flow battery (RFB) is one of the most promising new technologies to store and use very large quantities of renewable energy on a continuous basis. The energy efficiencies of flow batteries are often limited in part by slow electron-transfer reactions, and this challenge is driving new research to develop electrodes and redox couples that exhibit fast electron transfer kinetics. In this context, we are working to understand the influence of electrocatalysis on the practical performance of established and emerging flow battery chemistries. Our prior work focused on critically assessing rotating disk electrode (RDE) voltammetry techniques—which are widely used for kinetics studies in fuel cell research—for measuring electron transfer rates in RFBs. Based on the results, we concluded that the unique characteristics of flow batteries necessitate the development of new experimental techniques that better approximate their operating conditions. Our current approach employs microelectrodes in a flow cell to eliminate the confounding effects of mass transport and electrical resistance in RFB electrokinetics experiments. Results to date show that microelectrode methods can resolve electron-transfer kinetics at least an order of magnitude faster than conventional RDE experiments. We also found that flowing the electrolyte can mitigate electrode fouling effects in the Pt|FeCl 2 ||FeCl 3 |Pt material system, which yields better estimates of the true electron-transfer kinetics. Ongoing work in our lab is now focused on characterizing the kinetics of several RFB couples at carbon fiber microelectrodes in a channel-flow configuration, since carbon is desirable for use in RFBs due to its low cost.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Micro Heat Exchanger for Direct Methane to Methanol Oxidation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: This project aims to develop an integrated mixer-reactor-heat exchanger micro tube scalable module for the non-catalytic direct partial oxidation of methane in natural gas (NG) to methanol – what we will call “direct methane to methanol” (DMTM). We hypothesize that the required residence times can be reduced to <20 s by increasing reactor zone temperature to near 450°C. This is possible using an integrated micro tube-based mixer and preheater, a short, sharp reaction zone and a rapid quench. Advances in micro tube fabrication for high pressure (laser welding allows pressures >1500 psi or 100 bar) and temperature control (quench zones <1 cm length), combined with passivation of reactor surfaces, will make possible economical DMTM with air and without added radical initiators. This project’s experimentation to date consists of studying the passivation. We sulfided metal coupons using either elemental sulfur or liquid sulfiding agents such as dimethyl disulfide and dimethyl sulfoxide. The liquid agents are broken down into a mixture of elemental sulfur, hydrogen sulfide and light hydrocarbons (mostly methane) at 350-500°C, with N 2 or N 2 /H 2 at ~130 kPa, reacting with the coupons. Coupons tested included the steels I625, 904L, 304L and C1010, and Ni foil. These experiments were done over 3-20 day periods. The liquid agents proved better in forming coherent films on the coupons and the added H 2 was useful in breaking down the liquid agents. The sulfilded coupons were weighed and the films analyzed by X-ray fluorescence (XRF), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), atomic emission spectroscopy (AES), FTIR, and thermogravimetric analysis-differential scanning calorimetry (TGA-DSC). Once all data were analyzed, it was decided to use I625 for future work. Alloy I625 is a high Ni-Cr steel (58 wt% Ni min., 20-23% Cr); the Ni and Cr form surface sulfides, which from past work can be inert to oxidizing conditions. Suflided coupons are being tested under high-pressure air. The microreactor system, made entirely of I625 alloy, is being fabricated by Mezzo Technologies. Mezzo used its proprietary software to design the shell and tube sections. In the meantime, oxidation stability tests on previously coated coupons are taking place in the reactor system that was previously used in the sublimed sulfur agent reactions. These tests are also looking at the chemical inertness of the coupons.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Homogeneous Zirconocene Catalyzed α-Olefin Polymerization in a Microreactor with in-Situ IR Thermography
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: A 3D printed microreactor and IR camera are used to study a series of homogeneous zirconocene catalyzed α-olefin polymerization reactions. Microreactors have some advantages over batch reactors used in the study of chemical reactions. They use smaller volumes reactants and help save costs and minimize waste. The concentrations of the reactants and the temperature vary in the axial direction of the micro-channel. This allows the study of the full extent of a reaction by taking a snapshot of the reaction channel. Experiments are performed which demonstrate the practicality of studying exothermic reactions using IR thermography. An IR camera is placed facing the IR transparent top face of the microreactor. The reactor maintained a uniform temperature using a Peltier heating element. The setup is isolated inside of a vacuum chamber to minimize convection and thermal ‘noise’ recorded by the IR camera. Simulating hot fluid flow highlighted the channels in the thermal image and showed negligible heat conduction by the channel walls. The α-olefin, 1-Hexene and activator (B(C6F5)3) solution is reacted with a homogeneous zirconocene catalyst (SBI-Zr-Me2) solution by feeding the two streams into the microreactor. A thermal signature produced by the reaction was observed down the length the mixing region. Using an energy balance the total conversion can be determined at each point down the length of the channel. This ability to study the reaction with in-situ IR thermography opens the door to automated research of reaction chemistry and kinetics.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Hydrodeoxygenation of Guaiacol with Ru Catalysts on Various Activated Carbon Supports
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Bio-oil is a promising sustainable fuel alternative to traditional sources such as crude oil and natural gas. However, due to its high oxygen content, low heating value, and high viscosity, bio-oil cannot be used directly as a transportation fuel. Therefore, bio-oil requires additional upgrading to turn it into more valuable fuels. The hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) of bio-oil removes the oxygen groups in the bio-oil, turning it into lighter products. Activated carbon is known as a typical catalyst support for HDO reactions. In this study, various activated carbons were used as catalyst supports to load Ru. Commercial activated carbon (derived from fossil fuels) was first investigated for the HDO reaction. For comparison, activated carbon derived from food waste (FWAC) and miscanthus (MISAC) were also examined. Food waste was collected from UConn dining services, and then pyrolyzed into bio-char and physically activated by steam. MISAC was also prepared by pyrolysis and steam activation. All the supports were impregnated with 5% of Ru. The carbon supports were characterized by elemental analysis, N2 sorption-desorption, scanning electron microscope (SEM) and X-ray powder diffraction (XRD). In this study, guaiacol was used as a model compound in the HDO reaction. Decane was used as a solvent to dilute the reactant and octane was used as an internal standard. The reaction pathway was derived from the experimental data and kinetic parameters were calculated. 5% Ru-FWAC showed the highest reaction rate, probably due to its increased hydrophilicity. These results suggest that Ru metal on an activated carbon support is a highly active catalyst in the organic phase for HDO. There is also a great potential for using carbon supports derived from sustainable biomass sources like food waste.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Visible Light Induced Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution Using a CdS-Ni2P Hybrid Aerogel System
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Due to the increasing global energy demand and the climate change impact of CO 2 from energy production, it is essential to construct clean energy production and storage systems. Photocatalytic evolution of hydrogen from water by visible light serves as a promising and appealing pathway. CdS nanoparticles are good visible light absorbers but not efficient hydrogen evolution catalysts, while Ni 2 P is shown to be an exceptional electrocatalyst for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Integration of Ni 2 P nanoparticles with CdS nanoparticles using a sol-gel approach is expected to yield a hybrid system that will enable the efficient transfer of photo-generated carriers on CdS to catalytically active Ni 2 P sites. In this work, the assembly of pre-formed nanoparticles to make CdS-Ni 2 P hybrid aerogels will be described and photocatalytic HER data will be presented. The performance of these novel architectures will be compared to CdS nanoparticles and CdS aerogels. The role of interparticle coupling, porosity and surface passivation on catalytic efficiency will also be discussed. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Insights on the Synthesis of Nanostructured Non-Stoichiometric Mixed Metal Oxide Electrocatalysts Via Reverse Microemulsion Method
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Nonstoichiometric mixed metal oxides, such as perovskites (ABO 3-δ ), double perovskites (AA’B2O5+δ), and Ruddelsden Popper oxides (An+1BnO(3n+1)+δ) (where A is a lanthanide and/or an alkali earth metal and B is a transition metal cation), are recognized as promising electrocatalysts for oxygen reduction/evolution reactions - key reactions for a number of energy conversion and storage technologies. These materials are characterized by their excellent ionic-electronic conductivities, as well as thermal and redox stabilities. Recent findings have demonstrated a strong relationship between mixed metal oxide surface properties (i.e., structure and composition) and their electro/catalytic activity. However, the traditional synthetic methods employed for synthesizing these oxides offer little to no control over the surface structure or composition of these materials. Moreover, high calcination temperatures are traditionally needed to obtain pure oxide phases, which lead to agglomeration of the oxide nanoparticles, decreasing their final surface areas. In this direction, the reverse microemulsion approach has emerged as synthetic method for successfully producing complex oxides with controlled surface properties along with high surface areas. However, limited understanding of the synthesis parameters that govern the final particle properties and the universality of applying this synthesis method to a wide range of mixed metal oxides of different compositions/structures exists. In this contribution, we investigated the effect of key synthesis parameters of the reverse microemulsion method on the properties of the resulting oxide nanoparticles. We found that the condensation reaction rate within the reverse micelle (intramicellar exchange) is an important parameter controlling the final particle morphology. Overall, higher concentrations of the precipitating agent resulted in fast reaction rates, leading to formation of short nanorods, while lower concentrations led to slower reaction rates with longer nanorods being produced. This is owed to the compromise between intramicellar and intermicellar exchanges, where the growth of rods is sustained by slowing the intramicellar condensation rate (precipitation of metal hydroxides within the reverse micelle), which allows for intermicellar exchange (fusion of metal containing reverse micelles) to take place. Furthermore, we provide insights on the universality of this synthetic approach to a wide range of mixed metal oxides with varying crystal structures and compositions.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Design Strategies for Efficient Non-Stoichiometric Mixed Metal Oxide Electrocatalysts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Design Strategies for Efficient Non-Stoichiometric Mixed Metal Oxide Electrocatalysts Krishna Patel, Samji Samira, Xiang-Kui Gu and Eranda Nikolla Department of Chemical Engineering and Materials Science, Wayne State University, Detroit Non-precious mixed metal oxides belonging to the pervosite family with a general composition of A n +1 B n O 3 n +1 ( n = 1, 2, 3 ... ; A = alkaline earth (or) rare metal; B = transition metal) are ideal candidates for cost-effective catalysts for oxygen electrocatalysis [1]. When n = 1, oxides belong to the first-series Ruddlesden-Popper (R-P) phase, while as n→∞ , they exhibit a perovskite structure. These non-stoichiometric oxides exhibit mixed ionic and electronic conductivities as well as high surface oxygen exchange rates which are crucial properties for electrocatalysts [2]. Further, these oxides can also accommodate >90% of the metals in the periodic table giving rise to a vast phase space of material compositions [2]. However, a wide range of phase space makes it difficult to identify optimal oxides for targeted chemical reactions. Also, the complexity of these oxides has resulted in using bulk descriptors as there is no surface related experimentally measurable descriptors [2]. Therefore, it is imperative to develop structure-performance relationships that can guide the identification of active oxide electrocatalysts. In this presentation, a combinatorial approach involving theoretical studies and precisely-controlled electrochemical measurements is used to identify measurable activity descriptors that can guide the identification of active nonstoichiometric oxides. Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) plays a major role in efficient and sustainable electrochemical energy storage and conversion technologies [1, 2]. ORR was used as a probe reaction to describe the activity and stability of these oxides. The effect of composition and crystal structure for a vast phase space was studied. A variety of oxides were synthesized using a citric acid based sol-gel method followed by surface characterization using TEM imaging. We show that the experimentally measurable parameter, surface reducibility, can be used as a descriptor to predict the electrochemical activity and stability of oxides, thus leading to the identification of highly active and stable catalysts for oxygen electrocatalysis. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Carbon dioxide upgrading is motivated by the issues humanity is facing because of global warming. This is due to the anthropogenic CO 2 emissions such as the burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, and fertilization etc. Numerous methods such as reusing, recycling, use of alternative transportation methods, reducing meat intake, and planting more trees are suggested in order to reduce the global carbon footprint. A possible remedy would be to use the emitted CO 2 in order to produce value-added products, such as liquid fuels, to meet the world’s ever-increasing energy demand. Carbon dioxide is an extremely stable molecule; thus, its reduction is an energy-intensive process. Efficient and robust catalysts are needed in order to lower the high activation energy barrier of CO 2 conversion. For this project, monometallic and bimetallic basic copper chloride nanomaterials were prepared by pulsed laser in liquids synthesis by my faculty advisor Astrid M. Müller as electrocatalyst precursors; ad-metals were Sn, Bi, or In. Pulsed laser in liquid synthesis was used for its ability to control the size and composition of the catalyst and for faster synthesis. We employed scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with elemental mapping by energy-dispersive X-ray analysis to image these catalysts and determine the metal ratios.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Ab Initio Study into the Thermodynamic Stability and Intrinsic Activity of La 0.75 Sr 0.25 MnO 3 Vacancies As Bifunctional Oer/ORR Catalyst in Alkaline Media
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Density Functional Theory (DFT + U) study of stability and electrochemical activity for (La 0.75 Sr 0.25 ) 1+x MnO 3-δ perovskite oxides was conducted. For investigation of thermodynamic stability, phase diagrams were constructed using total energy values calculated from DFT + U. Additionally, vacancy formation energies were determined by means of chemical potential for both oxygen rich and poor conditions. As a measure of activity in the Oxygen Evolution Reaction (OER) and Oxygen Reduction Reaction (ORR), the overpotential of various perovskite oxides were calculated. The free energies of the intermediates in the OER/ORR mechanisms were required to determine the overpotentials; as a result, free energies were determined by combining the total energies of the intermediates with zero-point energies (within the harmonic approximation) and finite temperature terms. Through comparison of the overpotentials, DFT + U predicts that some of the vacancies have higher intrinsic activity than pristine La 0.75 Sr 0.25 MnO 3 . Furthermore, the enhanced reactivity of (La 0.75 Sr 0.25 ) 1+x MnO 3-δ oxides is correlated with the oxygen p-band center distance from the Fermi level. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Electrocatalytic Hydrogenation of 4-Propylguaiacol, a Bio-Oil Model Compound
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Conversion of lignocellulosic biomass to renewable hydrocarbon fuels involves biomass deconstruction, which follows either a biochemical or thermochemical pathway. Fast pyrolysis is a thermochemical process that involves high temperature heating of lignocellulosic biomass for short times in the absence of oxygen, yielding approximately 70% bio-oil by weight. The physical and chemical properties of bio-oil hinder its use as a drop-in replacement for fossil fuels. Bio-oil contains reactive oxygenates and it is corrosive, which impede long-term storage and transportation. Processing it in refineries to make transportation fuels using classical petroleum-style hydro-treatment is possible provided it is first upgraded. E lectro c atalytic H ydrogenation, ECH is proposed as an upgrading technology that operates under mild conditions (temperatures less than 80°C and atmospheric pressure). It involves in-situ hydrogen production by water electrolysis, which is reacted at the cathode to hydrogenate bio-oil and increase its stability and energy density. In this process, intermittent renewable electricity from solar and wind energy is stored in chemical bonds formed with hydrogen atoms. In this study, the ECH of 4-propylguaiacol (2-methoxy-4-propylphenol), a lignin derived bio-oil model compound, was performed using a ruthenium-based electrocatalyst. The effects of temperature and cell voltage were investigated to observe differences in product speciation and yields. Products were analyzed using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC/MS ). Using relatively high temperatures of 80°C and cell voltages of ~50 volts resulted in increased conversion of 4-propylguaiacol to propylcyclohexane.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Role of Proton Source in Lithium-Mediated Ammonia Synthesis
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Electrochemical ammonia synthesis has attracted a lot of attention as a possible alternative to the Haber-Bosch process, as it allows for supplanting high reaction pressures and temperatures with electric potential. This may allow for a more modular and lower capital cost method of ammonia fertilizer production. Many chemistries have been reported to produce ammonia at ambient conditions in aqueous solutions. However, many of them suffer from low rates and low selectivities for ammonia due to competition from the hydrogen evolution reaction. Nonaqueous methods hold promise due to the higher nitrogen solubility in nonaqueous solvents, as well as the ability to control proton source activity. One nonaqueous chemistry that has shown promise in the literature is the lithium metal-mediated one. Lithium-mediated ammonia synthesis uses metallic lithium’s reactivity toward nitrogen to fix it, forming lithium nitride. The lithium nitride then reacts in situ with a proton source to produce ammonia and lithium ions. The lithium ions and an electric current are used to regenerate metallic lithium. This work studies the role of proton sources in the process, which are important for protonating the lithium nitride, as well as for activating the lithium for nitrogen fixation. A wide array of proton sources, with different proton acidities and levels of steric hindrance, was examined systematically to determine their performance. Performance at high currents density was correlated to proton donor properties, creating a predictive model of proton source activity. The concentrations at which ammonia Faradaic efficiency is maximized was determined for each proton source at low current density, in order to minimize transport limitations. Faradaic efficiencies well above previously reported values were observed.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: The Impact of Low Molar Doping of Low Valence Metals on Sm 2 O 3 Catalysts for the Oxidative Coupling of Methane
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Approximately 85% of natural gas is composed of methane. Converting methane to higher value molecules has been a major focus in the field of catalysis for decades. Ethylene is of particular interest as a target molecule as it has a variety of applications such as it’s polymerization into polyethylene, the most used plastic in the world. Converting methane to ethylene through the oxidative coupling of methane (OCM) is a catalyzed process. An ideal catalyst requires the presence of basic sites and a high active surface area. While these properties can be quantified and understood easily, the interactions between a catalyst and various dopants are not fully clear. Synthesizing an effective catalyst for OCM requires an understanding of these interactions. Understanding the effects of certain dopants on a catalyst provides valuable information on how that dopant impacts catalyst performance for a variety of catalysts. In this study, the effects of molar doping at 0.1% and 1% of low valence metals onto samarium oxide (Sm 2 O 3 ), were investigated. Sm 2 O 3 was chosen as the base catalyst because it is one of the most active and stable single oxide catalysts for the methane coupling reaction, so understanding the behavior of the metals doped into Sm 2 O 3 can help in the synthesis of more effective catalysts for OCM. It was found that several dopants such as lithium and silver improved the conversion and selectivity of the catalyst. At certain molar doping percentages, both the activity and stability of Sm 2 O 3 was improved. Increasing the amount of dopant did not improve performance variables for all catalysts indicating the uniqueness of each dopant and the balance needed to find an optimal dopant concentration.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Homogeneous Hydrolysis of a Thermally Degrading Tracer
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: A major obstacle in commercializing geothermal resources is predicting the potential for cooling of production wells, particularly in the presence of cold water reinjection. Thermally degrading tracers such as phenyl acetate may enable advanced warning of “premature thermal breakthrough” if compounds with appropriate and known temperature-dependent reaction kinetics can be identified. This work investigates the potential for accelerated reaction rates in the presence of mineral surfaces (i.e., a heterogeneous reaction path). A homogeneous aqueous solution buffered with citric acid and sodium phosphate dibasic was spiked with phenyl acetate and the hydrolysis reaction was measured by spectrophotometry for temperatures ranging from 20 to 50 °C. The activation energy and pre-exponential factor were calculated from the Arrhenius equation and the hydrolysis of phenyl acetate displayed a low activation energy. This means that phenyl acetate could be a suitable chemical tracer for a wider range of temperatures and have useful applications as a well maintenance tool for low-temperature geothermal energy wells.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: TiO 2 Catalysts: Micropowders and Nanofibers in Sustainable Reactions A. Jernigan 1 , S. Nealy 2 , W. Maniukiewicz 3 , M. Modelska 3 , M. Binczarski 3 , T. Maniecki 3 , I. Witonska 3 , and A. Stanishevsky 2 , C. West 1 1 Department of Chemical Engineering, University of South Alabama, USA 2 Department of Physics, University of Alabama at Birmingham, USA 3 Institute of General and Ecological Chemistry, Faculty of Chemistry, Łódź University of Technology, Poland Catalytic technologies are vital in the advancement and development of many industries, including chemical, biological, and environmental. One area of focus in catalysis for several decades has been trying to find an efficient means of generating clean hydrogen, as this remains a barrier to widespread implementation of environmentally friendly hydrogen fuel cell technologies. An abundant source of hydrogen is water but liberating hydrogen from water is limited by both reaction kinetics and thermodynamics. Using photocatalysis with readily available biofuels as sacrificial reagents addresses those issues in part and presents the opportunity to harness solar energy to drive the reaction. The most studied photocatalyst is titania, and this work investigates the potential of titania nanofibers for those applications. Some of the inherent disadvantages are addressed using small amounts of other metals, such as its relative inactivity in the visible light range and rapid reversal of electron excitation. One metal incorporated is platinum, which is known to improve hydrogen generation rates, but other, less expensive metals are to be to reduce the amount of platinum needed and thus reduce the catalyst cost. In catalyst optimization, there is always a focus on finding ways to increase the available surface area and thus the efficiency and rate of reaction. Amid this push for smaller technologies, attention has been recently drawn to the potential of nanomaterials as an alternative to micromaterials in catalysis. Nanofibers are gaining significant interest as an alternative to micropowders with the advantage of greatly increased active surface area without the issue of agglomeration as is seen in nanopowders. In this work, TiO 2 nanofibers synthesized using needleless AC electrospinning were prepared for comparison to TiO 2 micropowders through the screening reaction of photocatalytic reduction of CO 2 to produce methanol. Future plans are to compare the sustainable production of hydrogen by photoreforming of ethanol on TiO2 nanofibers and micropowders doped with CuO and Pt. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: The Synthesis and Reaction Kinetics of Reversible Epoxies in a Diels Alder Reaction
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Epoxies are an important class of thermosetting polymers for many long-term applications such as adhesives, structural materials, paints, and coatings. Due to their thermosetting nature, epoxies are hard and robust, unfortunately they also are hard to remove, recycle and reuse. Epoxies capable of reverse polymerization are being studied in order to address these issues. In this research, reversible epoxies were synthesized by introducing the Diels-Alder reaction groups to epoxy monomers. A Diels-Alder cycloadduct was formed from the reaction of 1,1'-(Methylenedi-4,1-phenylene) bismaleimide and furfuryl glycidyl ether. Formation of the Diels-Alder cycloadduct was confirmed using Fourier Transform-Infrared (FTIR) Spectrometry. Next, the forward and reverse Diels-Alder reaction – corresponding to re-polymerization and depolymerization, respectively – was monitored by FTIR measurements at 90 oC and 110 oC as a function of exposure time. FT-IR measurements were taken for the sample at various temperatures from 90-120°C. FT-IR absorption peaks relevant to the reverse Diels-Alder reaction were gradually stronger as longer exposure time at 90 oC and 110 oC. The equilibrium shift was observed toward the reverse reaction dominant side at higher temperature by comparison of FTIR spectra at 90 oC and 110 oC. The reversible epoxy resins will be cured with various curing agents and their reaction kinetics will be studied.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Metal Screening of Ceria-Zirconia Based Catalyst for Low Temperature Dry Reforming of Methane
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Low temperature reforming catalysts are desirable for intensification of the process for producing renewable liquid fuels from biogas. In this study, Ceria-Zirconia based catalysts with various metal loadings were synthesized and characterized for efficacy in the dry reforming of methane (CH 4 +CO 2 -->2H 2 +2CO). Building upon optimal combinations and suggestions found in literature 1 , various weight percentages of palladium (Pd), iron (Fe), ruthenium (Ru), or cobalt (Co) were loaded onto Ce 0.6 Zr 0.4 O 2 (CZO). Nickel and magnesium were also incorporated in predetermined weight percentages from published research to obtain a balance between catalyst activity and stability 2 . Characterization techniques included X-ray diffraction to identify bulk composition, hydrogen temperature programmed reductions (H­­ 2 -TPR) to determine activation temperatures of catalysts, and nitrogen physisorption to define pore structures. Temperature programmed reactions were executed to verify 10% and 50% conversions of both CH 4 and CO 2 for palladium and ruthenium samples; these were prioritized due to the promising low reduction temperatures found via H 2 -TPR. Ru samples gave the best performance in terms of lower reduction and conversion temperatures compared to the synthesized Pd samples and platinum (Pt) samples found in previous papers. 0.16Ru-1.4Ni-1Mg-CZO outperformed 0.16Pt-1.39Ni-1Mg-CZO and 0.16Pd-1.4Ni-1Mg-CZO by at least 20°C and 30°C, respectively. Considering the price of Ru has been, on average, 13 times cheaper than that of Pt over the past ten years 3 , Ru can serve as a replacement for Pt in terms of cost and performance. Future work related to this project will involve time on stream studies to test the stability of the ruthenium catalysts and post reaction characterizations of tested catalysts. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Phosphorus-Mediated Reductive C--N Bond Coupling: A Path to Functionalized Azaheterocycles
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Nitrogen heterocycles are of significant industrial interest due to their abundance in natural products and other organic molecules with great biological potential. As such, methods which can readily access C – N bonds are of great synthetic interest. Current prevailing strategies, such as the Ullman, Buchwald-Hartwig, and Chan-Lam coupling reactions, are transition-metal dominated, requiring the usage of either copper or noble metals. Researchers in the Radosevich group have previously synthesized a biphilic phosphetane catalyst which catalyzes bond formation between nitroarenes and phenylboronic acids. This new coupling strategy is fundamentally different from previous palladium-based methods in that it operates via a P III /P V =O redox cycle. While this phosphetane catalyst is easily synthesized and can be used at reasonable loadings (15%), its major drawback is that it is not commercially available. Phosphines, as O-atom acceptors, were of special interest as alternative reagents, although their nucleophilic nature ensures that they cannot be regenerated. In my research, we showed that stoichiometric amounts of triethylphosphine, an inexpensive commercial agent, can drive the deoxygenative coupling of nitroarenes and boronic acids to generate di(hetero)arylamine products in a direct synthetic operation without the need for any transition metal additives. A variety of diarylamine products were prepared in good yield using this method, revealing versatility with regards to functional groups on both coupling partners. Additionally, this method offers access to traditionally difficult substrates such as nitroarenes containing electron-withdrawing groups. These C--N coupling techniques can then be used to access difficult azaheterocyclic frameworks with multiple sites for reaction. If one were to add groups to a benzimidazole, the presence of two nitrogen atoms which can tautomerize ensures two possible sites for addition. When the molecule is symmetric—as is the parent nucleus—this is not a problem, but in asymmetric instances, it is nontrivial to ensure functional groups end up on the correct side of the molecule. Here, we use the phosphetane catalyst described earlier, which can also catalyze an intramolecular Cadogan cyclization, to synthesize various azaheterocycles. This method allows us to approach pharmaceutically relevant molecules, and has been successfully applied to the synthesis of oxindoles, indoles, quinoxalines, and benzimidazoles.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Oxidative Coupling of Methane Using Mn-Na 2 WO 4 /TiO 2 Catalysts: effect of the Support on Reaction Performance
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Ethylene is a vital chemical for the synthesis of most petrochemical products, and highly demanded in the industrial field. As the demand increases, various methods of converting abundant methane into useful ethylene are drawing more attention. The current commercial process of producing ethylene from methane is a two-stage process that first converts methane into syngas (steam reforming) and then synthesizes it with ethylene. However, this process suffers from low energy efficiency and high capital and operating costs. The OCM is energetically more efficient than endothermic steam reforming because it is exothermic, and this one-step process can reduce capital and operating costs. However, the OCM can proceed to deep oxidation and homogeneous reaction to form CO or CO 2 . Thus, avoiding formation of CO or CO 2 is critical for improving yield of C 2 products. The Mn- Na 2 WO 4 /SiO 2 catalyst has shown promise for OCM. In this study, the Mn-Na 2 WO 4 was supported with various types of TiO 2 (Mn-Na 2 WO 4 /TiO 2 ) to determine the most promising catalyst to enhance C 2 yield and methane conversion. These catalysts were also further compared to a previously studied Mn- Na 2 WO 4 /SiO 2 catalyst. Each catalyst was prepared using incipient wetness impregnation method followed by a specific calcination procedure. The tests were conducted over a range of temperatures from 725 to 800 o C in a fixed-bed reactor. The gases exiting from the reactor were analyzed using a gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector. The surface area and crystallinity of catalysts were analyzed using BET method and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. In this study, the best catalyst was determined to be 1.9% Mn – 5% Na 2 WO 4 /TiO 2 (A), which has the largest surface area among the examined TiO 2 supports, suggesting that an increased surface area of the supporting metal may result in enhanced C 2 selectivity and methane conversion. In this context, future investigations are necessary to understand relationship or correlation between catalyst performance and surface area of the supporting catalysts.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Role of Pore Structure on the Sintering Effect of Pt Diesel Oxidation Catalysts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The USDRIVE Low Temperature Oxidation Catalyst Test Protocol recommends an accelerated aging test for Pt diesel oxidation catalysts (DOCs) to be performed at 800 °C in flowing air. However, at such high temperatures, Pt sinters readily to form large particles due to significant vapor phase transport of PtO 2 . One approach we used to slow the rate of Pt sintering was by alloying Pt with Pd [1]. A second approach was to trap the mobile Pt species with an oxide such as PdO that reacts to form Pt-Pd bimetallic particles [2], or using CeO 2 , which traps Pt in atomically dispersed form [3]. Recently, we have explored the role of pore confinement to determine if it was possible to slow the vapor phase transport of PtO 2 , and therefore, the rate of Pt sintering. Since PtO 2 vapor has negligible binding to silica [4], it provides the ideal support to study the role of pore structure. We studied MCM-41 and SBA-15 as silica supports and found that, although they slowed the rate of Pt sintering after aging at 800 °C, the resulting Pt DOCs was not very reactive due to blocking of the pores by the Pt particles, which in turn blocked accessibility of the smaller Pt particles retained inside the pores. This inaccessibility is due to high pore diameter to length ratios of MCM-41 and SBA-15. Here we explore other silica with a more open pore structure, such as silica nanospheres with an open pore morphology exhibiting a lower aspect ratio than MCM-41 and SBA-15. We found that we could slow the rate of Pt sintering and improve the reactivity using a model reaction, such as CO oxidation. The results are then compared to Pt on a commercial Davisil silica support, which we use as the control for this study. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Synthesis of an Alloy-Based Ni-Fe/C Catalyst for the Alkaline Oxygen Evolution Reaction
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Hydrogen gas is industrially relevant as a raw material for numerous chemical processes, including high-volume industrial chemicals such as ammonia and methanol. Currently, hydrogen is produced using reforming processes that involve fossil fuels and result in large releases of pollutants like CO 2 . Hydrogen production using electrolysis is a benign alternative. Alkaline anion-exchange membrane electrolyzers are promising for clean hydrogen production because the noncorrosive environment of the alkaline electrolyte enables the use of non-precious metal catalysts. However, practical implementation of these electrolyzers is hindered by high overpotentials for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). The oxidizing conditions of OER also affect the stability and conductivity of catalysts, leading to poor performance. Ni-based catalysts are widely studied for OER in alkaline conditions; furthermore, incorporation of Fe into Ni catalysts has shown promise by decreasing the onset potential compared to pure Ni. We are studying Ni–Fe composites derived from homogeneous metallic alloy precursors with the goal of creating alkaline OER catalysts that exhibit improved electron transport properties than those derived from pure oxides. We synthesized Ni–Fe alloy nanoparticles on an oxidized Vulcan carbon support using a wet-impregnation technique. The as-synthesized catalyst was activated for OER using electrochemical cycling. Systematic variation of carbon and Fe content in the Ni–Fe/C catalysts showed that a catalyst with 70:30 ratio of Ni:Fe and 48 wt% carbon content gave the smallest onset overpotential of ~270 mV. This catalyst attained 10 mA/cm 2 at an overpotential of 300 mV in 0.1 M KOH. It also exhibited enhanced activity at higher electrolyte concentration and at elevated temperature, but its stability was poor in concentrated electrolyte. Work is now focused on understanding the origin of this stability limitation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Catalytic Methane Dehydroaromatization with Microwave Heating
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In industry, methane is converted into aromatics through an indirect route: methane to syn-gas and then syn-gas to aromatics. Methane dehydroaromatization (DHA) is a direct route that would be more economical. The DHA process we use is a catalytic reaction involving a zeolite, a microporous aluminosilicate mineral, for higher selectivity of desired aromatics. Due to the thermodynamic unfavorability of the reaction, high temperature operating conditions are required. At high temperatures, coking (solid carbon depositions) of the catalyst occurs and inhibits the reaction. Microwave (MW) heating of the catalyst is currently under investigation. The main advantage is selective heating which can reduce coking. By incorporating metals such as gallium, into the structure, the hypothesis is that the metals induce dipoles which can increase MW sensitivity. Current work involves synthesis of zeolites with different metal compositions and silicon to aluminum ratios in the framework to study how MW sensitivity is affected.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Learning on the Job: An Active Learning Calculator for Atomistic Simulations
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Neural network potentials have been used to accurately predict the energy and forces on atomic structures, acting as suitable substitutes for traditional electronic structure calculators. However, these predictions often diverge from true values when the neural network encounters images that deviate considerably from those found in the training set. In these cases, it would be desirable to include this image in the training set and re-train the network so it can better understand this region of the potential energy surface, but the manual selection of these images can be tedious and impractical. We present a method whereby a bootstrap ensemble of neural network calculators is used as a hands-free calculator that can identify poorly understood regions on the potential energy surface and retrain the calculator as necessary: for every image, an assessment of prediction certainty is made by evaluating the ensemble width, used as a measure for uncertainty. For images where the ensemble is uncertain, we call the electronic structure calculator and retrain the ensemble calculator on that image. A scheme for accelerated retraining of the neural network is also presented within. We apply this calculator to a 400-image sample of a single water molecule where one of the bond lengths and the bond angle is varied. We show the ability for the ensemble calculator to train itself when it is uncertain about an image, and display how retraining on just a few images allows the calculator to understand the region much better. This active learning calculator should allow for the hands-free training of accurate neural networks to perform electronic structure calculations through sample regions not covered by the training data, considerably reducing computation time and cost for future calculations that retread previously investigated sections of the potential energy surface.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Solar Water Disinfection Using Visible Light
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Abstract: Stable In Situ H 2 O 2 Generation from an Au nanoparticle/SnO 2 System Author: Sarah Glass Metal/Semiconductor heterojunctions are an attractive solution for photodisinfection of water. These systems use sunlight to oxidize water and reduce dissolved O 2 to form reactive oxygen species (ROS) which can kill bacteria and viruses in water. Commonly used semiconductors for these systems are TiO 2 and ZnO both of which utilize only the ultraviolet (UV) portion of sunlight (~5% of the spectrum by energy). This is due to the bandgap of these semiconductors being greater than 3 eV. If the visible portion of sunlight was able to be used, a more effective system could be made. Visible active semiconductors like C 3 N 4 have been widely pursued but suffer from instability in aqueous media. An alternative approach is to use metal nanoparticles to drive plasmonic and interband transitions to generate “hot” carriers (e.g. holes and electrons) that are separated at the metal/semiconductor junction. Gold nanoparticles are ultrastrong absorbers of visible light, which makes up 40% of the solar spectrum. This opens the opportunity for a more efficient system that uses ~8x more light provided by the sun. Here we present the Au-nanoparticle/SnO 2 system that uses a wide-bandgap semiconductor, Tin Oxide, and plasmon resonance effects from gold nanoparticles. Gold nanoparticles strongly absorb visible light through their plasmon resonances and interband transitions with an absorption spectrum that is highly tunable based on the size and shape of the particle and the local environment they are in. SnO 2 is a highly stable, wide bandgap semiconductor that does not absorb visible light due to its wide bandgap (e.g. > 3.8 eV). It also has a favorable conduction band alignment with gold accepting the hot-electron and driving O 2 reduction at the SnO 2 /water interface. Our Au nanoparticle/SnO 2 systems results show that visible light can be used to generate H 2 O 2 . The test results support our initial hypothesis that using a stable wide bandgap semiconductor in conjunction with metal nanoparticles will generate ROS using visible light (> 450 nm).

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Metal Containing ZSM-5 Catalysts for the Dry Reforming of Methane: Exploring Synergistic Effects
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The abundance of natural gas in the U.S. brought by the development of new fracking technologies for its extraction has triggered a notable renaissance of the U.S. chemical manufacturing industry. The selective activation of C-H bonds in the most abundant component in natural gas, methane, is one of the greatest challenges in catalysis. Methane can be converted into raw materials or commodity chemicals as follow: i) indirectly via syngas or ii) directly via, for instance, selective oxidation or dehydroaromatization. Along with methane, emphasis has been placed on the utilization of CO 2 to produce chemicals and fuels do to their abundance and negative impact to the environment. Both CH 4 and CO 2 are the main contributors of the greenhouse effect. As a result, Dry Reforming of Methane (DRM) is an attractive route to convert CH 4 and CO 2 into syngas with an H 2 /CO ratio of 1:1, which is the optimal ratio to produce liquid hydrocarbons through the Fischer-Tropsch process. However, among other factors, the multiple undesired side reactions such as methane thermal degradation, carbon monoxide disproportionation, and water gas shift has, have limited the potential application of DRM at an industrial scale. These reactions adversely affect the H 2 /CO ratio and the overall catalyst’s performance. The major challenge to address, as a result of the mentioned side-reactions, is the rapid catalyst deactivation due to the formation of coke. In this study, we aim to improve DRM using a series of Fe/Ni/ZSM-5 catalysts. First, various methodologies have been used to prepare these materials trying to determine the most important variables influencing the final bulk and surface structure of the catalyst. We use various characterization techniques such as N 2 -physisorption, X-Ray diffraction (XRD), X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and Raman spectroscopy. Reactivity tests are performed in a home-made reaction setup equipped with various mass flow controllers, a stainless-steel reactor, a tubular furnace with a temperature controller, and a gas chromatograph (GC) for the analysis of the products. Steady-state kinetics has shown a stable catalytic activity and selectivity towards syngas for Fe/Ni/ZSM-5 compared to the Ni/ZSM-5 catalyst, indicating that Fe is suppressing the formation of coke during the reaction. We aim to determine the variables and the optimal catalyst composition to enhance the catalytic performance of conventional Ni-based catalysts. We will also perform in-situ/opernaro Raman studies to compliment the kinetic data and stablish a more conclusive structure-reactivity/selectivity/stability relationship.
