https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Synthesis of Molybdenum Trioxide and Characteristics of H x MoO 3 Bronze Formation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Many modern chemical processes rely on highly polluting petroleum as a hydrogen source. Replacing petroleum with a cleaner alternative, such as water, could greatly enhance the sustainability of the chemical industry. Electrochemical methods allow the conversion of water into hydrogen; however, there is currently not a good understanding of how to integrate such electrochemical techniques into existing industrial reactions. With the goal of improving the sustainability of industrial chemical conversions, the gap between thermal and electrochemical catalysis needs to be bridged. Reducible metal oxides, such as tungsten trioxide (WO 3 ) and molybdenum trioxide (MoO 3 ), are useful models for these studies, as they can take up hydrogen both thermally (hydrogen spillover) and electrochemically (hydrogen intercalation). Our group recently reported on these processes in WO 3 , 1 but MoO 3 is known to have a higher hydrogen capacity. 2 This suggests that MoO 3 might exhibit enhanced reactivity, and so this work focuses on hydrogen uptake in MoO 3 . Two MoO 3 synthesis methods were investigated in order to produce a stable, reducible oxide. The selected method produced MoO 3 with an orthorhombic crystal structure, confirmed using XRD. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed to probe intercalation dynamics, where multiple discrete intercalation events were observed. Comparison to CVs of WO 3 reveal the MoO 3 has a lower overpotential for intercalation suggesting hydrogen insertion into MoO 3 is faster than into WO 3 . This study provides a foundation for further work on hydrogen uptake in H x MoO 3 and provides evidence that MoO 3 might be more useful than WO 3 for thermo-electrochemical hydrogenation chemistries. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Raman-Spectrokinetics for Gaining Insights on Support Effects of Supported Vanadium Oxide Catalysts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Understanding the link between observed structure and measured reactivity of supported metal oxide catalysts remains a challenging goal for the complex catalytic systems used in oxidative and non-oxidative dehydrogenation of light hydrocarbons. [1] Supported ternary metal oxide catalysts are one such system; their reactivity is influenced by catalyst coverage, relative amounts of species on the support, and the properties the of support. In the study presented, we used a combination of operando Raman spectroscopy and conventional time-resolved reaction kinetics to determine experimentally the redox reaction rates of surface species directly from the Raman spectra. This approach, coined Raman-spectrokinetic, overcomes a major limitation associated with elucidating kinetic parameters by conventional methods, via mass spectrometry (MS) and gas chromatography (GC). The Raman-spectrokinetic approach allows for observation of reaction rates at a specific catalytic site whereas conventional MS and GC analyses only provide the sample’s overall reaction rates (average rates from the entire samples’ sites). The study presented is a continuation of an earlier study which explored the oxidation of (VO x ) m /(NbO y ) n /SiO 2 catalysts. [2] Herein, we aim to elaborate on earlier work by reporting on the effects of catalyst support material by utilizing the Raman-spectrokinetic approach to gain new insights on the oxidation kinetics of supported vanadium oxide catalysts, following the evolution/depletion of the vandyl (V=O) vibration as a function of O 2 /H 2 concentration. With the knowledge that turnover frequency in catalysts remains constant as a function of coverage, our observation of the same phenomena via Raman-spectrokinetics renders support for the validity of the method. The goal of this study was to broaden our use of the Raman-spectrokinetic approach into reactivity of metal oxides at different MO x coverage (2D and 3D species), on different supports (SiO 2 , Al 2 O 3 , TiO 2 , ZrO 2 ), and with different surface structures. The insights gained in investigating the effects of these variables on reactivity and stability will further ongoing efforts to rationally design catalysts and achieve unprecedented catalytic performance with supported metal oxide catalysts. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Role of Confinement, Molecular Connectivity and Flexibility on Entropic Driven Surface Segregation of Polymer-Colloid Mixtures
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Relative surface affinity between polymers and colloids are leveraged in many applications like filtration, adhesion, bio-sensing etc. The surface affinity is governed by both enthalpic (relative interactions between the species and surface) and entropic (excluded volume) effects. Neglecting enthalpic effects i.e. for purely athermal systems, entropy is the only driving force that controls the surface affinity of the species in a binary or multi-component mixture. Many intensive (relative size of colloids, chain length, equilibrium bond angle, chain flexibility) and extensive (confinement, temperature) factors can dramatically change the entropy of the system and thus enhance or decrease the surface affinities of the constituent species. In this article, we use coarse grained metropolis Monte Carlo simulations to delineate the role of these factors on entropic surface segregation in binary mixture of polymers and colloids. At low number densities, excluded volume effects are negligible and we do not observe any entropic driven surface segregation. Therefore our system of interest is binary polymer-colloids mixtures at moderate to high number densities where excluded volume effects are predominant. Our results indicate that for flexible polymer chains, the surface is always enriched with colloids compared to polymers and this effect is enhanced for longer polymer chains. The configurational entropy of the flexible polymers is significantly reduced near the surface and therefore they prefer to stay in bulk (away from the surface). However this behavior can be completely reversed by introducing large degree of confinement and making the chains relatively rigid (less flexible). Our results show that polymer segregation of long stiff chains in slit pore geometry is driven by nematization near the surface while looping of polymers is observed under large degree of confinement. We observe that for longer polymer chains with an equilibrium bond angle (q = p), both confinement and chain stiffness enhance the surface segregation of polymers relative to colloids.However, the segregation behavior within a confinement is dependent on the polymer chain length. The surface segregation of polymers is dramatically decreased for chains with equilibrium bond angles; pi/3, pi/2, 2pi/3 and 5pi/6 independent of chain length and flexibility due to excluded volume effects as this leads to inefficient packing near the surface.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Applying Computer Science to the Development of Chemical Reactions: Applications in Heck-Type Cross-Coupling Reactions
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Organic chemistry and computer science have historically been immiscible. My research is focused on harnessing the power of computer science to streamline the development of chemical reactions, in particular using high throughput experimentation (HTE) to study Heck-type coupling reactions. These reactions require a metal center supported by a ligand, and reactivity and selectivity are dictated by the multifaceted interactions of the pairing. These reactions often produce mixtures of nearly identical products, commonly including enantiomers whose separation and classification prove uniquely challenging. Through the design of a novel program and user interface, we are able to parse large data sets of yield and selectivity - particularly those generated by HTE - and present the information in a meaningful way. Graphical representations, partially analyzed with MATLAB and Python and coupled with intuition and prior experience, aid chemists in rapid interpretation of these data sets. Challenges emerged in the design of the program: representations need to be generated quickly, be meaningful at a glance, and be created by users unaccustomed to data science. These considerations are being addressed in the design process.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Novel Energy Transfer Mechanism for Dielectric Cu 2 o Nanostructures in Photocatalysis.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Most Plasmonic Metal Nanocatalysts (PMN) are plagued by inherent joule loss, band-gap limitations and the inability to showcase strong magnetic fields. In addition, several of the metal catalysts currently being used in industrial and pharmaceutical applications are toxic in nature and require expensive downstream operations. Fortunately, in the past few years, copper-based photocatalysts have been identified as an alternative to conventional catalysts. These copper-based catalysts are appealing due to their relative abundance, low cost, low toxicity and heterogenous nature. Previous reports suggest that researchers believe copper-based photocatalysts undergo energy transfers via plasmonic mechanisms as a result of Localized Surface Plasmon Resonance effects (LSPR) and standard semiconductor mechanisms that come into play once the semiconductor material’s bandgap energy barrier is exceeded. A new energy transfer theory was developed. Through novel experimental modeling and computational methods (FDTD simulations), mechanism types were isolated and then tested for degradation under various conditions. The concept demonstrated in our study unveils a new way to conduct solar light harvesting and photocatalysis. Although we demonstrated the concept using Cu 2 O particles, this concept can be broadly applied to other metal oxide semiconductor particles including titanium dioxide. The successful degradations narrowed down the mechanism possibilities and provided statistical support for this theory in application in not only photocatalysis, but an abundance of industries such as but not limited to: pharmaceutical, energy fuels, thin film solar cells, CO 2 reduction, specialty chemicals, agrochemicals, as well as water decontamination among other related industries.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Quantifying United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Using Greenscope Indicators
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The 2015 United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals were created with ambition to construct a better world by the year 2030. These goals suggest how we should live, and how companies should conduct their businesses. However, they are quite broad with limited ways of quantification. This work proposes a framework that could be used to quantify such goals so that systems’ evolutions can be evaluated at different times in their operating cycles. Using the chemical process sustainability assessment tool GREENSCOPE, sets of indicators that represent specific UN Sustainable Development Goals are identified and used to quantify a given target within a goal. The identified indicators may be grouped in categories: resource efficiency, recycling, waste management, and resilience. After choosing a set of GREENSCOPE indicators, a case study of an Acetic Acid manufacturing simulation in CHEMCAD is analyzed. Sections of the manufacturing process are studied and discussed to determine their performance in terms of resilience and sustainability.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Mathematical Modeling of the Influence of Toxin Exposure on Rheumatoid Arthritis
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis is a debilitating autoimmune disease that attacks the joints in the body. These attacks cause chronic inflammation that degrades the surrounding bone overtime. This disease effects around one percent of the population globally, and women are three times more likely to be diagnosed with this disease than men. Rheumatoid arthritis research is broad with many scientific studies underway to identify causes, cures, and preventions. Previous studies have determined the mechanism of the disease once it becomes established in the body, but only limited published results focus on identifying triggers and mapping the physiological responses at the onset of arthritis. It is understood that environmental factors account for seventy percent of the disease generation, while genetics accounts for the other thirty percent. Recent studies have shown that the immune responses to environmental factors that lead to arthritis may begin in the gut, gums, or lungs years before symptoms appear. However, the links between the timing and extent of various environmental exposures on the onset and progression of arthritis are not clearly understood. Mathematical models can provide insights into explaining the complex linkages between molecular level actions of chemicals and their effects on the cellular, tissue, and whole body levels of physiology in a disease. We are building a model for the chemical and biological processes that are theorized to be involved in the onset of arthritis. To model how environmental toxins, such as herbicides and bacteria, stimulate chronic inflammation, we have combined two previously published models into a more complex and informative model. This model tracks how the concentration of tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a chemical that triggers inflammation, changes in the joints, the bloodstream, and the surrounding tissue. The model predicts TNF regulation by the inflammatory stress on the immune system. We will explore possible explanations for how specific toxins can alter TNF regulation to lead to arthritis. This work will impact society by improving fundamental understanding of the effects of toxins on arthritic autoimmune inflammation, laying the scientific foundation for advances in disease treatment and prevention.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Performing Quantum Chemical Computations at Different Levels of Theory to Predict Am(III) over Eu(III) Selectivity for DTPA-Based Ligands
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The presence of minor actinides (especially Americium) in spent nuclear fuel has posed a veritable challenge for the long-term storage of nuclear waste due to their high radiotoxicity and thermal emission. Minor actinides also have the potential to be reused in nuclear fuel cycle, making it further desirable for their extraction. However, despite the development of polyaminocarboxylate ligands that can achieve the problematic separation of Am(III) from trivalent lanthanides via selective complexation of the former, insufficient theoretical understanding of the molecular chemistry behind such complexation has hindered the design of more efficient and industrially attractive ligands. These theoretical obstacles arise primarily from challenges in computationally describing (1) heavy metal electronic structures and (2) the increase in covalent interactions between polyaminocarboxylate ligands and Am(III) compared to Ln(III). This work aims to determine a reliable computational protocol in predicting the Am(III) over Eu(III) selectivity of a polyaminocarboxylate ligand by evaluating the performance of ab initio quantum chemistry computations at various levels of theory, including density functional theory, Post-Hartree-Fock, and multiconfigurational methods. We also employed basis sets of varying degrees of flexibility for light and heavy atoms each. In our search for a protocol that provides reasonable accuracy while expending as few resources as possible, our results have potentially shown not only the importance not only of utilizing basis sets of sufficient size, but also of examining how a particular computational method accounts for electron correlation and relativistic effects. Further evaluation of these computational methods to other similar systems as well as comparing their results with experiment are needed in order to systematically corroborate their predictive ability.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Rapid Assessment of Chemical Toxicity Using Machine Learning and Combinatorial Quantitative-Structural Analysis Relationship Models
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Due to the nature of their work, United States Airmen and other members of the armed services can be exposed to harmful chemicals that may degrade their physical and/or cognitive performance. Additionally, on-the-ground personnel may require rapid assessment of a chemical’s toxicity; laboratory testing is often too slow to provide an adequate response. Therefore, there is a real need for rapid, robust, and accurate in-silico models that can computationally predict key toxicological activities. Quantitative structural-activity relationship models, or QSAR, are becoming popular as models of choice with the rise of machine learning in the field. The developed Python QSAR package, named as QSARBayesOpt, employs combinatorial QSAR, an emerging type of model in the cheminformatics community. Using consensus voting, the predicted values from each independent model are combined to increase the predictive power of the package as a whole. Through this automatic tuning framework, the package allows the end-user to easily change datasets using Bayesian optimization. Bayesian optimization is also an intelligent tuning method, learning from previous iterations to make smarter searches in the parameter space; therefore, significant amount of computational time and cost can be saved using this approach. Furthermore, we have tested this package against several datasets, including inhibition activity of acetylcholinesterase by organophosphates, where we saw 78% regression accuracy and 97% classification accuracy.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Nickel Oxide Silica Based and Commercial Nickel Oxide Nanosorbcats for Adsorption of Cationic and Anionic Dyes Followed By Thermo-Oxidative Decomposition
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Wastewater contains a variety of pollutants that are basically classified into organic such as dyes and inorganic substances. The contamination of surface and groundwater with synthetic dyes is a serious environmental problem and is a threat to human beings. These dyes could be cationic, anionic, or neutral. For instance, many industries use pigments to color their products such as textiles, plastics, paper, and so forth. The discharge of the produced wastewater effluents into the environment is worrying for toxicological and aesthetical reasons. Therefore, their removal from wastewater is of great interest. All processes for removing such pollutants from wastewater have their own limitations. However, the adsorption process is recognized to be an effective and economic process for cleaning wastewater. In addition, adsorptive remediation of wastewater on metal-oxide-based nanoparticles has been reported in the literature extensively. Recent studies showed significant awareness of metal oxides as nanoadsorbents and nanocatalysts (nanosorbcats) for cleaning wastewater, due to their individual chemical and physical properties, which make them ascendant to the conventional adsorbent/catalysts. Herein, in this study, the employment of in-house prepared nickel oxide silica-based (SBN)s and commercial nickel oxide (NiO) nanoparticles as nanosorbcats for cleaning up synthetic wastewater was investigated. Different model molecule pollutants; mainly methylene blue (MB) and bromocresol green (BCG) exemplifying cationic and anionic pollutants, respectively, were removed from synthetic wastewater samples by SBNs and NiO nanoparticles. Batch isotherm adsorption studies in addition to kinetics and thermodynamics were performed for the removal of both dyes from wastewater. The experimental adsorption data has been modeled using the Sips adsorption isotherm model to understand the adsorption behavior of these molecules. Fast adsorption kinetics of both nanoparticles have been observed; NiO nanoparticles took 60 minutes to reach saturation of BCG while SBNs took only 2 minutes for the case of MB. Moreover, both nanoparticles have shown high uptakes of about 99% and 96% at low concentrations of MB and BCG. Furthermore, thermodynamic parameters like the changes in free Gibbs energy (ΔG), enthalpy (ΔH), and entropy (ΔS) of the system were calculated. The catalytic activity behavior of spent nanoparticles was investigated via thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA), to check out the applicability of the nanosorbcats concept. Consequently, the regeneration, uptake saturation capacities and the performances of spent SBNs and commercial NiO nanoparticles after each adsorption cycle were studied and compared with the virgin ones. The detailed findings of this study will be discussed further during the poster presentation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: The Interaction of Azole Bio-Isosteres with Amino Acid Side Chains for Drug Design
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: There is significant interest in the design of new drugs with novel binding sites for interactions with specific peptides in proteins. The hydrogen bond is a key noncovalent interaction governing what happens between a drug molecule and its local environment. For drug molecules, this local environment can be a biological target, a biological off-target, aqueous solution, a lipid membrane, or even a crystalline solid. Consequently, hydrogen bonding impacts a wide range of molecular properties critical to drug design including potency, selectivity, membrane permeability, and solubility. This project is investigating the energetics of hydrogen bonding at the fundamental level to gain new insights into the basicity of a molecular site and its role in controlling hydrogen bond interactions as well as the possibility of proton transfer from one site to another. We are using the amide group as a model for the protein backbone as it can work both as a hydrogen donor and acceptor. At this point, there is no single model that explains the large range of binding energies exhibited by such hydrogen bonds. We are modeling the interactions of the basic amino acids, lysine, arginine and histidine with the non-classical amide bio-isosteres 3,5 dimethyl-1,2,4-triazole and 2,5-dimethyl-2H-tetrazole using computational electronic structure methods at the ab initio correlated molecular orbital theory and density functional theory levels. The structures are initially optimized using density functional theory to probe different conformations and binding sites. This information is used as input into more computationally demanding correlated molecular orbital theory calculations at the G3(MP2) level to predict the energetic properties of these azoles and their hydrogen bonding interactions with different amino acid side chains. Besides the gas phase calculations, the basicities and hydrogen bond energies in different solutions are predicted using self-consistent reaction field approaches to provide better insights into what is happening in a biochemical environment.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Simulation and Optimization of Epoxypropane Preparation Process Via Hppo Based on Aspen Plus
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: A continuous HPPO lab-scale pilot plant was designed for the production of propene oxide via HPPO (Hydrogen Peroxide Propene Oxide) process. It is necessary to optimize the technical parameters for improving epoxypropane yield. In this paper, Aspen Plus software was introduced to simulate the main units of Hydrogen Peroxide Propene Oxide, such as Epoxidation Reaction unit, Propylene Circulation unit, Epoxypropane Purification unit and Propylene glycol Purification unit. In the reaction, propylene is epoxidized with H 2 O 2 over a TS-1 catalyst using methanol/water as a solvent. The reaction occurs at a temperature and pressure of 52℃ and 3 MPa, respectively. HAZOP and P&ID were conducted for the reactor and distillation column. Aspen Sensitivity was employed to proceed the sensitivity analysis of dividing wall column (DWC), double effect distillation column, extract distillation column and azeotropic distillation column. The optimized key technical parameters were obtained by Aspen simulation. The main objective of the simulation is to complete the design and optimization of a plant that produces 337,000 metric tonnes per year (8000hr) of propylene oxide (PO) and 21,000 metric tonnes per year (8000hr) of propylene glycol (PG). Through simulation, the mass fraction of propylene oxide in the product is greater than 99.3%, and the mass fraction of by-product propylene glycol is greater than 99.99%. The model can be considered of high utility in designing and optimizing HPPO process, to achieve high reactants conversion and propene oxide yields.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Evaluation of Solvent Recovery Options for Economic Feasibility through a Superstructure-Based Framework
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: As the chemical market continues to expand, the concerns with regards to environmental sustainability have increased due to excessive disposal of chemical solvents. To date, there is no proper mitigation plan to handle such volume of chemical waste. Solvents are used in many industries for purposes such as reaction medium and as extraction, cleaning, and purification agents. These solvents can account for up to 90% of the process by mass and are often discarded after a single use. Incineration, the most widely used process for solvent disposal, is not a “green” method due to the potential detrimental effects to the environment. A systematic framework for solvent recovery has been developed which considers multiple alternative recovery and purification technologies to recover solvents simultaneously through a superstructure-based approach. These technologies are represented as mathematical models that are composed of material and energy balances, utility requirements, equipment design, and costs to assist in determining the most economical method for solvent recovery of any chemical waste stream. Two case studies involving simple binary solvent system and a more complex multi-component system were analyzed and formulated as mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. Selecting solvent recovery options required considerably lower cost in comparison to typical incineration. The solutions obtained from the case studies presented in this work demonstrated the capability of the solvent recovery framework to obtain environmentally friendly and economically viable solvent recovery pathways as an alternative to incineration.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Analysis and Simulation of FCC Unit Using Aspen HYSYS
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In the preliminary step of petroleum refinery, crude oil is processed and fractionated into lighter hydrocarbons which have lower ignition point i.e., petroleum naphtha, gasoline or diesel. Inherently, product stream of fractional distillation column other than the lighter hydrocarbons also contain heavier hydrocarbons which is often referred to as residue (gasoil). Due to the higher ignition point, it is deemed to be less economically valuable product. To serve this purpose, Fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) is employed to add more value to the heavier products. FCC is one of the most important processes in the petroleum refining industry for the conversion of heavy gasoil that provides about 35% to 45% of the blending stocks in refinery of gasoline. Various alkenes like ethylene and propylene are also produced by FCC for polymer applications. This work describes the model of FCC in ASPEN HYSYS that can simulate the behavior of FCC close to real work conditions. The FCC models mainly consists of riser, stripper, reactor and regenerator. In this work, a basic refinery process is designed and the vacuum gas oil from the vacuum distillation column is used as feed in the FCC unit. A sensitivity analysis is carried on parameters of interest i.e., pressure difference between regenerator and reactor, catalyst heat capacity, feed temperature , to determine the correlation that affect the FCC performance (mole-fraction of Butane is used to measure the performance) . The typical data in refinery is adopted, in which few changes were made in order to achieve proper simulation. The results of simulation predict the parameters which are more sensitive towards the performance of FCC, for example, performance of FCC is more sensitive to change in heat capacity of catalyst as compared to feed temperature. Hence, with this model, set of parameters are determined which have pre-dominant effect to FCC’s performance.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Mathematical Modeling of Mesangial Cells in Diabetic Kidney Disease
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease. About one out of four adults with diabetes has kidney disease. The kidney is supposed to filter wastes and extra water out of the blood stream to produce urine. When the kidney is damaged, it cannot filter blood like it should, which leads to waste build up and excess water in the body and eventually to death. One of the key cell types damaged in the kidney is mesangial cells. The mesangial cells and the surrounding extracellular matrix hold together the bundles of capillaries where blood is filtered in the kidneys. Experiments have shown multiple chemical pathways that change mesangial cells in diabetic kidney disease (DKD). It is challenging to describe how these chemical pathways interact with each other in mesangial cells over time. I have used mathematical modeling of differential equations to represent the chemical pathways in mesangial cells that are known to be affected by DKD. I have combined the separate pathways into a systems biology model that can consider the interactions between pathways and between multiple mesangial cells in the kidney. I will present model results for conditions that lead to expansion of the mesangial tissue (cells and extracellular proteins) during diabetic hyperglycemia.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Mathematical Modeling of Nephrin Loss in Diabetic Kidney Disease
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of kidney failure. The job of the kidneys is to filter the blood. However, when the kidneys are damaged, the filtration system is less efficient. In this project we focused on podocyte cells, which compose the outer filtration barrier. In between podocyte cells, a protein called nephrin connects the podocytes like Velcro. The blood is filtered through this area to excrete waste and excess water. Diabetes can cause the nephrin to lose its Velcro abilities causing it to disconnect from the podocyte cells and be excreted in the urine. The loss of nephrin causes the mountain and valley landscape of the podocytes and the gaps between them to become distorted. Diabetic complications can cause the nephrin to lose the Velcro ability and be excreted. We will present an empirical model for predicting category of proteinuria (protein in the urine) based on loss on nephrin expression using human biopsy data for Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes patients. Type 1 and Type 2 have different blood sugar landscapes, this potentially causes differences in nephrin loss. We will also present images from a graphical user interface that we developed, with graphs presenting nephrin expression in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes. The model relates the percentage of nephrin lost to the mRNA expression of nephrin and to the urinary protein concentration. This noninvasive modeling research provides quantitative guidance for the threshold where nephrin loss causes long-term damage to the kidney clinically detectable by the presence of protein in the urine.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Application of Machine Learning Methods to Improve Leukemia Diagnostics
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In 2019, there will be an estimated 1,762,450 new cancer cases diagnosed and 606,880 cancer deaths in the United States [1] . With both numbers increasing every year it is very important to be able to diagnose each and every patient in the most cost efficient and timely manner. Every patient that is suspicious of having any type of cancer will undergo multiple tests to find a correct diagnosis. It has become extremely important to assess the signs of cancer in patients with the most accurate test possible for efficient diagnosis. Biomarkers, external symptoms, and other important indicators allow medical professionals to evaluate the cancer status upon examination. One of the most prominent markers that appear within the blast cells of patients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is myeloperoxidase (MPO) [2] . This project has focused on the use of machine learning methods to evaluate the chances of a patient having AML or Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) based on the clinical variables obtained via morphological, and cytochemistry tests. The two machine learning methods used in this study were decision trees and neural networks. These methods require a data set to train the neural network or decision tree and then a testing data set to evaluate how accurately these machine learning methods identify each patient as having ALL or AML. The immunophenotyping (IPT) results serve as the confirmatory test for checking the solution accuracy. These machine learning approaches can possibly help to determine which symptoms/markers are most important to search for when diagnosing a patient with either AML or ALL. A marker is deemed to be significant when it is used as a node within the tree and as for the neural network there are weights assigned to each possible marker with the more important markers resulting in a higher weight. It will also help to inform doctors which tests will be most efficient in determining a diagnosis for patients. It was found that the decision tree approach was able to diagnose patients with AML 97.14% of the time when considering myeloperoxidase (MPO). The neural network that was created using the same dataset was able to classify patients correctly 100% of the time while assigning the highest weight to the MPO marker. To check for the significance of the MPO marker both the decision tree and neural network were recreated neglecting the MPO marker. Both machine learning methods had a drop in accuracy when classifying a patient with AML with the accuracy of decision trees falling to 91.43% and the neural networks decreasing to 90.91%.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Computer Modeling of Aerosol Diffusion through Lung Mucosa
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Diseases of the lung are some of the most common and deadly in the world. Existing treatments, if any exist, tend to be extremely invasive and time-consuming. Further, due to the poor bioavailability of drugs traditionally administered orally or through injection, these treatments are not very effective. Technology is emerging that allows an aerosolized drug dosage to be delivered directly to the diseased area; however, the mucus layer separating the airways from the tissue remains a barrier to this method. The mucociliary clearance mechanism in the lungs clears foreign particles (including cigarette ash, dust, and bacteria) and prevents infection. A layer of mucus on the surface of the inner lung is constantly pushed upward towards the throat by a bed of cilia, and most particles that impact on the mucus are cleared from the lungs quickly and without incident. Although mucociliary clearance aims to prevent a disease from being contracted, it remains a barrier to drug delivery, as drugs must cross the same thick mucus layer that is being swept away from the tissue. We used COMSOL Multiphysics software to develop a model of the mucosal interface between the airways and the lung tissues. Data from the literature is used to determine details like dimensions, velocity, and viscosity. The mucus layer moves upwards towards the throat in laminar flow, imitating the mucociliary effect, and the underlying periciliary layer has no net movement due to the regular beating of the cilia that move the mucus. The “drug” enters from the airway side and moves through the fluid by convection. Given these inputs, the model outputs the concentration distribution of the administered drug molecule or particle subject to diffusion through the moving mucosa. We aim to maximize the amount of drug that reaches the target lung tissue. The model is customizable, easily modified to simulate other drugs or any other particle so long as some properties are known. Variables have been specifically parametrized to find more complex relationships, like effective diffusivity, from an input of more readily available information, like particle radius. Lung conditions can also be altered to meet the needs of the application (for example, the mucus layer is much thinner in the alveolar region, and the mucus of cystic fibrosis patients is much denser than average). Thus, the model can provide insight into the efficacy of new lung treatments and aid in the design of drug transport properties.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Electronic Properties of Dicationic Ionic Liquids for Corrosion Inhibition
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Ionic liquids have been found to impart corrosion inhibition performance in industrial applications. In order to assess the corrosion potential of several imidazolium-based dicationic ionic liquids, quantum mechanical calculations were performed to predict their electronic properties. The structure of these dicationic ionic liquids was R 1 -Im-R 2 -Im-R 3 where R 1 , R 2 , R 3 are alkyl chains and Im are imidazolium rings. Three alkyl chain lengths (butyl, hexyl, and octyl) were studied for R 1 and R 3 , whereas ethyl, butyl, and hexyl groups were considered for the linker domain R 2 for a total of 15 cations. These cations were paired with two chloride Cl - , two tetrafluoroborate [BF 4 ] - and an equimolar mixture of Cl - -[BF 4 ] - resulting into a total of 51 cation-anion pairs. Population analysis was carried to obtain electrostatic potential maps and HOMO-LUMO energy gaps. The HOMO-LUMO gap and optimized structures were analyzed to discern patterns in their gas phase behavior based on length of alkyl chains and the configuration of anions. The HOMO-LUMO energy gap was found to be the most dependent on the anion, with pure Cl - exhibiting the lowest gap, while the pure [BF 4 ] - showing the highest when comparing structures with equivalent cations. The most important factor found to affect the structure of the studied ionic liquids was the length of the alkyl chain linking the two imidazolium moieties. From the structural respective, Cl - location in the optimized geometry was decided by the acidic hydrogen atoms on the imidazolium rings due to its tendency to hydrogen bond. [BF 4 ] - also participated in the hydrogen bonding, but increased area of negative charge in the anion allowed it to bridge the imidazolium rings more effectively. A novel behavior was found when the [BF 4 ] - anion was present along with the butyl group as the linker in which the cation curled up on itself, creating a large region of positive charge within the center of the molecule.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Binding of Lignin Dimers on MWW-2D Zeolite: Solvothermal Effect Study
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Lignin as the potential renewable source of biofuels, chemicals, and other value-added products has gained significant attention. However, due to its complex structural network, developing efficient depolymerization techniques are challenging. Lignin depolymerization is governed by reaction conditions (pressure, temperature, etc.), catalyst used, and the presence of solvent. In this work, the binding modes of different β-O-4 linkages have been analyzed using periodic density functional theory (DFT) with the optB88-vdW functional. The effect of how changing the ratio of H to OH on the catalytic surface, different temperatures, and different solvents affects the binding energy has been analyzed. Overall, model MWW framework zeolites are characterized by ab-initio first principle simulations, with the goal of gaining molecular level insights into the different binding modes of β-O-4 linkages on the catalytic surface.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Computational Screening of Environmental Barrier Coating Materials for Nuclear Thermal Propulsion Engines
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Although nuclear thermal propulsion (NTP) rocket engines have the potential to far outperform the state-of-the-art chemical combustion engines for interplanetary travel, corrosive interactions between the hydrogen propellant and the uranium fuel element acts as a serious barrier of entry for the application of NTP engines. Environmental Barrier Coatings (EBC) have been considered previously to protect the elements but coating techniques used did not enough control to be effective. This research investigated the use of Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) as a technique to coat fuel spheres with a nanoscale EBC to prevent hydrogen attack on the fuel. ALD allows a conformal, uniform, and nanometer thick coating on both the fuel spheres as well as the high aspect ratio channels of the fuel elements. The primary focus of this study was the coating material to be deposited via ALD. Potential candidates were selected based on low neutron cross sections and high melting points. Density functional theory (DFT), a computational quantum mechanical modelling method, was then employed to calculate energy barriers for a hydrogen atom to move through both the surface unit cells and the bulk unit cells of these candidate materials. Those with the highest barriers were deposited on surrogate materials and compared to materials previously investigated for this application. Samples were characterized to ensure deposition was successful and determine film thickness. Stability of materials in a high hydrogen environment was also studied with DFT. This predicted stability was then tested experimentally in a high temperature furnace system. Through this process, it was shown that nitrides are predicted to outperform pure metals when used as EBCs in NTP engines and many will remain stable at very high temperatures. It was also demonstrated that both tungsten nitride (WN) and molybdenum nitride (MoN) are not stable enough species for this application. Candidate materials from this work will be deposited on surrogate substrates to be experimentally compared to each other, as well as barrier materials previously investigated for this application, in future work.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Theoretical Design and Analysis of High-Spin Ground-State a-D-a-π Conjugated Polymers
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Theoretical design and analysis of high-spin ground-state A-D-A-π conjugated polymers John D. Teas , Md Abdus Sabuj and Neeraj Rai Dave C. Swalm School of Chemical Engineering and Center for Advanced Vehicular Systems, Mississippi State University, MS, 39762, USA. High-spin ground-state donor-acceptor (DA) conjugated polymers (CPs) used as organic semiconductors (OSCs) are prevalent in research spanning the fields of physics, chemistry, and materials science. The OSCs with open-shell character have applications in many modern technologies, including organic electronics, nonlinear optics, and energy conversion and storage. Alternating arrangement of DA CPs exhibit various properties, such as interactions with light, the ability to transport charges, and tunability through chemical modification, which also allow for the active usage of these OSCs in optoelectronic technology (London et al , 2019). However, due to the presence of unpaired electrons, these high-spin organic molecules are unstable and highly localized. Despite these challenges, computer simulation allows for the design and analysis of these high-spin organic materials. Here, we have designed three conjugated A-D-A-π polymer semiconductor structures that show signs of having a triplet ground state ( S = 1) in the long polymer chain limit. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations at the unrestricted (U)B3LYP/6-31G** level of theory were performed on the oligomers ( n = 1 to 5) to identify the evolution of their electronic properties. The diradical character index (0 < y < 1), which describes the contribution of the open-shell resonance form to the ground-state, was found to be y = 0.537 for n = 1 and y = 0.999 for n = 5. This implies the formation of a pure diradical ( y = 1) for longer polymer chain lengths. The singlet-triplet energy gap (ΔE ST ) decreases with an increase in the length of the polymer chain ( ΔE ST = 0.114 eV for n = 1 and ΔE ST = 2.7x10 -6 eV for n = 5), which shows the extent of electron exchange interactions from admixing of the HOMO and LUMO in the ground state. This study shows the possibility to synthesize new A-D-A-π polymers, which are stable at ambient conditions, with intriguing molecular and electronic properties.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Analytical Prediction of Non-Newtonian Concentration Profiles Using a Correction Factor
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Mathematical models are a vital part of chemical engineering. Modelling systems allows for predictions to be made in specific cases without a dependence on empirical data alone. In fluid mechanics, models of systems containing Newtonian fluids can be easily obtained by established methods. However, Non-Newtonian fluids are much more difficult to model. The introduction of a correction factor could allow for Newtonian models to be used for Non-Newtonian fluids. Due to the nature of dimensionless or reduced states, the non-dimensionalized models for two different fluids under the same conditions are equivalent. By non-dimensionalizing a Newtonian model and then applying a correction factor, the characteristics of the model could be adjusted to match the hypothetical non-Newtonian case. With this method, the documented solution for a system containing a Newtonian fluid could be used to generate a model of the same system with a non-Newtonian fluid. The use of a correction factor to obtain a model of a non-Newtonian system significantly reduces the amount of time and computational power that would typically be required for such a task. This contribution proposes a method to obtain velocity and concentration profiles of a system containing a non-Newtonian fluid through the use of a correction factor and the analytical solution to the same system with a Newtonian fluid. The proposed analytical solution will be compared to the numerical solution to prove the accuracy of this method.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Generalized Antoine and Wagner Equations Consistent with the Predictions of the Soave-Redlich-Kwong Equation of State Using Similarity Variables
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Chemical engineers use the Wagner and Antoine equations to correlate vapor pressure as a function of temperature for various substances; however, they do not describe the entire vapor pressure curve from the triple point to the critical point. Methods of finding generalized Antoine and Wagner equation constants consistent with the predictions of the Soave-Redlich-Kwong (SRK) equation of state were studied. Calculations were simplified using two similarity variables. Common adjusted temperature, η * , combined reduced temperature and acentric factor, and common adjusted pressure, ψ*, combined reduced pressure and reduced temperature. Results of an iterative SRK vapor pressure algorithm were transformed into a data set of the new similarity variables. Antoine and Wagner constants were empirically determined by nonlinear least squares to achieve less than 0.05 percent relative deviation from SRK predictions. Three common adjusted temperature subranges, from the critical point down to 0.23, were needed for the Wagner equation. Only the C constant was fitted by least squares for the Antoine equation, with the A and B constants determined by exact calculation at the endpoints of common adjusted temperature ranges. Five common adjusted temperature subranges, from the critical point down to 0.18, were needed for the Antoine equation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Computational Analysis of C-H Hydroxylation in Bio-Inspired Monometallic Complexes
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: With sustainable energy innovations on the rise but logistical and technological barriers preventing their widespread implementation, it is of paramount importance to increase the sustainability of conventional energy generation for the remainder of its lifecycle. Natural gas, despite being the most environmentally benign of the fossil fuels, is underutilized due to difficulties in storage and transportation. Catalytic C-H hydroxylation is achieved in nature by enzymes known as lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) . The goals of this research project are twofold: To quantify the difference in energy barriers faced by a singlet and triplet state catalytic complex To determine whether a one step or two step reaction mechanism is energetically favorable for this C-H hydroxylation process Computational methods are applied to bio-inspired catalytic systems, utilizing quantum mechanical algorithms to optimize initial and final molecular geometries and determine stable transition state structures. The relevant energy and entropy differences are then calculated and compared between the spin states and pathways, shedding further light on the nuanced and controversial mechanisms by which these biological complexes catalyze C-H hydroxylation, and potentially enabling more effective catalyst design. Tentative preliminary results are consistent with literature values.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Uncertainty Analysis with Geothermal Techno-Economic Tool Geophires v2.0: Model Development, Validation and Case Studies
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: GEOPHIRES v2.0 is an open-source techno-economic simulator used for modeling geothermal reservoirs. One of the challenges in geothermal reservoir modeling is handling uncertain parameters that are difficult to measure or characterize. Over the course of this project, three modules have been developed for GEOPHIRES v2.0 to address uncertainty in geothermal parameters: multiparameter tornado diagram analysis, single parameter sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo analysis. These modules provide the user with tools to assess the impact of parameter uncertainty on the technical and economic performance of a geothermal system. High performance computing capabilities have also been implemented to effectively perform the large number of GEOPHIRES v2.0 simulations required for Monte Carlo analysis. A geothermal plant in Paris was used as a case study, first to validate the GEOPHIRES v2.0 tool by comparing the output with the results from the System Advisor Model (SAM) and actual plant performance, and secondly to test the three uncertainty analysis modules. The uncertainty analysis indicated that drilling costs and geothermal gradient have a major impact on overall plant levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) or heat (LCOH), while reservoir rock properties only have a minor impact.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Volume Change of Vaporization from the SRK Equation of State Using a Similarity Variable
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Equations of state such as the Soave-Redlich-Kwong (SRK) equation are used to predict thermodynamic properties of chemical substances. Most commonly, PVT properties are directly calculated, but equilibrium properties such as volume change of vaporization may be calculated using more complex algorithms including fugacity calculations. In this project, direct calculation methods for estimating volume change of vaporization consistent with the SRK equation were studied. Reduced volume change of vaporization, ΔV R , was expressed as a power series of natural adjusted temperature η, a similarity variable combining reduced temperature and acentric factor. Starting from a previously determined reduced density power series, twenty series coefficients were derived. Series results were compared to exact SRK data for volume change of vaporization, and the relative deviation was less than 0.22 percent for natural adjusted temperatures between 0.0516 and the critical point. Work continues to find additional series coefficients and increase the range of natural adjusted temperatures while keeping the relative deviation within 0.5 percent, and to combine the reduced volume change of vaporization series with the Clapeyron equation to calculate heat of vaporization.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Generalized Antoine and Wagner Equations Consistent with the Predictions of the Peng-Robinson Equation of State Using Similarity Variables
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Chemical engineers use the Antoine and Wagner vapor pressure equations because of their relative simplicity; however, their accuracy is limited to restricted temperature ranges and they require substance-specific constants. Generalized methods were developed to find Antoine and Wagner equation constants consistent with the Peng-Robinson (PR) equation of state. Two similarity variables were introduced to simplify calculations. Adjusted temperature, η, combined reduced temperature and acentric factor. Adjusted pressure, Ψ, combined reduced pressure and reduced temperature. A PR vapor pressure algorithm generated a data set of these similarity variables, and a nonlinear least squares method was used to find generalized Antoine constants. When all three generalized Antoine constants were independently fit, the results matched PR vapor pressure predictions within 0.05 percent for twelve subranges of adjusted temperatures from the critical point down to 0.23. Fitting only the C constant by least squares with the A and B constants calculated by exact fits of the adjusted pressure at the endpoints of each subrange, only five adjusted temperature subranges gave the desired accuracy from the critical point down to 0.23. For the Wagner equation, only three adjusted temperature subranges gave the desired accuracy from the critical point down to 0.23.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: A Comparison of Methods for Predicting the Melting Point of Perarylphosphonium and Perarylsulfonium Ionic Liquids Using Molecular Dynamics
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Ionic liquids (ILs) are organic salts that have melting points below 100°C. Their unusual properties, such as non-flammability, negligible vapor pressure, and high tunability have made them of interest for industrial applications such as heat storage, fuel cells, and batteries. In most applications melting point is desired so that the IL remains pumpable at moderate temperature. Oftentimes the IL structure can be modified, which affects the melting point, however knowing what modifications must be made to lower the melting point remains a challenge. Molecular dynamics (MD) is a method to simulate the physical interactions and movements among a molecule and its atoms. Several different methods exist in MD to calculate the melting point of a compound; however, it is not entirely clear how well each of these methods perform for ionic liquids. Knowing which method performs the best would allow us to connect the changes in chemical structure of ILs with the melting point. In this work we compare the performance of three popular methods for computing the melting point of a set of perarylphosphonium and sulfonium ionic liquids: the void density method, the hysteresis method, and the solid-liquid interface-based (SLIB) method. Each of these methods requires prior knowledge of the crystal structure, which was obtained experimentally from X-Ray scattering. Furthermore, the experimental melting points were also obtained using differential scanning calorimetry, allowing us to compare these melting points with melting point predictions from each method. Once a model provides an adequate prediction of the melting point, the molecular interactions provided by that model are further studied to understand the molecular-level causes of melting point depression in these compounds. Understanding the molecular interactions of a complex ionic compound will assist in generating new ILs and altering newly formed complex ionic compounds.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Examining Potential Intermediates in the Electrochemical Synthesis of Ozone from Water
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Ozone can be produced by electrochemical water oxidation, yet there are many questions about how to engineer its reaction mechanism that involves six electron transfer steps. Understanding this reaction can offer insight into properties of intermediates along the reaction pathway, which can influence the activation energies and rate determining step of this reaction. Once this information is known, it may be used to determine the properties of a catalyst, which can ultimately improve the rate and the energy cost for this reaction. To properly understand this reaction, it is imperative to have an accurate understanding of the energetics and thermodynamic properties (e.g. acidity constants and standard redox potentials) of hypothetical reaction intermediates along the reaction pathway. We have used Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) along with implicit and mixed solvation models to determine these acidity constants and reduction potentials for a collection of oxygen containing molecules. A mixed implicit/explicit solvation model and the accompanying thermodynamic cycle has also been found to reduce errors in calculations compared to the available experimental data. After benchmarking this approach with available experimental data, we predict thermodynamic properties for different solvated reaction intermediates and determine which are relevant for the electrochemical ozone production reaction.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Analysis of Model Application Using CFD in Transition Mixing
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Mixing is a common practice used in a vast majority of industrial processing and manufacturing applications. Mixing is typically studied in either the laminar or turbulent flow regimes because the equations governing these regimes are well understood. Due to the complexity of transition mixing, minimal modeling is done in this regime. Certain industries naturally find themselves operating in and around the transition regime, but are unable to fully understand the process due to the inability of accurate modeling. The mixing of many personal care products fall into this category because they typically deal with complex non-Newtonian fluids. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is a tool that enables the modeling of various physical systems to analyze velocity profiles, streamlines, and numerous other fluid and flow parameters. Transient simulations of the mixing of Carbopol (a high molecular weight, crosslinked polyacrylic acid polymer) were run using CFD in order to compare the blend time results with real data. Analysis was done by looking at concentration profiles and volume fractions at various locations in the tank throughout the mixing process. The viscous models compared were the laminar and realizable k-epsilon. The mixture model was used to compare the two different phases identified by different dye color. The Carbopol viscosity was modeled using a non-Newtonian power law. The two different viscous models yield different blending results, neither of which match up with the real data, indicating a discrepancy between the models and mixing within the transition flow regime.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Developing Matlab Code for Analysis of Heterogeneous Engineered Cardiac Tissue during Contraction
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Title: Developing MATLAB Code for Analysis of Heterogeneous Engineered Cardiac Tissue during Contraction Primary Author (and presenter): Bush, Michaela, Z Additional Authors: Ellis, Morgan. Finklea, Ferdous. Lipke, Elizabeth Department: Department of Chemical Engineering College/School: Auburn University Description: Engineered cardiac tissue (ECT) is needed for treating various cardiovascular diseases, studying development and disease mechanisms, and for high-throughput drug screening, so we are producing ECT directly from human induced pluripotent stem cells. The ECT must have the appropriate phenotype, maturation, and functionality for downstream applications. One way we assess these properties of ECT is by analyzing the speed and duration of calcium propagation, necessary for cardiac function. Calcium propagation is measured using optical mapping; we record high-speed videos of ECT treated with a calcium-sensitive fluorescent dye that brightens in the presence of calcium, creating flashes that follow calcium propagation. The purpose of this project is to create a custom MATLAB ® program that can analyze these videos and extract the calcium transient duration (CTD), conduction velocity, and the heterogeneity index of the tissue. Due to the heterogeneous nature of 3D-ECT, not all pixels contain useable data. New features have been incorporated to remove unusable pixels based on their lower fluorescence or range. The program can filter data temporally to smooth the propagation waves and normalize it to remove variations in base fluorescence. Pixels that lack consistent propagation are then removed based on their dissimilarity to pixels with consistent propagation. From the remaining usable pixels, the number of calcium propagation events and the time these events occur is quantified and visualized using isochrone maps. The conduction velocity is calculated by choosing several pairs of points and calculating the time calcium travels between the points divided by the distance between the points. A new feature incorporating the MATLAB® gradient function allows direction of the velocity for groupings of pixels to be plotted to aid in visualization of the wave propagation and the optimal pairs that best represent the overall conduction velocity. A method of calculating the CTD, which measures the time between depolarization and repolarization, at any repolarization percentage was implemented using the luminosity at the peak and trough of each wave. The heterogeneity index measures the variance of the CTD which is relevant as cells in 3D-ECT are not distributed evenly. Using this data, we can determine the functionality of ECT and the quality of our current methods to create ECT.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Seek and You Shall Find: Where Do Faculty Obtain and Engage with Active Learning Resources
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Different types of active learning are commonly used within classrooms throughout primary and sometimes secondary schools, but upon reaching college classrooms active learning is still gaining traction. The use of active learning techniques can provide an energetic learning environment and has been shown to have a positive effect on student learning. Kinesthetic learning is a branch of active learning that actively and physically engages students with the material being taught through physical movement and/or exercises. Kinesthetic learning specifically moves students around the classroom instead of the traditional sitting for a 50 to 80 minute lecture. Some examples would be rotating stations around the classroom, acting out a process, or students drawing out a process or problem on the board. Kinesthetic and other active learning techniques face many barriers in being adopted in classrooms within the collegiate community. Faculty members can be resistant to changes to the traditional lecture style of teaching, which is possibly connected to a lack of former pedagogical training and awareness of the resources available to support active learning strategies in the classroom. There is also a difficulty in knowing where and how to effectively share materials with other educators when creating active-learning materials. This leads us to the research question: how do faculty members find resources to develop teaching methods for their classrooms? In terms of understanding how to integrate kinesthetic and active learning teaching techniques into college classrooms, information on how faculty members obtain pedagogical skills and methods should be considered. The study conducted seeks to identify where faculty members within engineering disciplines look for resources regarding teaching methods. With this information we can be determine what the best ways are to distribute active learning resources engineering faculty. Data collection through survey and interviews looked at the resources for active learning and how faculty are currently using or are willing to use them. The results lead to information on how to approach developing and disseminating resources to help and improve classroom engagement.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Nonlinear Dynamic System Identification of Monoclonal Antibody Production
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The demand for monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) has increased due to their high affinity and specificity to thousands of biological targets. Immunotherapy using mAbs are widespread in the treatment of various diseases including cancer and autoimmune disorders. The entry of biosimilars (variations of previously approved mAbs with similar efficacy and safety to its predecessor) into the market creates a need for production process intensification, and computational models are valuable tools which can be used for optimizations purposes. In this work, we identify data driven models that simulate the system dynamics of mAb (IgG4 cB72.3) generation in GS-NS0 cells in a semi-batch operation. Hammerstein Wiener and Nonlinear AutoRegressive models with eXogeneous (NARX), a subclass of Recurrent Neural Networks, are fitted to simulated data and compared for performance. The trained data driven models demonstrate good accuracy and reduce computational cost in comparison to the rigorous dynamic model. This potentially makes the data-driven approach a versatile tool for computationally demanding optimization studies. Results favor the Hammerstein Wiener model for multiple simulation datasets, and the NARX model for a single simulation dataset. Further exploration is under progress to determine the best surrogate model, which can be used for process optimization. *The first and second authors contributed equally to this work.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: 3D Printed Kidney Filters for Hands-on Learning
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In this project, I designed an anatomically correct 3D printed model of a part of the kidney and zoomed in at a more detailed level for a 3D printed component that mimics the filtration of blood by the kidney. I describe the motivations, the models, and their use in hands-on demonstrations for learning science and engineering concepts. The glomerulus, the functional unit of filtration in the kidney, removes waste from the blood while retaining important compounds needed for a healthy body. Glomeruli are a bundle of capillaries surrounded by a capsule and lined with specialized filtration cells. Through physical openings and chemical diffusion, the blood traveling through the capillary is filtered of its waste, which is then excreted as urine. Because the glomerulus is so important in blood filtration, it is a major component in kidney health and important for research studies related to filtration in the body. The glomeruli are found in the thousands in the human kidney but are invisible to the naked eye. With computer aided microscopy, images have been developed and circulated through current literature. However, this data has not yet been used with 3D modeling software to represent the anatomically correct microscopic glomerulus. I used SolidWorks was to model the glomerulus at different spatial scales for demonstration tools. The 3D model of a glomerulus capsule and capillary matrix follows current literature describing the size and volume of an average human glomerulus, which is approximately 200 micrometers in diameter, and considers both artistic renderings and microscopy images currently available. Standard 3D printers and splicing software were used to print each physical model. In this poster, I will justify the development of the 3D glomerulus model highlighting its purpose and use in demonstrations to increase scientific literacy in a variety of venues. I will show the accuracy of my model with respect to current findings on glomeruli size and features. I will also show how a simplified kidney filter was designed and 3D printed for engineering education workshops. Using descriptions and images of glomerular pores, I devised a simple cylindrical filter that when used in tandem with beads representing the various molecules and cells in the blood provides a simple hands-on demonstration of the process of glomerular filtration and how it changes between healthy and diseased conditions.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Understanding the Relationship between Engineering Identity and Academic Motivation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The primary goal in this research is to explore the connection between motivation and identity within undergraduate engineering students. Uncovering the relationship between these two constructs has the potential to inform techniques that encourage academic motivation. In turn, this could encourage a greater correlation between identity and engineering identity. Previous work shows that having a greater intersection between one’s career identity and other identities (i.e., social, demographic, etc.) increases motivation. We hypothesize that this could translate into an academic setting, in which academic motivation is more prevalent among those who have a secure sense of engineering identity. In the end, we believe this will correlate to overall higher success. The method used in this study involves analyzing an individual’s previous responses to failure as a measure of a student’s motivational behavior and comparing this measure to the strength of their engineering identity. The sample population consists of upperclassmen aeronautic and astronautic engineering students. Engineering identity is measured via an instrument created by Dr. Allison Godwin of Purdue University, West Lafayette. The instrument centers on uncovering how strongly students feel they identify as engineers, within categories of recognition, interest, and competence. This study also uses the critical incident technique. Students are asked to reflect upon a time where they successfully and unsuccessfully recovered from an academic or professional failure (the critical incident). Failure is a sensitive subject that provokes strong reactions within people, some greater than others. Thus, in analyzing these reactions, we can gain insight into different patterns of coping mechanisms and determine what patterns hinder or help motivational growth. We are interested specifically in the disciplinary distinction between astronautic and aeronautic engineering students. The subject population in this study is drawn from an upper-level systems dynamics course required for both majors. For students on the astronautic track, it serves as an integral part of their curriculum, while students on the aeronautic track take the course for a greater perspective. In analyzing the difference between majors within the same course, we demonstrate how the intersection between course content and major identity play in subsequent motivation to succeed in the class. This study aims to give educators greater insight into student behavior so they can adjust their teaching techniques to optimize student motivation or encourage greater identity correlation. In future work, we will continue to work through what exactly defines identity, manipulating certain variables to greater understand relationships.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Metrics of Student Success and Problem Difficulty Using Auto-Graded Online Homework
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Online homework and interactive textbooks are becoming more prevalent in university classrooms . Research suggests that students appreciate the immediate feedback as well as being given multiple attempts to earn points for a problem . However, determining the quality of auto-graded problems is still an open question . To develop a metric, o ver 700 questions were evaluated from a second-semester freshman course in Material and Energy Balances. U sing three years of data from over 250 students and more than 100 ,000 problem attempts were analyzed . Pr oblems consist of multiple parts with each part increasing in difficulty. A variety of problem types were used in including mul tiple choice, numerical response , and graph reading. Metrics used to analyze the que stions included number of attempts before a correct answer was given , total attempts , and success rate . Using these quantities , a point system was created to determine the quality and difficulty of problems based on student performance . Additionally, online homework questions were analyzed to correlate student success in the course with completion of the challenge activity questions. S tudents who complet ed more of the challenge activities had better success in the course as measured by final grade. Overall, web-based analytics of student success and attempts - before - correct can quantify the quality of hundreds of auto-graded problems.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Why Do I Have to KNOW This? Engineering in a Globalized Society
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: As society is becoming increasingly globalized, engineers must be able to integrate non-technical factors into their problem-solving and design. This research study investigates whether engineering students, engineering faculty, and professional engineers have similar thinking when it comes to solving problems within a global context. This is aligned with the ABET outcome that students must have “an ability to apply engineering design to produce solutions that meet specified needs with consideration of public health, safety, and welfare, as well as global, cultural, social, environmental, and economic factors,”. This student outcome is referred to as a professional skill. Professional skills were developed as a response to old accreditation standards being too stringent and that they stifled innovation. For engineers, professional skills includes the implicit knowledge of how one’s work impacts a globalized society. At most universities, bringing in global contexts into problem-solving is neglected until students’ senior-year capstone course. This study compares three populations, undergraduate seniors, engineering faculty, and practicing engineers, understanding of the significance of engineering solutions within a global context. Comparing the results from the three populations will provide insight into whether there are discernable differences between the group’s beliefs. Comparing the populations will also provide insight into whether ABET requirements are being met. The results from this study could be used to change how courses or programs are structured to help best prepare students professionally.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Effect of Tank Bottom Shapes on N js and Power Dissipation in Stirred Vessels Under Different Baffling Configurations
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Mechanically stirred mixing vessels are widely used in the chemical, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, food, and other related industries to homogenize the liquid content of the vessel and any phase dispersed in it, such as finely divided solid particles. The minimum agitation speed, N js , to just suspend finely divided solid particles in the liquid and the power, P , dissipated by the impeller in these systems are two of the most critical parameters for scaling up mixing processes from laboratory scale to industrial scale. In agitated vessels, the degree of solid suspension can be classified into three levels: on-bottom motion, complete off-bottom suspension, and uniform suspension. Enough agitation is important to completely suspend the solids off the vessel bottom. Below this needed agitation, the total surface area of the solid suspended within the liquid is not completely or efficiently utilized. Therefore, it is important to be able to determine the impeller agitation speed, denoted by N js , at which the just suspended state is achieved. Both N js and P (and its non-dimensional value P o) depend on several factors including type of impeller, its diameter, vessel geometry, and the dynamic conditions at which the mixing is operated (agitation speed). Although most correlations available in the literature for N js and P o were obtained at the laboratory scale using flat-bottom vessels, vessels with hemispherical or torispherical bottoms are much more commonly used in industrial applications. Until now, the effect of the shape of the vessel bottom on N js and P o has received little attention in the literature. Therefore, the main objective of this work was to experimentally determine N js and the power dissipation at these measured N js values for different tank bottom shapes using an axial-flow impeller (Lightnin A310). By using a method recently developed in the mixing lab at NJIT to measure N js , it was found that the hemispherical-bottomed tank dissipated about 15% more power than flat-bottomed tank when tested at the same agitation speed. Additionally, it was found that N js was higher in the hemispherical-bottomed tank than in the flat-bottomed tank. Therefore, the power dissipated in hemispherical bottomed to just suspend the particles was determined to be nearly 50% higher than that of the flat-bottomed system. The results obtained here can be expected to be of significant applicability to industrial systems, such as glass-lined vessels, typically used in the pharmaceutical industry.
