https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Increasing Chemical Engineering K-14 Involvement By Tackling Water Conservation Using Human-Centered Design
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: AIChE 2019 Chemical Engineering Division Increasing Chemical Engineering K-14 Involvement by Tackling Water Conservation using Human-Centered Design Anays Hernandez 1 and Sindia Rivera-Jiménez, Ph.D. 2 1 Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Florida and 2 Institute for Excellence in Engineering Education, University of Florida ABSTRACT How much water does the average person use at home per day? The U.S. Geological Survey reports that old showers may use up to 5 gallons of water per minute and water-saving shower heads produce about 2 gallons per minute. The agency recommends that taking a shorter shower using a low-flow showerhead saves lots of water. Even if an individual invests in a low-flow showerhead, they still need to figure for how long they are showering. A water consumption sensor that relatively anyone can install in their shower head can help to solve this problem. In addition, global market research reported that the environmental sensor market was valued at USD 1.22 billion in 2017 and is expected to reach USD 2.19 billion by 2023. The use of sensors in the K-14 classroom has shown to be of significant educational value because they can help address societies problems while integrating many disciplines such as chemistry, physics, mathematics, computer science, engineering, civics, among others. Exposure to the use of sensors to solve real problems can encourage students to follow career paths in Science Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM), particularly for underrepresented communities. The primary objective of this pilot project is to create a water consumption sensor that is easy to use, and cost-effective for the everyday individual. The integrated sensor system uses simple electrical equipment including photo-resistors, light sources, waterproof cabling, Legos, 3D printed parts, and Arduino. Ideally, this work will become an instructional module that can be used to increase the interest of K-14 students into the chemical engineering field by tackling environmental problems using a human-centered design approach where the needs and wants of the user are paramount for the designer.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Analytical Solution of the Heat Transfer Problem for Power Law Non-Newtonian Fluid
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Accurate predictions of velocity profiles for Non-Newtonian fluids has received considerable attention for about half a century. The specific rheology of these type fluids is well known has an impact on the concentration of species and the corresponding temperature profile in the bulk of the system when mass and/or heat transport occur. Significant research effort has been devoted to the analysis of kinematic viscosity and shear rate to characterize and model the deviation from the Newtonian postulate. However, Non-Newtonian behavior not only directly affects shear stress Newtonian viscosity but also transport of heat in its parameters, thermal diffusion and convective film coefficient. This contribution focuses on the analytical solution of the Energy and Navier-Stokes equations for the case of a Non-Newtonian behavior affecting the main transport physicochemical properties. The power law model, Ostwald-de Waele equation, has been adopted for the solution of the momentum equation. A similar power law expression has been use in the modeling and simulation of the energy equation. The solution strategy uses a similarity approach and the principle of recursion to obtain an explicit mathematical function. Furthermore, this study concentrates on the comparison of the numerical solution and the combined similarity-recursion solution to validate the accuracy of this last method and its predictions. A few different geometries have been chosen to further validate the approach and highlight its simplicity. Concluding remarks are presented to highlight the potential applications of this mathematical tool in the design of heat exchangers.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Investigation of Particle Noise Produced By Tip Sonication
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The tip sonication of nanoparticle solutions can create particulates in test tubes resulting in significant data misinterpretation and faulty results for researchers analyzing nanoparticles. The process of tip sonication is implemented by many researchers who work with nanoparticles to disperse particles. This method is fundamentally applied when nanoparticles are synthesized by nanoemulsion techniques. Low retention, plastic microcentrifuge tubes are typically implemented to store particles, however, previous research has discerned contamination following tip sonication in these tubes. The contamination generated by particulate noise from the tube potentially can result in major inaccuracies. We seek to optimize the process of sonication and reduce data misinterpretation through determining conditions which minimize the contamination particulate formation. In these experiments, ultrapure water is tip sonicated using a Qsonica sonicator and the resulting concentration of contamination particles is measured by nanoparticle tracking analysis. The conditions we have tested include brand of tube used, amplitude and process time. These all impact the concentration of particulate noise produced. Furthermore, several cleaning procedures on the tubes were tested to determine if debris in the tube was the source of the contamination. In addition, we have conducted experimentation to confirm that the particulates we are examining are not bubbles by measuring each sample twice following varying time gaps of ten, twenty and thirty minutes.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Carbon Monoxide in Electronic Cigarette Effluent
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The electronic cigarette market has an estimated market value of over $10 billion dollars (2018). While some e-cigarette users are former smokers trying to quit, many youth report e-cigarettes being their only source of nicotine. E-cigarettes are still relatively new devices and their design continues to evolve rapidly. There are many different types of electronic cigarettes on the market, ranging from miniature disposable electronic cigarettes to Advanced Personal Vaporizers (APVs). Some modern e-cigarettes offer customizable temperature/power levels as well. Research on the health effects of these devices is still emerging. However, e-cigarette effluent has been shown to contain formaldehyde, other aldehydes and ketones, other carbonyl compounds, reactive oxygen species and chloropropanols, volatile PAHs and aluminum. It has now been shown, using diode laser absorption spectroscopy, that e-cigarette effluent also contains carbon monoxide (CO). The concentration of CO produced varies as a function of the power of the e-cigarette and the flavor of the e-liquid heated. The CO concentrations ranged from 0 ppm to more than 180 ppm at a high power. CO is a well-known toxicant which when inhaled at high concentration over long periods can lead to death. Short duration exposures are not as well characterized but have shown deleterious health effects.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Effect of Gamma Irradiation on Antioxidant Activities of Molle ( Schinus molle ) and Guaviduca ( Piper carpunya ) Essential Oils.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Molle ( Schinus molle ) and guaviduca ( Piper carpunya ) are Ecuadorian endemic species traditionally used as medicinal plants since they have several biologically active components and they are even attributed culinary properties. In this research, the effect of a treatment with gamma radiation on the antioxidant capacity of molle and guaviduca essential oils was evaluated. The essential oils were extracted from dry leaves through hydro-distillation. The irradiation was carried out with a Cobalt-60 source in the raw materials or in the essential oils. The evaluated doses were 10, 15 and 20 kGy. The antioxidant capacity of the oils was determined with the ABTS radical cation and with the DPPH radical methods. In the Schinus molle essential oil irradiated with a dose of 20 kGy before the extraction, the antioxidant capacity increased from 7,71% to 11,07%, while in the Piper carpunya essential oil, the antioxidant activity decreased in all cases due to the irradiation. These results suggest that the ionizing radiations are able to modify the composition of essential oils and modify their properties.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Lower Extremity Flailing Motions in Response to a Hypothetical Rear-End Vehicular Impact
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Occasionally a victim of a rear-end car crash will experience a lower extremity injury (for example, a patella fracture). One mechanism that has been suggested for such injuries is the result of "flailing" motion (involuntary motions) of the lower extremities that may occur during the impulse phase of the rear end collision. To date, there has been no peer-reviewed literature that indicates that such flailing motions occur that can be causally related to any lower extremity injuries. The purpose of this study is to explore various combinations of driver body geometry (particularly lower extremity dimensions and angles), vehicular interior structure locations (particularly underneath the dash area, steering wheel, and other interior surfaces directly ahead of the driver, and seat positioning. Measurements will be made under two conditions: 1) normal driving position; and 2) after subjects rotate their legs upwards as a simulation of "flailing". First contact point and (if it occurs) 2nd contact points will be documented. Note that a rear end collision is not actually occurring, i.e., only a single stationary unpowered vehicle is employed.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Microbial Electrolysis Cell Bio-Degradation of Alkane Compounds
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Alkanes are simple carbon chain molecules that are used in the fuel industry to be combusted to utilize their stored energy. Alkanes are pumped at gas stations across the world for consumers to use, but a majority of gas stations have some amount of alkane contamination that occurs in the surrounding soil that pollutes the environment. In this study, we test a mixed culture of bacteria in a Microbial Electrolysis Cell (MEC) to bioremediate two alkanes, octane and decane, to produce a current to ensure there is activity. The MECs were 120 mL reactor vessels ran in duplicates that contained a graphite anode connected to a Titanium and a stainless steel mesh cathode connected to a 316 stainless steel wire. A voltage of .7 volts was applied to the MECs by a power source and the output voltage from the exoelectrogenic organisms was recorded by Kiethly recording software. We found that a current was produced when the microorganisms found in the soil obtained from a closed gas station near Raleigh that was assumed to have contaminated soil were fed alkanes. The 2 types of alkane reactors produced a current while the control reactor vessels containing acetate, a commonly oxidizable compound, produced no current alluding to the presence of exoelectrogenic microorganisms that could only oxidize alkanes being present in the contaminated soil. These results show promise for bioremediation of alkane polluted soil but it also gives possibility to the potential for co-metabolization to bioremediate other pollutant compounds with similar chemical structures.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: On-Site Extraction and Electrochemical Analysis of Heavy Metal Pollution in Soil, Plant, Air, and Water Samples
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Heavy metal pollution is a worldwide problem. Within the US these metals are leached into the environment from landfills and from the thousands of mines across numerous mountain ranges (e.g. such as in the infamous Gold King Mine Spill). It is crucial to be able to quantify and identify metals in water, soil, plant, and air to reduce exposures and inform remediation efforts. Currently, the metal testing process often takes days to weeks and requires an equipped laboratory with trained technicians. But imagine if there was a simple integrated device that could not only give you results in minutes but is able to be used on-site. Through a collaboration between Colorado State University and Access Sensor Technologies, we have created a system to do just that. Soil and air filter samples can be immediately placed in a solution capable of extracting metals. Once the extraction is done and adjusted to optimal conditions for the experiment, stripping voltammetry is performed to identify and quantify several different metals including lead and cadmium. In the past, electrochemical techniques have been limited because of the many interferences within the solution, leading to nonsensical results or masking the presence of the metals entirely. However, by modifying the extraction solution and holding at the correct pH we have found many of these interferences disappear, making stripping voltammetry practical for use not only in the lab but also out in the field, where we can determine concentrations down to single part per billion (ppb) levels.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Narcotics Consumption Trends at a Southwestern U.S. University Campus in 2018 Tracked By Wastewater-Based Epidemiology
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Current methods measuring the consumption of prescription and illicit drugs are often hampered by innate limitations, which can impact the relevance and robustness of the associated data. Here we applied wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) as a metric to measure trends in the consumption of twelve narcotics within a collegiate setting from January 2018 to May 2018 at a Southwestern U.S. university. Local legislation, put into place because of the opioid crisis, has decreased the number of opioid prescriptions in 2018 by 36% compared to 2016. We hypothesize that per-capita estimates of heroin and fentanyl (illicit alternatives) derived from campus-generated wastewater will be significantly higher (α = 0.05) from the previously sampled academic semester. An initial study, completed for the campus from August 2017 to December 2017 (Fall semester) identified consumption of select narcotics, in units of mg/day/1000 persons in the following order: cocaine (551 ± 49), heroin (474 ± 32), amphetamine (256 ±12), methylphenidate (236 ± 28), MDMA (88 ± 35), oxycodone (80 ± 6), methadone (72 ± 8), alprazolam (60 ± 2), codeine (50 ± 4), and morphine (18 ± 3). The present follow-up study was designed to identify potential changes in the consumption patterns of prescription and illicit drugs as the academic year progresses as well as the occurrence of narcotics not previously investigated at this location. Seven consecutive 24-hour composite raw wastewater samples were collected each month ( n = 70) from two sites that capture nearly 100% of campus-generated wastewater. Samples were extracted using a Dionex 280 AutoTrace solid phase extraction (SPE) system with Oasis Hydrophilic-Lipophilic Balance (HLB) SPE cartridges. Internal standards for target analytes were used to quantify losses during sample processing. Extracted samples were analyzed by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry for the following parent drugs and metabolites: alprazolam, amphetamine, buprenorphine, cocaine, codeine, fentanyl, heroin, MDMA, methadone, methylphenidate, morphine, and oxycodone. Chemical analyses are in progress for the January 2018-May 2018 samples. Forthcoming data will be shared immediately with public health officials to help address the health crisis and to showcase the use of WBE as a tool to directly measure the impact of an implemented public health intervention (i.e., opioid prescription reduction).

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Ultrasound-Assisted Post-Pyrolysis Magnetization of Biochar without Adsorption Reduction: Effective Removal of Heavy Metals
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Low cost and efficient adsorption of heavy metals from wastewater and thorough removal of adsorbent after water treatment has become the two essential needs. Hence, the main objective of a series of our studies is to develop an advanced acoustic-based method for activation of carbonaceous structures which can be effectively used for adsorption and easily removed from the aqueous solution. Biochar, the solid byproduct of pyrolysis with microporous carbonaceous structure, has been increasingly recognized as an efficient adsorbent for a vast number of pollutants. Magnetization, though eases the separation and reuse of biochar, significantly reduces its adsorption capacity to a comparatively much higher extent.. In this study, a hybrid post-pyrolysis modification was developed which sustained and even significantly increased the adsorption capacity of biochar. The process included i) structural modification of biochar under ultrasound waves, ii) magnetization with magnetite (Fe 3 O 4 ) nanoparticles and iii) functionalization with 3-aminopropyl triethoxysilane (APTES). Low frequency ultrasound irradiation exfoliates and breaks apart the irregular graphite layers of biochar, and creates new/opens the blocked micropores, thus enhancing the biochar’s porosity. On the other hand, APTES stabilizes the nanoparticles on the biochar surface, while it participates in water treatment. Preliminary results showed that acoustic-based magnetic biochar exhibited a much greater ability to remove Ni and Pb, with 124% and 31% higher adsorption compared to raw biochar. This high performance can be attributed to the synergistic effect of ultrasound activation on increasing the porosity and surface area of biochar and its further interaction with amine functionalization using APTES.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Rapid Photo-Catalytic Oxidation of Dissolved Manganese with TiO 2
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Manganese(III/IV) (hydr)oxides (hereafter Mn oxides) occur ubiquitously in terrestrial and marine systems, and play crucial roles in natural electron and element cycles. However, the understanding of their occurrence is limited due to the slow oxidation of Mn 2+ (aq) to Mn(IV) which precedes the formation of Mn oxides. Through the photocatalytic process with TiO 2 (the 9 th most abundant compound in the Earth’s crust), we found very fast oxidation of Mn 2+ (aq) to Mn(IV). The reaction rate is even much faster than microbial processes, which has been believed to be the primary mechanism for the oxidation. We studied the oxidation process under a variety of conditions, such as different TiO 2 structures (anatase vs rutile), different solvents (saltwater vs freshwater), and different atmospheric conditions (open air vs nitrogen). These analyses show that the fast photocatalytic oxidation occurs primarily due to direct electron transfer between Mn 2+ (aq) and photo-excited TiO 2 . This understanding will enable us to explain the abundance of natural Mn oxides on rock surfaces. In addition, because the redox process of Cr and Tl, which are newly emerging paleoredox proxie, is significantly governed by Mn oxides, understanding of Mn oxide formation will help to calibrate the redox proxy systems for oxygen evolution on early Earth.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: A Study of the Physical Properties of Plastic Derived Fuel Oil Produced from Waste Plastic
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Plastic waste around the globe has become a massively detrimental issue that can lead to health complications and destruction of the environment. Studies and prior experimentation suggest that thermally decomposing plastic will cause the carbon bonds to break apart and form a fuel oil similar in composition to diesel. Using a low-cost and simple processor called the Trash-to-Tank (3T) processor developed by the University of Kentucky Appropriate Technology and Sustainability (UKATS) Research Team, waste plastic can be converted into fuel, known as Plastic Derived Fuel Oil (PDFO) and sold as a diesel alternative. The 3T processor has been specifically designed to be appropriate for underdeveloped regions where access to sophisticated literature are often lacking. Currently, the UKATS Research Team is conducting a pilot study in Uganda to assess the performance of the 3T process. In order to ensure that the fuel meet all appropriate regulatory requirements for use as a motor vehicle fuel in Uganda, emissions testing has been commissioned from the Ugandan Bureau of Standards. The laboratory results for the PDFO will be presented and compared with traditional number 2 fuel oil. The 3T process has been implemented in Uganda and has the potential to provide a low cost way for rural communities in developing regions to take ownership of the waste plastic problem in their communities. This process is part of the establishment of locally managed decentralized circular economies in underdeveloped regions and further can give women and other people living in poorer regions the ability to become entrepreneurs.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Competitive Adsorption and Photocatalytic Degradation of Alizarin Red S and Bromocresol Green Anionic Dyes Using TiO 2 nanoparticles
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Water contamination is a widespread problem that jeopardizing life on earth. The fact that water is capable of dissolving many different substances makes it uniquely vulnerable to pollution. Many human activities are causing direct and indirect water pollution such as landfill, industrial runoff, leaks and spills, mining, etc. Therefore, major steps forward should be taken to treat those water bodies. Cutting edge nanotechnologies are currently invested in order to mitigate water contamination problems and provide environmentally sound solutions. Adsorption and photodegradation using photoactive nanomaterials are considered one of the states of technologies that are used in industrial water purification. This study evaluates the effective photodegradation properties of TiO 2 brookite nanoparticles for the removal of binary aqueous mixtures of the anionic dyes: Alizarin Red S (ARS) and Bromocresol green (BCG). Batch adsorption experiments were conducted to investigate the effect of dyes concentration, contact time, and temperature effect. The adsorption isotherms were fitted for the single adsorption using the models of Langmuir, Freundlich and Sips, while the binary adsorption isotherms were fitted using the Extended-Sips model. The photodegradation experiments for the adsorbed dyes were achieved using UV light irradiation (6 W, λ max = 312 and 365 nm). Overall, post-adsorption photodegradation preliminary results showed high selectivity towards ARS molecules in the presence of BCG molecules. In addition, the adsorption process was spontaneous in nature with endothermic behavior for both anionic dyes. The TiO 2 nanoparticles were successfully regenerated using UV irradiation. Moreover, molecular dynamic computational modeling was performed to understand the molecules optimum coordination, TiO 2 geometry, adsorption selectivity, and binary solution adsorption energies. The outcomes of this study will be showcased and discussed in detail.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Point of Entry Water Purification System in Quiché, Guatemala
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The design of a community-wide point of entry water purification system is presented. The system will provide water for up to 600 people in a rural May an community in the Department of Quiche, Guatemala. In the past year, a piping system was installed from a spring located 13 kilometers away. This system relies on gravity to provide water to the homes in the community. The large-scale purifier will be installed at the point of entry to a storage tank. It utilizes solar panels to power the unit and an ultra-violet photoreactor to purify the water and inactivate waterborne pathogens. The design considerations for the purification system included: volumetric flowrate through the system, prefiltration for sediment removal, photovoltaic and battery system for power, and the ability to stop water flow in case of photoreactor failure. The system is designed to exceed a 14 gallon per minute flow rate such that a need for a pump to overcome pressure drop is obviated. When designing the prefiltration, which is necessary for maximum sterilization through the photoreactor, pressure drop measurements were taken to designate which option would best fit the flowrate and pressure drop considerations. The photovoltaic and battery system was designed so that the purification system would be able to run without power from the solar panels for a day and a half. The worst-case scenario for the global horizontal irradiance for the Quiche, Guatemala location was used to calculate how many solar panels and what size battery would be required to do this. A solenoid valve was added to the design to stop the flow of water in case of photoreactor failure. A bypass valve was added prior to the unit, per the communities request, so water could continue to flow in the event of full unit failure. This project was designed and implemented in just under one year. Throughout the year-long journey, one goal was sought after; providing clean water to a developing and well-deserving community in Guatemala as clean water is a human right.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Multi-Modal Resins for the Adsorption of Nitroaromatics
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Legacy munition constituents (MCs) including nitroaromatic compounds (TNT, RDX, HMX), along with insensitive high explosives (IHE; NQ, DNAN, NTO), and their degradation products are hazardous molecules that could negatively impact environmental waterways if not removed from wastewater. Although there are remediation techniques in place, new generations of MCs and IHEs are not readily treated. Advanced oxidation processes, such as the Fenton reaction, have been utilized for treatment but are not cost-effective, especially in dilute concentrations, so new technologies are needed. In this work, we propose synthesizing porous, multimodal resins that utilize coulombic interactions, hydrophobic interactions, and hydrogen bonding to improve selectivity for nitroaromatics and overall adsorbent lifetime. Resins synthesized from the monomer glycidyl methacrylate are particularly attractive because they contain reactive epoxy groups which provide a tailorable surface chemistry. Resins are synthesized through suspension polymerization. Properties such as bead size, pore volume, and surface area were manipulated by changing variables such as polymerization temperature, agitation speed, crosslinker ratio, and presence of a porogen. We hypothesize that (1) macroporous resins will provide greater access to binding sites than nanoporous resins and (2) multimodal ligands will exhibit higher selectivity for nitroaromatics than traditional ion-exchange groups. To test the first hypothesis, porous resins are synthesized by including a cyclohexanol and tetradecanol mix in the suspension polymerization reaction. To test the second hypothesis, ligands with multiple modes of binding (i.e. varying degrees of hydrophobicity, H-bond donors, and polarity) were incorporated via epoxide ring opening reactions. Resin functionalization was monitored with Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) by collecting spectra before and after reaction. Resin capacity and binding affinity were studied through equilibrium batch adsorption tests with organic adsorbates phenol, pyridine, picolylamine and benzene. While these are not explosives, they represent adsorbates with varying propensity for H-bonding. Adsorbate concentration in solution is measured by ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy. This work can be extended beyond explosives, because understanding the role of molecular-level interactions in binding affinity will allow for the design of adsorbents that can capture other emerging organic contaminants.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Oxidation of Reactive Blue 4 through the Use of a Heterogeneous Fenton Catalyst
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Organic aqueous dyes are commonly found in the wastewater of textile companies. Unfortunately, the treatment of these chemicals tends to be complicated, due to their natural resistance to degradation, filtration, and centrifugation. For industrial use, it is important to develop a fast, reusable, and green method to treat and degrade these organic dyes. Therefore, we chose to make use of a Fenton catalytic pathway in the form of Fe 3+ ions. Loading these iron ions on a mesoporous structure, such as SBA-15, was explored to find a way to make the Fenton catalyst more reusable in industry. In other words, to turn a homogeneous catalyst into a heterogeneous catalyst. The heterogeneous catalyst will theoretically be able to retain more of the iron ions than the homogeneous ions after filtration, while still providing active sites for the Fenton pathway. It was found that the iron loaded SBA-15 worked better at oxidizing the reactive blue 4 dye, around 70% oxidation, than just the reagents without the catalyst; however, the experiments ran into complications when an unexpected product was formed within the reaction chamber. With this unexpected product in play, more research will be needed to increase the efficacy of the catalyst as it failed to match up to the homogeneous catalyst.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Study of How the Concentration of Ozone and α-Pinene Precursor Gasses Affect the Hygroscopicity of the Resultant Secondary Organic Aerosol Particles
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Cloud-related phenomena are the largest source of uncertainty in climate models. Thus, many researchers are investigating how various particles interact with water (their hygroscopicity) to form clouds in order to improve these climate models. While the interactions of some chemical species, specifically inorganic salts such as sodium chloride or ammonium sulfate, are well understood, other chemical species are less well understood. One class of particles, called secondary organic aerosols (SOA) which forms from the reactions of gasses in the atmosphere, fall into this class of poorly understood interactions. The reaction of alpha-pinene with ozone to form aerosol particles is a suitable model as both gases are abundant in the atmosphere. Alpha-pinene is a biogenic species that is emitted in by vegetation, while ozone, an inorganic molecule, has both natural and anthropogenic origins. Various methods have already been used by different research groups to investigate the hygroscopicity of the SOA model. However, due to a lack of standardized experimental set-up, comparing results is difficult. To relieve ambiguity, our research group established and used a standardized procedure to explore the effect of different initial concentrations of alpha-pinene and ozone on hygroscopicity.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Economic Analysis of Waste-to-Energy Technologies for Urban and Rural Areas
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The average amount of waste generated in the United States is 4.4 lbs/day/person, and the majority is landfilled. The energy contained in these wastes presents an opportunity for renewable energy production. Renewable energy production methods that are more environmentally friendly are needed. Therefore, it is crucial to implement waste to energy technologies to reduce landfilling and minimize environmental impact. Municipal Solid Waste can undergo processes like Anaerobic Digestion (AD), Incineration or Gasification to produce biogas or syngas. Harmful gases produced in landfill can also be used as an energy source. These gases can be upgraded to be used in energy recovery methods like combined heat and power units (CHP), Fischer-Tropsch Synthesis (FTS) for the production of liquid fuels, or the production of Compressed Natural Gas (CNG). All of these technologies are new and minimal data has been reported for their operation. A limitation encountered when trying to implement/build one of these plants is that there is no set tool that compiles the techno-economic and environmental data of existing plants and can provide fast cost estimation for the development of these projects. The goal of this research is to create a software tool based in Excel to assist decision makers such as municipalities and waste management companies. Using this tool, the user is able to select the technology desired: AD, Gasification or Landfilling, as well as the energy recovery method: CHP, liquid fuel or CNG production. The user will also provide the feedstock type (Municipal Solid Waste, Food Waste, Animal Manure, Farm Waste), feed properties and plant capacity. The software tool is set to provide the user with the capital and operational cost requirements and energy profits from the process. Additionally, Carbon balances, biogas production rate and its composition are calculated. The calculator also includes the cost of biogas purification based on the purity requirements for each energy recovery technique. The use of the tool is illustrated using a base case AD plant that generates biogas used to produce liquid fuels via FTS. The plant processes 60,000 dry tons/year of MSW with a 30% moisture content. Using the calculator, the capital cost of the entire system is $17.0 MM and the total operational expenses are $4.46 MM /year. The revenue from tipping fees and liquid fuel sales are $8.6 MM/year. The software tool provides the user with the ability to compare and contrast alternative waste-to-energy options and incentivize building these plants.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Performance Evaluation of Two Cost-Effective Particulate Matter Sensors Under Ambient and Controlled Conditions
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: NASA’s Multi-Angle Imager for Aerosols (MAIA) investigation is currently in development for the purpose of studying linkages between different types of airborne particulate matter (PM) and human health. The investigation requires the MAIA satellite instrument to be complemented by networks of surface PM monitors, and will focus on a selected set of major metropolitan areas around the world. In target areas with insufficient surface monitor coverage, the MAIA project will supplement existing reference-grade monitors with cost-effective sensors. To support this objective, we evaluated the performance of PurpleAir-II (PA) and Alphasense OPC-N3 (AS) optical particle counters (OPCs) against size-binned particle counts measured by GRIMM EDM 164, a transportable version of the EPA-approved GRIMM EDM 180, as well as a Differential Mobility Analyzer/Condensation Particle Counter (DMA/CPC). Experiments were performed in indoor and outdoor (i.e., ambient) environments with the PA, AS, and GRIMM, and under controlled laboratory conditions with DMA/CPC in addition to the 3 OPCs. The DMA allows for differentiation of particles based on size, and the CPC grows the particles to larger size for counting. For laboratory evaluations, narrow size distributions of NaCl particles were generated and an airtight aluminum chamber was used to isolate these particles from the external environment. In general, correlations between the low-cost sensors and the GRIMM were a function of particle size and concentration and were generally linear with varying slopes and offsets. In the outdoor environment, PA and AS consistently had R 2 >0.9 for PM 1 and PM 2.5 (particles below 1 µm and 2.5 µm in diameter respectively). PA demonstrated the highest R 2 for most of the PM and counts measurements. In the laboratory, high R 2 was observed in correlations of total counts between GRIMM and DMA/CPC, supporting the use of GRIMM as a reference for size-binned comparisons. For NaCl particles generated with a narrow size distribution (0.5 ± 0.1µm), the OPCs put most of the counts in the smallest size bin (0.3-0.5 µm), but some counts were misclassified to into larger bins. To our knowledge, this study is unique in comparing the response of multiple OPCs to aerosols with controlled narrow size distributions.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Destabilizing Nanosized Biochar
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Biochar has been widely developed as a low-cost and environmental-friendly carbon material for its application in energy, environment, and agriculture. Its applications are largely due to its physiochemical characteristics such as its outstanding porous structure, large surface area, and abundant functional groups which all contribute to its adsorption abilities of contaminants. Recently, a novel method, ball milling has been investigated to enhance the adsorption abilities of biochar in removing organic and inorganic pollutants from contaminated sources. As a new type of engineered biochar, ball-milled biochar (BMB) presents outstanding porous structure, larger surface area, and more abundant functional groups than pristine biochar. Due to its nanosized structure, however, BMB also displays increasing stability and suspension in aqueous environments, which hinders its separation in regard to regeneration and waste disposal. The goal of this research is to investigate to what extent conventional coagulation and flocculation methods could effectively destabilize BMB from aqueous solutions.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Conceptual Design of Glycol Recovery Method for the Treatment and Disposal of De-Icing Fluid Run-Off and Stormwater Management at Vancouver International Airport
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: During the winter months, Vancouver International Airport (YVR) performs de-icing operations during which aircrafts are sprayed with de-icing fluids containing ethylene glycol. The wastewater generated from this process contains ethylene glycol, a component of de-icing fluid, and consequently has a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD). This wastewater is harmful if it is released into the environment untreated, as high BOD levels reduce the dissolved oxygen (DO) levels and adversely affects the ecosystem. YVR currently implements a periodic offsite disposal system, in which the spent de-icing fluid is collected and sent to Annacis Island Wastewater Treatment plant for further treatment. In addition, the airport’s stormwater runoff periodically exceeds the Canadian Glycol guideline, which mandates that the glycol runoff must not exceed 100 mg/L. The purpose of this project is to present a conceptual design option for the treatment, transport, and disposal of de-icing fluid run-off and management of stormwater runoff. This project analyzes alternative options to YVR’s current waste management method of offsite disposal, with a focus on methods of recovering glycol from spent de-icing fluid. The solution meets environmental regulations, current and future capacity until the year 2050, and manages stormwater run-off outside of de-icing periods. The effects of climate change, airport expansion plans, and flow and loads are taken into to account. A thorough economic study is performed to ensure that the solution is a feasible alternative to YVR’s current operations. The system that is determined to be the most optimal path forward consists of recovering the spent de-icing fluid onsite by utilizing an electric heater and mechanical vapor recompression system, as well as selling the recovered product to a third-party glycol supplier.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Study of the Degradation of Chlorinated Pesticides Atrazine and 2,4-D By Continuous System Ozonation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Atrazine and 2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic Acid (2,4-D) are chlorinated pesticides used for weed control in corn and sugarcane crops; Its presence in water can cause an environmental problem and damage to human health. In Ecuador, the presence of these compounds or their treatment in wastewater has not been investigated, but it is known that the treatments are not specific for their degradation, because these molecules are relatively stable. The project included the study of treatment of synthetic effluents containing atrazine and 2,4-D, through advanced oxidation processes. A continuous ozonification reactor was designed and built with a longitudinal diffuser consisting of two concentric cylinders. The outer cylinder of PVC, 8 mm in diameter and 200 cm in length will be divided into four sections of 50 cm by means of valves for the collection of samples. The ozone diffusion system consists on a silicone cylinder with a diameter equal to 4 mm, with holes of 0.5 mm in diameter to bubble the ozone along the reactor. The effluent entered the reactor with a peristaltic pump and ozone was supplied at rate of 0.84 mg/s through a “PHILAQUA” ozone generator. Atrazine solutions 1.53x10-4 M (33.0 mg / L) and 2.4 D 1.53x10-4 M (33.8 mg / L) were prepared, which were treated in “Batch” and continuous system at different pH values. In continuous system, degradation of atrazine equal to 53.8% was reached at pH 11, and 77.3% of degraded value was mineralized. 250 mL of Atrazine solution were treated in the "Batch" system, in 285.7 s it was affected by the same degradation as in the continuous system and 240.86 mg of Ozone was used. In the continuous system a degradation of 2,4-D equal to 54.4% is detected at pH 11, and 45% of degraded value was mineralized. 250 mL of 2,4-D solution were treated in the "Batch" system and in 424.33 s it was affected by the same degradation as in the continuous system and 357.7 mg of ozone was used. Therefore, continuous system was 2.28 times more efficient than "Batch" system for the treatment of Atrazine and 3.38 times more efficient for the treatment of 2,4-D.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Vancouver International Airport (YVR) airside operations de-ice aircraft during winter and utilize an offsite disposal system to manage the spent de-icing fluid and storm-water runoff. The aircraft de-icing fluid (ADF) contains ethylene glycol which is collected on the de-icing pad and conveyed to a ten million litre lagoon and is then transported to the Annacis Island Wastewater Treatment Plant for further treatment. Without being adequately treated, the de-icing fluid and storm-water run-off result in wastewater being generated with a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and is toxic if released into the environment. The purpose of this project is to design and analyze biological treatment as an alternative to offsite disposal of the ADF and present the treatment, conveyance and disposal of fluid and present an economic and environmental justification to support the implementation of the solution. The design process involves examining several biological treatment options to meet design constraints of not interfering with airside operations, maximizing the use of existing assets when possible, not attracting wildlife and can be built within the confines of the airside boundaries. A hydraulic feasibility study, life cycle analysis and economic study are conducted to determine the most ideal and viable option. The biological treatment chosen and designed is an artificially aerated engineered wetland system which can withstand current and future capacity until the year 2050, meets all municipal provincial and federal regulatory requirements and can store storm-water runoff outside the de-icing periods.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Ionic Strength Effects on Flocculation Performance in Taylor-Couette Flow
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The removal of flocs, which are aggregates consisting of solid particulate, from source water is an essential part of the drinking water treatment process. To improve flocculation, salt can be added to increase the solution ionic strength. This creates a charge screening effect, which allows for aggregation of particulate. However, increasing the salt concentration would increase the load on reverse osmosis filters down the line, which is cost prohibitive. The addition of long-chained, charged polymer flocculants makes the flocculation possible without need for excess salt. Flocculation in a treatment tank is subject to a variety of hydrodynamic flow states, and isolating how they affect flocculation is difficult. A Taylor-Couette (TC) cell, which consists of two concentric cylinders where the gap between the cylinders can be filled with fluid, can generate precisely defined flow states at specific rotational speeds. The Dutcher group has built a TC cell with radial injection capabilities from the inner cylinder, therefore flocculation can be captured via image analysis from the start of the process. This TC cell will be used to study how different concentrations of NaCl impact flow dynamics and floc size, growth rate, and configuration.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Proper characterization of atmospheric brown carbon (BrC), its formation, and its absorbance effects are critical to understating the aggregate effect that these materials have on overall aerosol climate forcing. Since a vast of chromophoric compounds can be produced from a single dicarbonyl/ammonium pairs, it is impractical to identify every specific chromophoric species that comprises an aerosol's overall absorbance spectrum as a reaction system ages. Therefore, we present an alternative method of representing UV-visible absorbance spectra as a composite of multiple, dynamic spectral line shapes. Previous work demonstrated that a model with four fitted Gaussian curves with magnitude following first-order kinetics achieves accuracy within 66% in the 200-350 nm range to track the absorbance behavior of single carbonyl/ammonium reaction systems (methylglyoxal and glyoxal) with different reagents concentrations and aging times. This research aims to verify the validity of this model on a complex carbonyl mixture (methylglyoxal and glyoxal)/ammonium reaction system. Absorbance data for varying concentrations of methylglyoxal and glyoxal in ammonium sulfate solutions were measured and modeled. Results were compared to the model gained by directly adding up the model of individual reaction systems. Residual analysis indicated that instead of fix at 220 nm, the peak of one of curve was within the range of 215 to 220 nm. Finally, a new peak was formed at around 225 to 230 nm. Therefore, a new Gaussian curve and the interaction parameters were added to track the result of the interaction between methylglyoxal and glyoxal.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The ability to detect and specify trace concentrations of uranium in groundwater is crucial to addressing public health concerns associated with uranium in groundwater and restoring adversely impacted lands. Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) detection of trace concentrations of uranium on polymer mats has been previously reported using amidoximated-polyacrylonitrile (AO-PAN) mats and carboxylated gold nanostars, but a reproducible method of determining uranyl species in aqueous solution is still needed. In this project, we seek to utilize Aliquat 336 polyacrylonitrile (Alq-PAN) mats to isolate the original uranyl species from solution, followed by separation analysis at trace concentrations based on unique vibrational frequencies in SERS spectra with gold nanostars. To observe how efficiently Alq-PAN mats isolate and uptake negatively-charged uranyl species, we varied the uranyl-to-oxalate concentration ratios (5:50, 5:100, 5:300) of the aqueous solution and incubated Alq-PAN mats within the aqueous solution. We hypothesize that increasing the number of oxalate ligands, or increasing the uranyl-to-oxalate concentration ratio, will increase the number of negatively-charged uranyl-oxalate species in solution, thus promoting uranyl uptake and SERS detection. Understanding the interaction between Aliquat and uranyl-oxalate complexes will allow us to extend the speciation analysis to other aqueous samples with different negatively-charged uranyl species, such as uranyl-carbonate or uranyl-phosphate.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Water is one of the world’s most valued commodities, and antibiotic-resistant bacteria are one of the emerging pollutants of concern. The aim of this project is to test the use of biochar columns as an effective and inexpensive form of stormwater treatment. Biochar is biomass that has undergone pyrolysis. It serves as an adsorbent for contaminants in water including antibiotic - resistant bacteria. It is commonly used in land applications as a soil amendment, but there are concerns as to how long biochar is effective and what occurs once the biochar is saturated. Three infiltration columns will be tested; one containing biochar, one with soil and biochar mixed in a ratio typically seen in a soil amendment, and one with soil. Using culture-based methods, E. coli in the synthetic stormwater will be quantified before and after treatment through columns in triplicates. The ability of the columns to both remove and retain an adequate concentration of E. coli will be analyzed to determine the best step for future use of biochar.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Open Borehole Cross-Contamination: A Unique Opportunity to Evaluate Natural Attenuation of Mixed Organic Contaminants in a Sedimentary Rock Aquifer System
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: At a site in Wisconsin, organic chemicals were released into the subsurface resulting in the formation of a persistent, dense non-aqueous phase liquid (DNAPL) source between 46 and 55 m below ground surface (bgs) in a fractured sandstone. Since 2003, researchers have applied various hydrogeological measurement and modeling techniques to characterize the flow system, contaminant mass, and phase distributions. In July 2017, three holes were continuously cored to 100 m bgs, downgradient of the source zone (MP-23D, MP-24D, and MP-25D). The cores were geologically logged and sampled (about 5 per 1.5 m) for contaminant analyses by removing a puck from the core, crushing it in a hydraulic press, and placing about 15 g of the rock into a pre-prepared vial of high purity methanol for contaminant extraction. The rock core results quantify the total (i.e., dissolved, sorbed, NAPL) contaminant mass in the rock matrix pore space. Then the coreholes were logged using geophysical and hydrophysical methods in the open and FLUTe™ sealed boreholes. Prior to multilevel system (MLS) installation, the holes were sealed with FLUTe™ liners unless open hole measurements were being made. Each borehole was instrumented with high resolution (20 monitoring intervals over 40 m) Westbay® MLS in November 2017 and used to sample groundwater in June 2018 and 2019. These MLS samples represent the water and contaminant mass in the fractures. The rock core was expected to have high, quantifiable results through 55 m bgs. Therefore, permanent casings were set at 60 m bgs before proceeding with coring. The rock core data showed consistent, high concentrations through 62 m bgs and sporadic quantifiable concentrations separated by non-detects were identified to 83 m bgs. In contrast, high, quantifiable concentrations were observed from 60–98 m bgs in groundwater samples from all three MLS. The discrepancy between the rock core and MLS groundwater data suggests the boreholes became cross-connected during open hole conditions. Repeat groundwater sampling in the MLSs show concentration declines in the deepest portion of all three holes and drastic compositional changes for all MP-25D ports. The cross contamination of these boreholes provides an opportunity to study natural attenuation of these chemicals in a sedimentary rock aquifer system with baseline conditions obtained from rock core VOC data. Future work will consist of comparing the depth discrete groundwater concentration trends to hydrophysical data quantifying active flow regions in each hole and analyzing mechanisms and rates of the natural attenuation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The goal of this research is to observe the effects of surface energy on the attachment of algae with specialized attachment mechanisms to substrata in stationary environments and small, controlled flow environments. Reactor channels were 3D-printed from PLA filament and a standard glass microscope slide and pressed PLA were used as the substrates for attachment. The algae species in focus for this experiment are two types of filamentous green algae, Oedogonium and Stigeoclonium. Oedogonium is known to have root-like structures, called holdfasts, and mucilage basal pads as a specialized attachment mechanism. Stigeoclonium is a freshwater algae that has a specialized “star-like” attachment mechanism that is known as basal rhizoids. In nature, multiple algae types grow together on rocks and surfaces, but the factors affecting algal attachment are not fully understood. Different types of algae are preferred for different commercial applications, such as pollutant removal, nutrient supplements, and biofuel production. The economic viability of algae cultivation could be improved if the details governing algal attachment were better understood.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Historical mining practices have contributed to long term environmental impacts to soil and water and may pose a risk to public health if not managed appropriately. The focus of this study is to phytoremediate soil and water with elevated levels of radionuclides, including radium and uranium, at a legacy uranium mine in northern New Mexico. Uranium present is undergoing radioactive decay, producing radium as one of decay products at levels that require remediation before the land can be returned to other uses. Part of a proposed closed-loop system to remediate the water and soil affected involves using plants to remove uranium and radium from the soil. Here, greenhouse studies are being conducted to determine which plants are most effective for uptake of the heavy metals. In the first greenhouse study (summer 2019), spring canola (Brassica napus var. L140), safflower (Carthamus tinctorius var PI544006), guar (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba var. Kinman), carinata (Brassica carinata0, confectionary sunflower (Helianthus annus var. Red River 2215), and several native grass species were germinated and placed in pots containing contaminated soil collected from the legacy mine site. Of these plants, the confectionary sunflower, guar, spring canola, and carinata grew sufficient biomass for analysis. One challenge noted was the heavy texture of the soil, which limited root penetration of the transplanted seedlings into the contaminated soil and which affected plant-available water. Soil properties, and nutrient and metal levels, were measured using inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), gamma spectroscopy, and liquid scintillation counting before transplanting and after harvest. For the second greenhouse study (winter 2019-2020), winter canola (Brassica napus) and hemp (Cannabis sativa) will be added to the studied species, a new contaminated soil sample with lighter texture will be used in the pots, and plants will be directly seeded. Special attention will be paid to the soil moisture content. Results from the greenhouse studies will be used to inform design of an on-site study at the legacy mine site.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Environmental Fate and Transformation of Dichloroacetamide Herbicide Safeners
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Dichloroacetamide safeners are a class of agrochemicals co-applied in large scale with chloroacetamide herbicides to protect crops from herbicide toxicity. Although all four dichloroacetamide species have been detected in Midwestern surface waters, safeners are currently regulated as “inert” constituents under the U.S Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act, and as such, have received meager attention in the peer-reviewed literature. Recent studies suggest that some dichloroacetamide safeners are reactive in aquatic systems and can yield products with increased bioactivity which may pose risks to human and environmental health. To evaluate the fate and transformation of dichloroacetamide safeners, we measured timescales (i.e. half-lives, sorption rates) for predicting safener persistence, determined the effects of water chemistry (i.e. pH, DOC) on the rate and extent of hydrolysis and sorption processes, and quantified sorption parameters for active herbicide co-formulants and mixtures. We found that most dichloroacetamide safeners undergo both acid-catalyzed and base-catalyzed hydrolysis, and we identified two hydrolysis products for benoxacor, the most widely-used dichloroacetamide safener. Sorption studies revealed limited uptake of safeners and herbicide co-formulants, with more sorption to soil with a high organic carbon content. In general, dichloroacetamide safeners demonstrated reduced uptake onto soil compared to their chloroacetamide herbicide co-formulants.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Exploration of the Efficiency of Surfactant Extraction from High Internal Phase Emulsions
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Clean water and clean air filtration are essential for environmental sustainability, in which there is a need to provide efficient ways to process both fluids to help communities have healthy lifestyles. One component that can improve the filtration is the use of foams. Foams are porous substances that have a combination of a continuous phase and an internal (or dispersed) phase. Pores of the foams consist of the dispersed phase of the foam formed in conjunction with surfactants. Surfactants are substances that lower surface tension between two immiscible phases, which results in a more stable interface between both phases. In more general applications, surfactants are used in conventional products such as soaps and detergents, in which the surfactants help with filtering any unwanted chemicals and compounds. In the emulsification process, the surfactant gets mixed in with the high internal phase emulsions and gets washed off using soxhlet extraction. However, there has not been any studies on the quantity of surfactant that is washed off. This is an issue due to the fact that surfactants will contain unwanted contaminants in which will cause toxicity in water quality. In this project, we investigated the process of polymerization of a water/monomer system, more specifically the step of washing the surfactant off. This step of the process is essential because, in most applications, the surfactant is washed off to decrease in the possibility of contaminates still present and can cause impure products. The parameters that will be tested are (1) how long does it take to wash out the surfactant, (2) what solvent works best to wash out the surfactant as well as to analyze what surfactant we are using (for this experiment we will be using Polysorbate 80, Polysorbate 20, Span 20, and Span 80), and (3) how can we quantify how well the surfactant is washed off. UV-visible spectrometry was in this experiment as it can analyze the absorbance of a solution with light. With this and Beer-Lambert’s law, which states that the absorbance of the compound is directly proportional to the concentration of the solution, we can produce conclusions on the washing off of surfactants and how we can manipulate the step to efficiently provide filtration mechanisms. The resolution before and after the wash of the surfactant can easily be measured and help understand the parameters of this part of the process related to emulsion-based polymerization.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Leachates from spent ore piles and mine tailings, and small particles moved by the wind, have enriched uranium and its decay products (radium) in the soil and water near legacy uranium mines in northern New Mexico. Evaluation of the phytoremediation efforts requires quantification of uranium, radium, and other metals in the water, soil, and produced biomass. Given the low concentrations of the metals and the occasionally small sample sizes, quantification involves multiple strategies. Plants are partitioned into roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and (oil)seeds. Each part is analyzed to help understand the movement and aggregation of radionuclides in plants. The overarching goal is to be able to produce fuels from the plant material that remains uncontaminated while reducing waste volume and preventing further spread of contamination. The analytical techniques being considered are inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) for heavy metals and higher levels of uranium; high-resolution, dual channel ICP mass spectroscopy (ICP-MS) for low metal concentrations and radium; gamma spectroscopy, and liquid scintillation counting. Most of these analyses require multi-step sample preparation including drying, ashing, acid digestion, filtering, ion exchange chromatography fractionation, and spiking with standards. Here, we present preliminary results about phytoremediation efficiency and the potential for value-added use of the produced biomass.

All cultures are grown in photobioreactors that are irradiated using fiber optics simulated sunlight (initially earth irradiation is tested then simulated Mars sun-irradiated will be tested using specialized lamps). The overall process flow diagram, theory of conversion, simulated yields, and initial results will be presented in the poster.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The international community faces an imminent global phosphorus crisis. When switched to anaerobic conditions, PAOs will then release phosphate and obtain energy through the cleavage of polyphosphate. The Gu Research Group in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Cornell University partnered with the Cornell Biological Field Station to examine the presence and abundance of polyphosphate and PAOs in Oneida Lake. Further experiments, such as colorimetric analysis, ion chromatography, and NMR, need to be conducted to confirm the absolute concentration of polyphosphate in the sediment samples. The findings from this study can benefit the search for PAOs to mitigate the global phosphorus crisis.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Scale-up of Moringa Coated Sand Filters
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Clean drinking water is a global issue, affecting more than 844 million people around the world. The proposed project is to scale-up and redesign a Moringa seed coated sand filter to remove bacteria from wastewater with locally accessible and affordable materials. Moringa seeds contain a cationic protein that can create electrostatic forces between negatively charged microbes, removing the pathogens present in the water. For the purpose of this study, the lab-scale glass columns used for the filters were replaced by PVC pipes, using a binary mixture of collector size and increasing the column diameter and flow rate according to the Clean Bed Filtration Model to obtain the EPA standard approved removal. To prove the functionality of the filters, fluorescent E. coli bacteria was first utilized to quantify the experimental removal. It was then noted that when treating water spiked with E. coli and TOC, the organic matter (TOC) competes with the bacteria for protein sites, impeding the proper removal. To address this problem, an activated carbon pre-filter was implemented. The results showed that, when this pre-filter is applied, the TOC sticks to the activated carbon particles, allowing the f-sand filter to function properly and remove bacteria above the EPA standard approved removal.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Phosphate Adsorption Using Nitrogen Doped Biochar from Egg Shells and Egg Carton Feedstock
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The project discusses the potential use of biochars produced from waste for phosphate(P) removal. Different series of biochar were produced from different ratios of eggshells and egg cartons to find the optimal ratio of eggshells to egg carton for the adsorption of phosphates. The biochars were produced through pyrolysis of feedstock under a nitrogen gas atmosphere at 750 C. In order to characterize the biochar, the samples were analyzed using TGA, BET surface analysis, CHN, FTIR and pH. Elemental and proximate analysis showed that eggshells have a high concentration of ashes and nitrogen. The pyrolysis decreased the carbon content in the 1:1 shell to carton biochar but increased the nitrogen content. The best variation of biochar produced was an eggshell biochar under nitrogen at 750 C and had a peak adsorption capacity of around 955 mg PO 4 /g of biochar. This was promoted by the basicity of the solution which was measured to be 12. The eggshells promoted chemical adsorption through precipitation. Langmuir isotherms were fitted to all data sets but only ratios with equal or more carton fit the isotherm. The BET analysis showed increased surface area in samples produced from higher levels of egg carton. The mixture of 1:3 shell to carton had a surface area of 241.24 m 2 / g and the eggshell alone had a surface area of 12.82m 2 / g. Eggshell samples had smaller surface area but high adsorption capacity due to presence of Calcium (Ca) that allowed for the formation Ca-P crystals. This project shows that eggshells could be applied as a source of calcium to produce biochar with high phosphate adsorption capacity.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Microbial EPS Impact on Residual Water Saturation in Emulated Soil Micromodels
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Microbial communities are an integral part of soil environmental conditions. Within soil, bacteria contribute to moisture retention by secreting extracellular polysaccharides (EPS). EPS helps regulate moisture retention by reducing water evaporation, in turn promoting plant growth. EPS mitigates water loss at pore-scale by (i) acting as a hydrogel, which will swell during wet conditions and retain moisture in dry conditions, (ii) promoting soil aggregation, resulting in porous microstructures that increase the interparticle capillary forces, and (iii) altering soil surface properties such as hydrophobicity. Studies on moisture retention at bulk scale have few chances to uncover these intricate interactions among microbes, soil and solution systematically. Here, we employed an emulated soil micromodel to examine the mechanisms of moisture retention on EPS collected from Sinorhizobium meliloti cultures and compared them to the drying effects of deionized water, dilute glucose solution, and artificial groundwater (AGW). The results showed that EPS reduce the evaporation rate and promoted residual saturation at equilibrium compared with AGW and DI water within identical physical geometry. Dilute EPS (0.006%) in AGW solution had an average residual saturation of 2.8 ± 2.94% after 16 hours drying. Comparatively, deionized water reached 0% residual saturation after 6 hours drying, artificial groundwater reached 1.6 ± 3.19% saturation after 6.5 hours, and dilute glucose in AGW solution (0.006%) reached 3.6 ± 3.61% saturation after 8 hours. In this study, we confirmed the effect of EPS on moisture retention at pore-scale and provide a platform to understand microbial-mediated moisture retention. Ultimately, we hope this work to aid in implementing sustainable agriculture leading to increased food production and less water usage.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: E. coli Removal in Moringa-Coated Sand Using Binary Mixtures
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Providing access to clean water is one of the 14 grand challenges on engineering. 1 billion people do not have access to clean drinking water more than 4,000 children under the age of five die daily due to diarrhea diseases linked to drinking unclean water. This study offers moringa oleifera seed coated sand solution as an option for sustainable water treatment. The moringa seed is readily available in countries that need safe drinking water the most. One tree produces 15,000 seeds in one year and the seeds contains 1% cationic protein allowing it to act as a coating for sand. The charge on the seed attracts to the sand, reversing the charge of the sand surface. Coating very fine sand (106 micron) with moringa seeds removes 100% of E. coli from our lab-scale columns and satisfies the EPA standard. However, the removal decreases significantly with larger sand size and the limited access to this size sand defeats the purpose of our solution. One solution is to mix this small sand with practical sieved sand to produce binary mixtures. Our hypothesis was that this mixture will provide the same hydraulic conductivity and bacterial removal. Our experiments confirmed this hypothesis. The hydraulic conductivity experiments showed that binary mixtures of 40% sieved sand and higher should behave the same as the successful 100% 106-micron columns. The E. coli removal experiments proved this hypothesis correct, showing binary mixtures of 40% and higher have similar removal as 100% 106-micron sand. The next steps in this project include scaling up the column containing the binary mixtures, and using activated carbon to remove organic matter in real water.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Modulation of Cationic Nanocarrier Properties for Penetration of Blood-Brain-Tumor Barrier and Glioblastoma Treatment
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme is a Grade IV malignant invasive tumor of the central nervous system that has a 3-5% 2 year survival rate. Treatment is made difficult by the inability of chemotherapeutics to effectively penetrate the blood-brain-tumor-barrier (BBTB), a highly selective interface that only allows the intercapillary transport of small (50-100 nm), lipophilic molecules; these properties are not present in modern chemotherapeutics. Previous research in the Peppas lab has produced pH-responsive polymeric nanocarriers capable of drug complexation and targeted therapeutic delivery. To apply these nanocarriers to glioblastoma treatment, their sizes and surface charges must be controlled at the synthesis stage to fit the required parameters. The purpose of this experiment was to optimize the synthesis of these nanoparticles for glioblastoma treatment applications. The nanoparticles were synthesized using emulsion polymerization via ARGET ATRP synthesis, a technique that allows for control over chain length and small amounts of catalyst. The organic monomers were emulsified with crosslinker, surfactants, and ATRP reagents and reduced in an oxygen-free environment. They were then purified through centrifuging and their size/charge properties were characterized through DLS and zeta potential techniques, respectively. Varying experimental factors affected the properties of the nanoparticles. It was found that increased initiator and reducing agent concentrations resulted in a loss of swelling capabilities but increased surfactant concentration led to smaller nanoparticles. The results indicate successful synthesis of the desired nanoparticles, but further experimentation is required to confirm the properties, chemical composition, and reproducibility of these particles as well as their potential as therapeutic agents.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Elucidating Metabolism of E. coli double Knockout Strains
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Determining the metabolic effects of gene knockouts in workhorse microorganisms such as Escherichia coli is an important topic for metabolic engineering since it allows for the elucidation of kinetic limitations within those organisms that are essential to understand when designing them in industrial contexts. Most studies in the past have focused on strains with single gene knockouts; this project extends this analysis to double knockouts, which are significant since they allow for the restriction of fluxes to one of the three glycolytic pathways present in E. coli and the complete elimination of reactions catalyzed by multiple isozymes. In this study, adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) was performed on Δ pgi Δ gnd , Δ pgi Δ edd , and Δ rpiA Δ rpiB double knockouts for around 1 month to maximize their growth rates on minimal medium with glucose. At the end of this time, they were grown with 13 C-containing glucose tracers, their amino acids and carbohydrates were collected and analyzed with GC-MS, and the isotopic labelling implied by the GC-MS data was used to reconstruct metabolic fluxes using the Metran metabolic flux analysis software. A comparison was made between the glucose uptake-normalized and absolute fluxes of the Δ pgi Δ edd strain. Future work will include continuing this ALE for a longer time period and with more sets of gene knockouts, as well as sequencing the genomes of the evolved cells to determine which mutations allow them to grow faster.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Synthesis and Characterization of Poly(hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (PHEMA) Hydrogels for Drug Delivery Applications
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Nanoparticle based drugs offer immense possibilities as a next-generation medical technology, but currently lack a nontoxic, reliable method of targeted delivery. Due to its biocompatible nature, flexible cross-linked structure, and numerous accessible hydrogen bonding sites, PHEMA hydrogels may be viable candidates as encapsulating materials for targeted nanodrug delivery. The primary objectives of this study are the systemic synthesis of PHEMA hydrogels via radical polymerization of and the multimodal materials characterization of PHEMA hydrogels. Material and structural properties of the PHEMA hydrogels were evaluated using scanning electron microscopy, fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, and ultraviolet visible spectroscopy. The influence of pH on hydrogel swelling behavior over a period of 48 hours was investigated in this study. To verify its efficacy as a targeted drug-delivery agent, PHEMA hydrogel’s overall retention and release of iron oxide nanoparticles was measured through dynamic light scattering and ultraviolet visible spectroscopy. The results of this study will be highly significant in the design of higher-efficacy vehicles for targeted drug delivery.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Depolymerization of Polyethylene Terephthalate Plastics By Ozonolysis
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is the most abundant of the seven categories of recycled plastics due to its affordability and desirable chemical properties for use in diverse applications such as the ubiquitous containers and synthetic fibers. The improper disposal of plastics contributes to environmental pollution adversely affecting nearly all types of ecosystems. Beyond washing and reusing consumer plastics, chemical or tertiary recycling breaks plastics down into constituent monomers which may be transformed to make new consumer products. However, such techniques are still in the research and development stages. Herein, we investigate a new method that attempts to break down PET using ozone (a powerful oxidant that is also used in water purification and deconstruction lignin, a naturally occurring biopolymer) to decompose the polymers into smaller molecules for reuse. To perform ozonolysis, a solvent that dissolves PET and is itself inert to ozone is essential. Among various solvents [acetic acid, tetrahydrofuran (THF) and trifluoroacetic acid (TFA)] in preliminary studies, TFA demonstrates high PET solubility as well as compatibility with ozone. Bubbling ozone (9.4 mole% in O 2 ) through such a PET solution produces several smaller molecules including terephtalic acid (TPA) as inferred by NMR spectroscopy. These initial results are promising as TPA is a starting material for producing PET plastic. They provide guidance for future research towards making chemical recycling practically viable, thereby improving environmental sustainability.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: KRAS Digital PCR Screening Optimization for the Detection of KRAS Mutations in CTCs and Exosomes in Patients with Pancreatic Cancer
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and exosomes can be identified in the peripheral blood of patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), and can inform cancer diagnosis and treatment effect, thus avoiding an invasive primary tumor biopsy. CTCs are rare cells shed from a tumor and into the blood stream, increasing the risk of metastasis. Exosomes are secreted extracellular vesicles that carry proteins and RNA. For this investigation, samples from patients with PDAC were processed using the Labyrinth, a high-throughput microfluidic CTC isolation device, and exosomes were obtained through ultracentrifugation. After isolation, we used digital PCR (dPCR) to screen the CTCs and exosomes for the presence of KRAS mutations, which occur in >90% of PDAC primary tumors. dPCR is an ultrasensitive technique enabling single molecule detection, critical in low input samples. Here, we present the optimization and validation of a KRAS mutation detection assay for CTCs and exosomes, which simultaneously screens for the 7 most frequent clinically detected mutations in the G12/G13 region of the KRAS gene. We compared master mixes (Bio-Rad Supermix vs TaqMan Genotyping), varied concentrations of KRAS screening assay primers and probes, tested lower concentrations of cell spike samples to mimic patient samples, and did a comparative analysis of the assay’s effectiveness in CTCs and exosomes. We also report our initial findings in patient samples. Preferred results include a combination and balance of high levels of amplification as well as detectable separation between wild type (WT), mutation, and empty PCR reaction droplets. Ultimately, this assay could be used to screen high risk patients for development of PDAC and improve cancer care.
