https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Determining Pharmaceutical Powder Wettability
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In this work different methodologies that are used to measure the wettability of powders are studied in detail. It has been recognized that the different manufacturing process would significantly change the wetting behavior of material. In addition, the wetting properties of raw and intermediate material directly affect the dissolution performance and bioavailability. For this reason, the characterization of wetting properties is inevitable for quality control in advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing. Several techniques have been developed to identify wettability of powders. These include the sessile droplet, capillary rise, immersion and condensation methods. The sessile drop method (i.e. drop penetration method) is the most common method. In this method a single liquid droplet is released to a powder bed and the contact angle of the liquid is then measured on the powder bed. This method is the easiest to replicate, but it is also very sensitive to powder bed condition. For instance, air may get trapped inside the powder bed. The capillary rise method is a layer of powder and the fluid is pushed up through it. In the immersion method the powder bed is placed under the liquid and the phase interaction between the solid and liquid is observed. In the condensation method the resting drops on the surface are analyzed. Another frequently used technique is the capillary rise method. Here, the powder will be packed into a tube and the test fluid can interact with the powder by moving up the tube. Sources of error in this method are the possible movement of the tube during testing as well as the inability that occurs due to use of non-Newtonian liquids or liquids with contact angles over 90°. The immersion method involves taking the powder and submerging it into a pool of test fluid, while the condensation method involves making the test fluid into a saturated vapor and having the vapor condense into droplets on the powders surface for analysis. The immersion method can be difficult to replicate because the adhesive that is used to adhere the powder to the solid may lead to a wrong perimeter of the particle being recorded, that would lead to an incorrect conclusion. It is also likely that due to the liquid imbibition, the reported contact angle would be too small. Both immersion and condensation are harder to replicate and for that reason less commonly used when testing the wettability of a powder.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Aggregation of Gold Nanoparticles and Virus Complexes with Osmolytes
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Detection of viruses is difficult because they are some of the smallest microorganisms in the world. Typical virus detection techniques utilize expensive reagents and require highly-trained personnel. One alternative method to detecting viruses is through use of citrate capped gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) and osmolytes. When in the presence of osmolytes, viruses and AuNP complexes will aggregate due to hydrophobic interactions, increasing the hydrodynamic diameter of the AuNPs. Size changes can be detected using methods of dynamic light scattering (DLS) and a red shift in ultra violet visual spectroscopy (UV-Vis). The research conducted consists of multiple trials using 15 nm AuNPs to detect the behavior of aggregation with two model viruses. AuNPs were synthesized by reducing gold (III) chloride trihydrate using trisodium citrate. The size of the synthesized AuNP was confirmed using dynamic light scattering (DLS), which measures size and UV-Vis absorbance, which measures the absorbance of light. Next, the virus was purified via dialysis with 1000 kDa dialysis tubing in 4.3 mM pH 7.2 phosphate buffer (PB) and size exclusion chromatography. Once purified, a 1:10 dilution was performed to obtain 5 different concentrations of virus. Additionally, 1 nM and 1 μM bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 4.3 mM PB alone were used as controls to show that only virus-AuNPs complexes were aggregated by osmolytes. AuNPs were coated by rotating for 20 hours. Once coated, a benchmark measurement was taken before aggregation with osmolytes and salt. To aggregate, the coated samples were spun down, the supernatant was removed and the samples were resuspended in 1 mL of 1 M glycine, mannitol, or sodium chloride. Finally, the aggregated samples were measured using UV-Vis and DLS. Two viruses were used to test the ability of AuNPs to detect virus. It was hypothesized that a 1:1 ratio of AuNP diameter to virus diameter would provide the best results because it would be easier for similarly sized particles to interact with each other’s geometries. Different concentrations of porcine parvovirus (PPV), diameter 18-26 nm, with 15 nm AuNP complexes showed conclusive aggregation when 1 M mannitol was added. Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV), diameter 40-60 nm, and 15 nm AuNP complexes showed concentration dependent aggregation with 1 M mannitol as well. The data provides evidence that the use of osmolytes to induce aggregation of AuNP and virus complexes shows promise as a simple, inexpensive virus detection method.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Elucidation of the Ochratoxin A Biosynthetic Pathway via Heterologous Expression in Aspergillus nidulans
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Ochratoxin A (OTA) is a secondary metabolite produced by the Penicillium and Aspergillus fungi genera. OTA is a food toxin that has been shown in previous studies to be carcinogenic, immunotoxic, and genotoxic, and has been found to be produced under shipping conditions in cereals and fruits. Consensus biosynthetic pathways have been found in Aspergillus carbonarius , but biosynthetic pathways in other species have not been verified. The current biosynthetic pathway utilizes polyketide synthase (PKS), non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS), Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases and halogenase enzymes to synthesize OTA. We first verify the biosynthetic pathway of OTA via heterologous expression in Aspergillus nidulans . Our experiments yield the OTA intermediates 7-carboxymellein and 7-methylmellein via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), indicating that the proposed biosynthetic pathway failed to yield ochratoxin B at the peptide sythetase step. The absence of phenylalanine ethyl ester indicates either the failure of phenylalanine to esterify properly or the absence of non-ribosomal peptide synthetase for lack of transcription factors to activate the gene encoding NRPS. Transcription factors were found in Aspergillus carbonarius and OTA was heterologously expressed again in Aspergillus nidulans. Future directions include investigation of the possibility of hybrid PKS-NRPS genes in OTA production. Furthermore, characterization of the domains of PKS and NRPS can elucidate the mechanisms by which the 7-methylmellein and ochratoxin B is formed, respectively. Upon elucidation of these mechanisms, possibilities of gene regulation via gene therapy or similar approaches can be used to mediate OTA production in food production and transport.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Development of RNAi Tools for Gene Knockdown in Rhodosporidium toruloides August Finke 1 , Anne M. Ruffing 1 , James Kirby 2 , and John M. Gladden 2 Bioenergy and Defense Technologies, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM Biomass Science and Conversion Technologies, Sandia National Laboratories, Emeryville, CA Rhodosporidium toruloides is a yeast used to produce biofuels due to its fast growth, high lipid production, and ability to use different carbon sources for growth. The bisabolene and GFP knockdown exhibited a positive correlation, showing that the RNAi successfully knocked down the whole mRNA that coded for the GFP-bisabolene fusion gene. This RNAi technique can be applied to knockdown genes that would improve biofuel production in R. toruloides . https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Selective Precipitation of Haptoglobin from Human Plasma Fraction IV
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Haptoglobin (Hp) is the serum protein responsible for scavenging cell-free hemoglobin (Hb), the oxygen storage and transport protein of red blood cells (RBCs). During states of hemolysis, such as extensive blood transfusion, sickle-cell anemia, or Malaria, cell-free Hb is released from RBCs into the blood stream. Cell-free Hb is toxic and can lead to tissue oxidation and hypertension. Yet, when cell-free Hb is bound to Hp, these toxic effects are inhibited, making Hp a promising therapeutic for treating states of hemolysis 1 . Unfortunately, Hp is difficult to produce and expensive. Fortunately, Hp is present within Fraction IV (F-IV), a byproduct of the Cohn process used for purification of human serum albumin 2 . However, F-IV contains various additional serum proteins and insoluble material. This study sought to determine the optimal concentration of ammonium sulfate [(NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 ] to isolate Hp from F-IV via selective protein precipitation. Increasing amounts of (NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 were added to 100 F-IV suspensions, creating solutions ranging from 0%─70% saturation of (NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 . The resulting mixtures were centrifuged and the amount of Hp and total protein in the pellet suspension and supernatant were quantified. Total protein was quantified via the Bradford assay. Hp was quantified by reducing samples with known excess of Hb and using the spectrophotometric difference between the deoxygenated Hb-Hp complex and deoxygenated Hb to determine the Hb binding capacity (HbBC) 3 . Initially, samples had a total protein concentration and HbBC of and , respectively. Increasing amounts of (NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 led to a linear decrease of the total protein. At 40% (NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 saturation, 70% of total protein remained in solution and more than 90% Hp with HbBC was also present. Increasing saturation to 50% lowered the HbBC in the solution to 2.1% and lowered total protein concentration to 50.7% in solution. Overall, the optimal concentrations for selective precipitation of Hp with (NH 4­ ) 2 SO 4 was determined to be 50% which separated half of the starting proteins in solution. Furthermore, after resuspension of precipitated Hp, bringing the solution back to 40% saturation could further remove unwanted proteins with minimal 4 . The results of this study will aid further downstream purification of Hp.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Using CRISPR Cas13a to Combat the Flu Virus at the Genetic Level: A New Approach to Flu Treatment
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The influenza vaccine normally provides protection from three to four strains included in the formulation. However, since the flu viruses constantly mutate, the vaccine protection decreases because it can only protect against strains included in the vaccine but not the new ones. As a result, it needs to be reformulated each year to accommodate the new strains. The vaccine is also unable to protect against pandemic strains. As a treatment approach, antiviral medications can be administered to infected patients, but often the strains are resistant to the drugs. The long-term objective of this research is to develop a new flu medication that uses CRISPR technology to target the viral genome. Highly conserved sequences in the genome are targeted by Cas13a proteins using specially designed CRISPR RNA (crRNA). Cas13a is highly selective through the use of the crRNA, which attaches to the complementary sequence in the virus genome and designates the location the Cas13a protein should cut. As a result, the flu RNA will be cut, thereby preventing viral replication, hence treating the infection. Since the crRNA targets the highly conserved regions of influenza viruses, the treatment is expected to be broadly effective against different viral strains.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Comparison of Keit Irmadillo™ and Mettler Toledo Reactir for Pharmaceutical Process Chemistry Reaction Monitoring
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In-situ attenuated total internal reflection fourier transform mid-infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) with the ATR probe placed in the reaction vessel is a well-established technique for monitoring pharmaceutical process chemistry reactions that can reveal reaction component concentration trends, such as starting material consumption, product formation, and reaction intermediates if present. The Keit IRmadillo™ is a relatively new ATR-IR spectrometer that is being marketed as a rugged instrument for monitoring reactions in liquids and slurries and is certified for use in hazardous and potentially explosive industrial environments. The Mettler Toledo ReactIR 702L is another new ATR-FTIR instrument marketed for chemical reaction monitoring, but is a more compact unit primarily intended for use in research and development laboratories. This poster compares the IRmadillo and ReactIR 702L with the Mettler Toledo ReactIR iC10, an older ATR-FTIR instrument used extensively at GlaxoSmithKline. A major operational difference between instruments is that the ReactIR iC10 requires liquid nitrogen to cool the detector, whereas the IRmadillo and ReactIR 702L do not, which enables them to start more quickly and to run unattended indefinitely, important advantages for both lab and plant operation. However, the corresponding higher detector temperatures used by the IRmadillo and the ReactIR 702L are also expected to decrease the instrument sensitivity and increase noise, which could negatively impact reaction monitoring performance. Results from monitoring two example reactions will be presented. The first example compared all three instruments using a pharmaceutical intermediate compound manufacturing process where the slurry reaction endpoint time can vary based on certain process parameters. To compensate for this uncertainty, ATR-FTIR is used to track the reaction intermediate concentration and determine the appropriate timepoint to sample the reaction for endpoint confirmation by HPLC analysis. The second example used the well-known homogeneous solution reaction of acetic anhydride with methanol to further evaluate the IRmadillo and ReactIR iC10 instrument sensitivity, ability to detect transient reaction species, and performance with high concentration components.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Fundamental Analysis of Aqueous Humor Dynamics in the Human Eye
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Fluid mechanics is an essential part in numerous aspects of the composition and pathology of the human eye. In particular, glaucoma, a condition caused by an increased amount of intraocular pressure, is heavily dependent on the proper flow and drainage of aqueous humor in the eye. Currently, the most popular approach to impeding the disease is through numerous types of surgeries, such as laser or incisional surgery, which reduces intraocular pressure by creating a pathway to the Schlemm’s Canal. However, minimal research has been done to improve the drugs administered to glaucoma patients nor the proficiency of the drugs being delivered to the trabecular meshwork, for example. A fundamental analysis has the potential to aid in a better comprehension of the velocity and concentration profile in the human eye to improve in the administering of drugs and validate the effectiveness of surgery on patients without damaging other functional aspects in the eye. In this contribution, the focus is on the analysis of the mathematical models used to solve fundamental differential equations describing the velocity and concentration profile in the human eye. The Navier-Stokes equation is solved using a creeping flow assumption to obtain velocity profiles within the trabecular meshwork. The resulting velocity has been coupled with the corresponding molar species continuity equation to obtain drug concentration profiles in the same local area. A summary of these findings will be provided with significant insight on improved drug treatment and the effectiveness of surgery to glaucoma patients.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: With the imminent needs of a rapid, accurate, simple point-of-care system for global healthcare industry, electrochemical biosensors have been widely developed owing to its cost-effectiveness and simple instrumentation. However, typical electrochemical biosensors for direct analysis of proteins in human biological sample still suffer from complex biosensor fabrication, lack of general method, limited sensitivity, and matrix caused biofouling effect. To resolve these challenges, we developed a general electrochemical sensing strategy based on a steric hindrance effect on an antibody surface layer. This strategy utilizes the interaction pattern of Protein-G and immunoglobulin G (Fc and Fab regions), providing steric hindrance effect during target capturing process. The provided steric hindrance effect minimizes matrix effect caused fouling surface and altered the path of electron transfer, delivering a non-fouling and high-sensitivity detection of protein in complex matrix. Also, an enzyme based horseradish peroxidase/hydroquinone/H2O2 transduction system can also be applied to the system, demonstrating the versatility of this sensing strategy for general electrochemical sensor application. We demonstrated this platform through the detection of Tau protein and programming death ligand 1 with a sub-pico molar detection limit within 10 min, satisfying the clinical point-of-care requirements for rapid turnaround time and ultra-sensitivity.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Optimization of the Chocolate Process Using Rheology.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The science behind why some chocolates are more appealing than others is based on the optimization of the entire chocolate-making/production process. This process involves cocoa nib processing, mixing, refining, tempering and molding. Proper parameters, such as conch/melanger timing, seed chocolate and temperature, will affect the final taste. Since the appeal of chocolate is based on the chocolate’s balance of viscous and elastic behavior, comparing physical properties evaluated from rheological studies can determine the optimal procedures. The Casson model is commonly used to model food dispersions and is commonly used in chocolate manufacturing. The Casson parameters, Casson yield stress and Casson plastic viscosity, define the characteristic chocolate texture and flavor. The Casson yield stress is the minimum stress required to initiate the flow and marks the transition from the solid viscoelastic stage to the liquid stage. The Casson plastic viscosity is the resistance to flow. These parameters are identified by fitting the Casson Model parameters to the steady state flow curve. Chocolate is a complex multiphase material and the transition from a solid to liquid depends on its evolving, stress dependent microstructure. In this study, more contemporary thixo-elastic-visco-plastic (TEVP) rheological models are compared to the traditional steady state Casson model. The TEVP models fit steady and transient data, with a yield stress and plastic viscosity parameters to be compared to the Casson parameters. This research highlights the tempering and refining of the United States Military Academy chocolate making process. Chocolate tempering and refining techniques are studied to determine the impact on the chocolate’s complex behavior, yielding optimal rheological parameters. First, the tempering process was analyzed by varying the seed chocolate. The viscosity of each chocolate sample was then tested using a rheometer to collect the flow curve data. Then the refining process was analyzed by varying the length of time the chocolate remained in the melanger. Again, each chocolate sample was tested using the rheometer to determine the samples’ viscosity/elasticity. Finally, the rheological parameters using the Casson model and other contemporary TEVP models were identified by fitting the models to the experimental data and then comparing to the results of a blind taste test. Models will be compared by ability to predict large amplitude oscillatory shear flow.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Development of an Osteochondral Implant Using Microencapsulated Mesenchymal Stem Cells
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Osteoarthritis remains a poorly treatable outcome of traumatic cartilage injury as cartilage is unable to self-repair. Transplantation of an engineered, osteochondral tissue plug has been proposed as a better way to achieve repair of cartilage defects with implants that can readily integrate with the subchondral bone. Composite materials composed of chitosan and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) have been shown to support rapid invasion and integration with host tissues post-implantation and are a promising platform for assembling such an osteochondral implant. In this study we explored the use of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) within glycosaminoglycan-chitosan capsules as a platform for generating spherical cartilage and bone tissue “modules” for use in assembling an osteochondral construct. Rat bmMSCs were suspended (1×10 7 cells/ml) in a solution of 1.5 wt% carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), 4 wt% chondroitin 4-sulfate (CS), and 1 mg/ml collagen type I. The suspension was then electrosprayed to generate uniform droplets that were captured into a stirred and grounded chitosan solution (0.6 wt%). Electrostatic interactions between negatively charged GAGs and positively charged chitosan results in the formation of hollow microcapsules (300-500 µm in diameter) entrapping MSCs at high density. The encapsulated MSCs were cultured under static conditions in either osteogenic or chondrogenic induction medium for either 28 days (osteogenic) or 42 days (chondrogenic). Between 28 and 42 days osteogenically induced capsules were maintained in MSC growth medium. Capsule cultures were sampled at intervals and analyzed to evaluate cell/biomaterial morphology, DNA content, and extracellular matrix composition. After loose capsule culture, osteogenic and chondrogenic capsules were used to generate osteochondral constructs as follows. Cultured capsules were first briefly washed with 0.1 wt% chitosan followed by a wash with 0.1 wt% glycidyl-methacrylated polygalacturonic acid (GMA-PGA) to deposit a photocrosslinkable polyelectrolyte film. A transparent cylindrical mold was then loaded with a 4 mm layer of coated osteogenic capsules followed by a 4 mm layer of coated chondrogenic capsules. The mold was then immersed in PBS and capsule fusion was induced by photocrosslinking with 400 nM light using LAP as the photoinitiator. The fused constructs were then cultured for an additional 15 days in MSC growth medium. Results to date demonstrated the feasibility of the culture, coating and photocrosslinking method of osteochondral assembly using long-term cultured GAG-chitosan capsules. In addition, GMA-PGA was found to be an efficient, photocrosslinkable surface coating for generating fused capsule constructs.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Microfluidic Synthesis and Purification of Protein Nanoparticles
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: MICROFLUIDIC SYNTHESIS AND PURIFICATION OF PROTEIN NANOPARTICLES Nanoparticles have revolutionized the field of colloidal science and have been applied for a myriad of purposes in medicine, coatings, and even electronics. Many such applications, especially in medicine, necessitate precise control over parameters including size, polydispersity, and chemical content. Protein nanoparticle systems, like Abraxane®, are successful drug carriers due to their biocompatibility and biodegradability. However, nanoparticle synthesis procedures are limited in their scalability due to the critical interplay between particle size and solution conditions. Furthermore, medical applications necessitate the removal of trace chemicals and cytotoxic impurities – a challenge for nanoparticle suspensions. Here we present a scalable microfluidic process that addresses the need for high-throughput continuous production of homogenous, size-tunable, purified protein nanoparticles . Our platform takes advantage of laminar flow to enable the reproducible synthesis of monodisperse protein nanoparticles. Nanoparticle synthesis occurs via protein desolvation and controlled aggregation in the presence of ethanol, followed by cross-linking with glutaraldehyde. Laminar flow facilitates the precise control over protein, solvent, and cross-linker concentrations within the device, allowing for tuning of nanoparticle size. We validated the efficacy of our platform with the synthesis of bovine serum albumin (BSA) nanoparticles. Our results contrast with reports on the bench-scale synthesis of the ~50 nm BSA nanoparticles necessary to avoid an immun e response. Such efforts have traditionally suffered from increased polydispersity. The particles produced by our platform demonstrate superior stability and size tunability. Our system provides a 33% reduction of required solvent, and an 80% reduction of crosslinking agent compared to benchtop BSA nanoparticle synthesis. Furthermore, our platform can produce 16.2 mg/hr of crosslinked protein nanoparticles, compared with 11.3 mg/hr for benchtop synthesis. Purification is also an important challenge in nanoparticle synthesis because the removal of small molecule cytotoxic impurities typically requires time-intensive centrifugation processes. The H-filter in our platform enables purification of nanoparticles in a continuous manner by exploiting differences in diffusion times between small molecules and nanoparticles. Therefore, our platform can remove excess solvent and crosslinker, eliminating additional purification steps. The present process introduces significant improvements to current protein nanoparticle synthesis processes, potentially enabling new applications in drug delivery . The approach is general and future work includes extrapolation into a plethora of other protein and polymer-based nanoparticle systems. Additionally, the planar chip design allows for the process to be easily scaled-out for a variety of academic and industrial applications.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Screening Powder and Binder Combinations for 3D Printing Personalized Medication
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Screening Powder and Binder Combinations for 3D Printing Personalized Medication Leila Sorrells 1,2 , Shing-Yun Chang 2 , Kavin Kowsari 2 , Karthik Nagapudi 3 , Koyel Sen 2 , Bodhi sattwa Chaudhuri 2 , Anson Ma 2 1 University of South Florida; 2 University of Connecticut; 3 Genentech, Inc. Binder jetting printing is a form of 3D printing that has recently become the preferred additive method for creation of drug tablets due to its precise printing and control of drug release. It operates using inkjet print heads and a moving print bed where prints are created by repeatedly layering a powder, binding the powder with fluid, and rolling another layer of powder on top. This research focuses on using disintegration and hardness testing to determine the best combinations of powders and binders to use as a matrix for holding an active drug component for 3D printing drug tablets. Eight polymer-based binders were tested against fifteen powder mixtures created from varying concentrations of lactose monohydrate (LM), calcium sulfate hemihydrate (CSH), and sodium croscarmellose (SC). The goal was to find a combination or combinations that would reach a hardness of roughly 15 kgf and a disintegration time less than 15 minutes in 36 °C water. For all binder types, increasing CSH percentage leads to an increase in hardness. However, the binder that consistently created samples that best aligned with the hardness and disintegration goals was Kollidon, which can be introduced in the powder or in the liquid form as an aqueous solution. Samples prepared from the same percentage of Kollidon, regardless of the method of introduction, have similar properties.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Investigating Health Effects of Aerosol Particles on Single-Cells in a High-Throughput Air-Liquid Interface Platform
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Air pollution and its detrimental health effects have been an increasingly alarming concern for the world. Cardiovascular diseases, chronic respiratory diseases, and different types of cancers can all be linked to air pollution effects. Furthermore, over 8.9 million people die per year from the direct effects of ambient particulate matter. One conventional method for studying the health effects of aerosol particles is to collect particulate matter (PM) from the atmosphere, resuspend the PM in cell culture media, add the PM/media to cell cultures, and assess single cell oxidative stress. However, this method does not resemble the in vivo conditions of alveolar macrophages. Alveolar macrophages are found in the alveoli of the lungs where the oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange between blood and air takes place and are a key cell type that is affected by PM. In this project, we aim to create a microfluidic air-liquid interface environment that mimics how alveolar macrophages are exposed to PM in order to study effects of PM at a single-cell level. Utilizing a microfluidic platform provides uniform microenvironment and enables high-throughput and high content single-cell analysis for hundreds of cells. We adapted a previously developed microfluidic single-cell analysis technology and developed a method for exposing cells to an air-liquid interface. We then characterized cells by microscopy and LIVE/DEAD staining to assess if cells remain viable during air exposure. Following this validation of the air-liquid interface platform, we will use it to study the single cell responses of intracellular reactive oxygen species in exposure to aerosol particles.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Wnt family members play an important role in many developmental processes in humans and other animals, they also have been linked to tumorigenesis. A gene named WISP1(Wnt inducting signaling pathway1), is a member of this family, it's expression is increased in melanoma(a deadly type of skin cancer) and is associated with reduced overall survival of patients diagnosed with primary melanoma. The goal is to find the role WISP1 plays in melanoma metastasis. Zebrafish was the model selected for this purpose,because they have melanocytes that can become malignant and develop melanoma through specific mutations. Zebrafish also have two homologs of the gene WISP1 in their genome. Here, we knocked down each homolog of WISP1 separately in wildtype zebrafish, using MOs (Morpholino oligonucleotides) and compared their phenotype to other control groups to understand what role WISP1 plays in Zebrafish morphology and then perform a dose control experiment to ensure that the resulting phenotype is a result of the knockdown, and not any other off-target effects. Results so far indicate that knockdown groups exhibit a distinguishable phenotype compared to control groups. After determining the ideal dose to knockdown the gene of interest, we would then incorporate the hWISP1 gene in the minicoopr,introduce this modified plasmid in Casper zebrafish and test for changes in melanoma development. The minicoopr plasmid would rescue melanocytes via re-expression of mitf while introducing specific mutations that will promote melanoma development

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Non-Standard Amino Acid Incorporation in Proteins for Biofilm Surface Attachment
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Biofilms are consortiums of microbes in which cells stick together or on a surface embedded within a slimy extracellular matrix composed of extracellular polymeric substances mainly polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and DNA. The biofilms formed on living or non-living surfaces prevalent in hospital settings are generally by pathogenic microorganisms such as Staphylococcus spp, Escherichia coli, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa leading to numerous health infections. Microbes form biofilm in response to various factors, which include nutritional cues, or in some cases, by exposure of planktonic cells to sub- inhibitory concentrations of antibiotics. A cell switches to the biofilm mode of growth undergoes a phenotypic shift in behavior in which large suites of genes are differentially regulated and gradually develop resistance to conventional anti-microbial drugs. Therefore, in this study we are exploring the interaction of probiotic and pathogenic bacterial species to make a monolayer probiotic biofilm on any surface to prevent pathogenic biofilm attachment and formation. Usage of probiotic bacteria might lead to a possible alternative solution for inhibiting and killing pathogenic microorganisms rather than developing a new array of antibiotics.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Multi-Epitopic Down-Regulating Antibodies for Cancer Immunotherapy
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: CD8 + effector T cells are the cytotoxic force of the immune system, and their activity is carefully regulated by signaling through their cell surface receptors. The signals delivered through these receptors can be either stimulatory or suppressive; in particular, activation of immunosuppressive proteins on the T cell surface (known as immune checkpoint receptors) dampens T cell activity and leads to exhaustion or anergy. Tumor cells have evolved to exploit this immunosuppressive pathway to evade clearance by the immune system, contributing to cancer progression. To circumvent this issue, antibody drugs have been developed against immune checkpoint proteins to competitively block their activation, allowing for efficient anti-cancer T cell activity. Although this approach has demonstrated clinical success, the majority of patients do not respond to treatment, and most responses are only partial. We aim to improve upon immune checkpoint blockade by engineering novel therapeutics that act through alternative mechanisms. To do this, we engineered bispecific antibodies that simultaneously bind to 2 non-competitive epitopes on the same immune checkpoint protein (termed multi-epitopic antibodies). This design is advantageous because in addition to blocking ligand binding, the bispecific antibody can induce cross-linking of adjacent receptors to induce receptor down-regulation. We used the yeast surface display directed evolution platform and magnetic- and fluorescence-activated cell sorting to isolate novel antibodies targeting immune checkpoint proteins, which were then used as the basis for formulating multi-epitopic antibodies. Preliminary results indicate that these engineered antibodies efficiently down-regulate immune checkpoint receptors, presenting a promising new approach for cancer immunotherapy.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Elucidating Protein Remodeling Mechanism By Molecular Chaperones
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: HtpG is a molecular chaperone protein found in Escherichia coli . This protein belongs to a family of ATP-dependent molecular chaperones and couples conformational changes from ATP hydrolysis to protein remodeling; HtpG assists other proteins in reaching their native conformation, preventing aggregation, and mediating targeted unfolding and disassembly. In this study mutants of HtpG defective in ATP binding or substrate binding were constructed. HtpG mutants E34A and W467R were made by site directed mutagenesis. HtpG wild type and mutant proteins were overexpressed in E. coli, collected, and purified using Fast Protein Liquid Chromatography. The purified proteins were tested for ATPase activity, stimulation of ATPase activity by substrate proteins, and prevention of aggregation assays. Both mutants studied, HtpG E34A and W467R, were defective in chaperone activity and prevention of aggregation. Comparing these mutants with their wild-type form, they exhibited decreased rates of ATP hydrolysis and were not stimulated by model substrate proteins such as rhodanese and citrate synthase. Also, in the prevention of aggregation assay using urea- denatured Rhodanese, HtpG wild-type and ATP and substrate defective mutants were unable to prevent aggregation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Examining Siglec Signaling in Alzheimer’s Disease
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is a form of accelerated neurodegeneration and the most common form of dementia. There are currently few therapeutic options for AD patients, but the immune inflammatory response presents a potential therapeutic target once there is understanding of the underlying cellular signaling networks. We aimed to see if we could identify new targets in the immune system using an untargeted approach to signaling analysis. Using mass spectrometry to evaluate changes in protein phosphorylation of multiple mouse models of AD compared to aged matched controls, we have identified a Siglec signaling receptor that is activated on disease-associated microglial cells. We developed an expression system in BV2 cells with the wild type Siglec-F receptor, as well as inactive receptors where one or both cytoplasmic tyrosine residues have been mutated to phenylalanine. We assayed apoptosis to determine if altering functional tyrosine residues of these receptors will impact cell death and found that cells expressing wild type Siglec-F undergo significantly more apoptosis compared to those with mutated sites. We then treated BV2 cells with SHP099, an inhibitor of inflammatory transcription changes, to identify SHP-2-dependent and -independent signaling networks. This analysis identified other signaling proteins that could potentially be targeted to inhibit apoptosis. From these results, we see a potential to dissect signaling pathways activated by Siglec-F and target distinct phenotypic responses for inhibition. This approach could create a new avenue of therapeutic development for neuroinflammatory diseases.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Oral Delivery of GLP-1 for the Treatment of Diabetes
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Diabetes is a tremendous health epidemic; it is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, affecting more than 30 million Americans [1]. The vast majority of cases are Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) which is characterized by insulin resistance and high blood sugar levels that can cause severe damage to the eyes, nerves, and organs, as well as increase the risk of cardiovascular disease [1]. A promising treatment for T2D utilizes incretin glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), which serves to enhance and promote insulin secretion while decreasing glucagon secretion by the pancreas [2]. Currently available treatments deliver GLP-1 via subcutaneous injections, which present complications including patient noncompliance, injection pain, and needle phobia [3]. Therefore, development of an oral delivery method would improve patient compliance and offer a safer, easier way to deliver drugs, improving outcomes and quality of life. We are developing a novel technique for oral delivery of GLP-1 using PLGA-PEG nanoparticles as a delivery device to remove the barriers caused by daily injections. The major challenges in administering oral therapeutics are protecting the drug against degradation in the harsh environment and fluctuating pH levels throughout the gastrointestinal tract, while facilitating drug delivery across the intestinal epithelial barrier layer. In this research, we synthesized and optimized the formulation of PLGA-PEG nanoparticles, then encapsulated GLP-1 in PLGA-PEG using a water-in-oil-in-water double emulsion. We characterized the size distribution of the GLP-1 loaded nanoparticles using Dynamic Light Scattering and tested the encapsulation efficiency and drug loading capacity using High Performance Liquid Chromatography. A Caco-2 epithelial cell monolayer was used to perform nanoparticle transport experiments. Transepithelial/transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) was performed to characterize the cell seeding density and optimize the monolayer’s readiness for the transport experiments. Nanoparticles were conjugated with fluorescence and permeability through the cell monolayer was tested. Based on these results, we will move forward with conjugating IgG antibodies onto the nanoparticles to facilitate transport across the intestinal epithelium. References: Type 2 Diabetes . https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Extraction of Biologically Produced Indigo Dyes
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Indigo is a chemical that is used to dye clothing such as Levi Blue Jeans. The original method to produce dyes was extracting dyes from plants. However, this method took more than two weeks to ferment making it inefficient when the blue jean industry became popular. The current methods for producing clothing dyes are synthetic processes containing toxic and harmful steps. In order to reduce the health and environmental hazards, a biologically produced dye is being investigated as an alternative. In a previous study, it was found that a mutation in the enzyme, toluene ortho-monoxygenase, (TOM) of the bacteria Burkholderia cepacia would cause a change in color in rich media. The mutation A113V in the TOM enzyme results in the production of indigo. Using E. coli TG1, extraction and reduction methods are being investigated to develop a process for the production of indigo for use as a clothing dye. E. coli TG1 is grown for 48 hours with Isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) added at the 24-hour mark. The IPTG activates the production of indigo. Once cells are grown, the cells are pelleted and frozen to rupture the cells walls. Currently, chloroform is being used, but different solvents are being investigated for indigo extraction. Other solvents being studied include dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), tetrahydrofuran, and transcutol. Testing various solvents will help determine a chemical that decreases health and environmental hazards. After extraction, the dye is insoluble in water and must be converted into the leuco-form by a reduction mechanism. The leuco-form is water soluble and will adhere to the clothing. The current industrial method uses sodium dithionite which cannot be recycled, so other methods are being investigated such as biological and electrochemical methods. After the clothing is dyed, air oxidation converts the dye back to its original form, fixing it in the clothing.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Development of a Microfluidic Device to Study Cell-to-Cell Communication By Dynamic Sampling of Paracrine Factors
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer related death in American women. Cancer cells signal to surrounding tumor stroma to produce cancer associated adipocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages while secreted factors from stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment induce drug resistant and metastasis in cancer cells. Co-culture and conditioned media-based experiments have demonstrated that paracrine factors induce drug resistance. While multiple co-culture techniques exist, no of them are capable of dynamic sampling of extracellular media during an experiment to investigate cell-to-cell communications. To address this, a novel microfluidic device was designed, fabricated, and tested to study intercellular communications during co-culture. The device consists of three parallel channels connected by an array of 30 µm wide by 100 µm long microchannels spaced 75 µm apart to facilitate the orthogonal diffusion of biomolecules. COMSOL Multiphysics was used to model the mass transfer in the device to optimize channel length and width. The optimized device consisted of three parallel 1500 µm long with the two outermost channels for static cell culture and the center channel connected to a peristaltic pump to allow for continual perfusion and circulating of medium. The operating length of the three channels was 20 mm to allow for sufficient cell numbers for sampling of paracrine factors. Circulating media flowrates of 5, 10, and 15 µL/min were tested, with 5 µL/min providing sufficient mass transfer across the three channels with minimal shear effects on the culture cells A test device was fabricated using a combination of soft lithography and polydimethyl siloxane (PDMS) replication. The device utilized a peristaltic pump with clear, flexible tubing for constant flow of media and a three-way junction incorporating into the tubing outside of the device for dynamic sampling. Pipette-tip reservoirs were positioned at the inlets and outlets of the culture channels for media replacement. Peristaltic pump performance was characterized by running water through the tubing and timing the water collection at different pump speeds. The pipette-tip reservoirs were observed during testing to ensure media replacement without the introduction of bubbles during sampling. A careful sampling technique, which included clipping the opposite junction during sampling, was also developed to address this issue. This novel microfluidic device will be used to analyze the cell-to-cell communications between MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells, a triple negative cell line, and adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) to study how stromal cells enhance the proliferation and drug resistance of cancer cells.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Release of Griseofulvin from Spray-Dried Nanocrystal–Amorphous Solid Dispersions (HyNASDs): Impact of Surfactant
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Over the last few decades, majority of the new chemical entities (NCEs) in the drug discovery pipeline are poorly-water soluble, and their slow dissolution turns out to be the rate-limiting step during intestinal absorption. Among different approaches to enhance bioavailability, two platform approaches have gained prevalence both in the scientific literature and marketed products: nanoparticle-based dosage forms (nanocomposites) and amorphous solid dispersions ( ASDs ). In the nanoparticle-based dosage form, dissolution rate is improved due to the dramatic increase in the surface area of the drug crystals via size reduction down to the nanoscale. On the other hand, amorphous form of the drug can offer significant enhancement in the extent–rate of dissolution due to its higher free energy and higher apparent solubility. A major shortcoming of drug nanocomposites as compared with amorphous solid dispersions (ASDs) is their limited supersaturation capability in dissolution media. Here, we prepared hybrid nanocrystal–amorphous solution dispersions (HyNASDs) in order to boost the drug release performance of traditional nanocomposites while elucidating the impact of a common anionic surfactant, sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), on drug release in dissolution tests. Wet-milled suspensions containing 1:1 to 1:5 GF:polymer mass ratios, with and without SDS, were spray-dried. Hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) and Soluplus (Sol) were used as suspension stabilizers and matrix-forming polymers. XRPD and DSC results suggest that nanocomposites and nanocomposites with notable amorphous GF (>10%), HyNASDs, were formed upon spray-drying. Redispersion of the spray-dried powders revealed the criticality of SDS in nanoparticle recovery from the nanocomposites/HyNASDs, which could be explained by GF wettability enhancement by SDS, as inferred from the modified Washburn experiment. Results from in vitro dissolution tests suggest that enhanced wettability with SDS and smaller spray-dried particle sizes led to faster GF release. For 100 mg GF dose (above thermodynamic solubility), Sol provided higher GF relative supersaturation, e.g. 250% for the HyNASDs (1:5 GF:Sol with SDS) vs. 30% for the nanocomposites (3:1 GF:Sol with SDS), than HPC (up to 50%) owing to Sol’s stronger intermolecular interactions–miscibility with GF and its kinetic solubilization–recrystallization inhibition of GF. SDS provided enhanced wettability, allowing for fast supersaturation from Soluplus-based HyNASDs (~300% within 20 min), while higher Soluplus loading led to higher supersaturation. Finally, this study demonstrates how drug release from traditional nanocomposites could be boosted upon incorporating a drug-miscible, solubilizing polymer with a low GF:polymer mass ratio and an anionic surfactant.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Synthesis and Characterization of Novel Phospholipid-Conjugated Topotecan Prodrugs for Lipid Vehicle Delivery
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Current anticancer therapies face the innate challenge of proper targeting and dosing of chemotherapeutic agents. Low selectivity is a characteristic trait of many existing drugs, which results in unintended damage to healthy tissue alongside cancerous tissue that may cause dangerous short and long-term side effects. Our mission is to modify commonly used anticancer drugs (cytarabine, gemcitabine, topotecan, and others) to increase their selectivity through incorporation into lipid vehicles for ultrasound-mediated delivery. Currently our focus lies on topotecan—a topoisomerase inhibitor used in the treatment of solid-tumor cancers—onto which phospholipid tails were conjugated to form a prodrug that can be loaded into lipophilic environments without premature leaking. We hypothesize that topotecan is then released from the prodrug at the treatment site via non-specific esterase cleavage. 2T-T (“Two-Tailed Topotecan”) prodrug was successfully synthesized by conjugating phospholipid tails to the parent drug via Steglich esterification. The resulting compound was purified with chromatographic separation, producing a yield of 24%, and characterized with 1H and 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (NMR). The prodrug was then loaded into liposomes and tested for biological activity via MTT cell proliferation assay. Biological effectiveness was verified by comparing 2T-T activity to the activity of parent topotecan. 2T-T showed comparable IC50 values to the parent drug at the nanomolar level, supporting our hypothesis that topotecan is released from 2T-T prodrug in its biologically active form at the cancer site. Future work includes further characterization as well as improvement of yield and biological activity. Drug modification such as this paves the way for future anticancer drugs with vastly improved safety and effectiveness.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Developing a Scalable Model for Optimum Growth in Stirred Tank Bioreactors
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Stirred tank bioreactors are commonly used in many laboratory and industry applications. These reactors are often utilized in chemistry, biology, and pharmacy fields to examine important parameters. The most significant parameter of a bioreactor is the volumetric mass transfer coefficient (kLA) of oxygen. The kLA of oxygen is essential to measure efficiencies and scale-ups, and is widely affected by air flow rate, impeller type, impeller speed, and temperature. The experiment was first conducted in a 1L cylindrical glass reactor with a dished bottom. In this reactor, the kLA was measured using a gas cylinder that contains nitrogen and air. To test both the concentration and temperature of nitrogen and air, a dissolved oxygen and temperature probe were used. Nitrogen was measured by waiting for the oxygen concentration to decrease down to zero. After the oxygen concentration reached zero, air was measured until the dissolved oxygen completed 100% saturation. Depending on the amount of time is takes for nitrogen to reach zero and air to reach 100% saturation, different flow rates were adjusted so that the duration would run smoothly. Various types of impellers and impeller speeds were tested to see how the amount of time is affected as well. A 3L reactor was then repeated with same process that was done with the 1L reactor. This process was completed, and currently, the 3L bioreactor is being utilized to produce bacteria growth and cell culture. The bacteria being used in the process is Escherichia Coli due to its wide industrial use and fast-growing abilities. From using Escherichia Coli in the bioreactor with the various flow rates, impellers, and impeller speeds, we can see how fast the bacteria can absorb the oxygen and grow. To measure the concentration of the bacteria growth in the bioreactor, Optical Density (OD) measurements are recorded. This project is being tested in India as well by measuring bacteria growth and culture in larger reactors such as 5L and 7L. By doing these experiments on a smaller scale and a larger scale, we will be able to find the optimum parameters for a scalable model.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Supramolecular Filaments As Inhalable Drug Carriers for Lung Disease Therapies
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Drug carrier systems that are capable of increased deposition, prolonged retention, and drug release in the lungs are extremely powerful in the treatment of diseases such as lung cancer, COPD, asthma, and tuberculosis. Supramolecular filaments (SFs) are a class of nanostructures formed by units such as peptide amphiphiles (PAs) ; peptides conjugated to alkyl chains and assembled through non-covalent forces. SFs can be “loaded” with therapeutic agents and controllably release these drugs upon filament disassembly. We take advantage of this technology to produce biocompatible PA-based drug carrier systems. Here, we provide key insights into PA design parameters necessary to deliver therapeutic agents effectively, a proof-of-concept in jet nebulization’s ability to effectively deliver drug-loaded supramolecular filaments, as well as a proposed mechanism of SF breakdown during nebulization.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Engineering a Split Ubiquibody for Inducible Control of Protein Interface
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Similar to humans throwing away trash, the cells in our body need to discard proteins that aren’t being used to prevent buildup. This process of protein degradation is accomplished through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP), which tags the proteins to be degraded with a marker called ubiquitin (Portnoff, Stephens, Varner, DeLisa 2014). This pathway has been harnessed by several techniques to reduce levels of selectively targeted proteins by providing a method of eliminating proteins in the cell that are stable, but might be detrimental to cell function and life. Such techniques successfully enable degradation of targeted proteins, but are not modular, which requires an optimization for each new target protein. The goal of this project was to engineer a split ubiquibody, where the two ubiquibody domains (catalytic and binding) are expressed separately and dimerize in the presence of a chemical rapamycin. The results yielded a successful engineering of a split ubiquibody fused with either the FRB and FKBP protein. Before testing the dimerization of the two split complexes, the individual expression of each construct was tested to ensure that the individual complexes themselves could express well in mammalian cells. When testing these split ubiquibodies for expression using a Western Blot using both the FLAG and HIS tag, the complexes containing the binding domain expressed well consistently; however, catalytic domain had low expression indicating that the structure itself was not yet optimized for dimerization of the overall complex. To address this problem in the future, the complex with the catalytic domain is being redesigned with a linker and different orientations to improve stability and optimize expression.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Evaluating Transport and Intracellular Uptake of a Protein Nanocarrier in 3-D Tumor Spheroids
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The delivery of therapeutics into cells could open up many treatment options for various diseases such as cancer and neurological disorders, but these intracellular targets have been considered largely “undruggable” by small-molecule drugs that can penetrate the cell membrane. Delivery of antibodies directly to these targets would allow for more direct interaction with intracellular proteins, but intracellular antibody delivery remains an issue. To combat this, our lab has previously developed the Hex carrier, which can bind up to 3 antibodies per carrier and deliver them intracellularly in their functional form. Previously, I have shown via flow cytometry that HeLa cells treated with Hex-bound fluorescently labeled rabbit Immunoglobulin G (IgG Rb ) show a statistically significant increase in intracellular florescence compared to treatment with unbound IgG Rb . To further expand on previous studies of uptake in 2-D cell culture systems, the evaluation was extended to a 3-D tumor spheroid model. 3-D multicellular spheroids are very common models used to evaluate nanoparticle delivery, as they better mimic actual tumors as they would appear and behave in vivo. This allows for a more realistic assessment of nanoparticle transport and uptake at the tissue level. The intracellular uptake of fluorescent IgG Rb was assessed by flow cytometry to confirm that intracellular delivery is maintained in a complex, 3-D system. After being cultured and treated, the spheroids were digested with trypsin in order to break up the spheroid into individual cells for flow cytometry. Results of this analysis indicated positive fluorescence of the spheroids’ cells, indicating successful intracellular delivery despite the more complex system. This successful delivery of Hex in 3-D tumor spheroids provides further evidence of the improved delivery of antibodies by the Hex carrier. Future work will involve using confocal microscopy to evaluate transport of the Hex-antibody complex across the extracellular matrix into the interior of the spheroid, providing further support for Hex as an antibody delivery vehicle.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Development of Wearable Cortisol Biosensor for Medical Application
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Anxiety and depressive disorders alone affect over 400 million people and costs of over 1.5 trillion dollars per year. Although many people are affected, the psychiatric field still suffers from minimal understanding. There is a need to directly observe the essential biological nature of these disorders and move into objective, readily available indicators that can guide care. Cortisol, the body’s main stress hormone, is one of the most interesting biomarkers for many psychological disorders. There is a correlation between cortisol levels and several neurological disorders such as major depression, bipolar disorder, and anxiety. Cortisol levels can be measured using sweat, saliva, or blood. The current state of the art for measuring cortisol levels is phlebotomy, which uses blood samples, is invasive, and not applicable to tracking a patient continuously. The ability to continuously monitor cortisol levels could potentially give great insight into biological nature of these disorders and make way for a form of a diagnostic biological test which is currently nonexistent. It has been shown that the cortisol levels in sweat have a good correlation with those levels in blood. We believe that body sweat is a valuable source of biological information that can be used readily and monitored continuously. We chose commercial available metal oxide silicon field effect transistors (MOSFET) with an extended gate design as our sensor due to their high production speed, mechanical compatibility with skin, and low cost. Using competitive immunoassay, cortisol, a small molecule without charge removes the antibody from the surface of the extended gate displaying the large signal change necessary for our sensor. We are integrating this biosensing method into the extended gate MOSFET design due to the need to miniature the device for wearable application. Since one possible rout for sensing with extended gate structure is detecting the charges of the biomolecules, the research presented analyzes the effects of the buffer solutions Debye length, the scale which traveling charge carriers screen out electric field in conductors on the drift of the signal. The research presented will also detail the signal changes of the sensor as different MOSFETS with capacitances ranging from picofarad (pF) to nanofarad (nF) are paired with extended gate varying in surface area. By changing the surface area we can increase and decrease the total capacitance of the extended gate since the inherit capacitance is defined by the chemical functionalization itself.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: The Role of dach1 in De Novo Formation of Collateral Arteries in the Uninjured Heart
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD), is the leading cause of death in the US, accounting for 1 in 3 deaths annually. CAD occurs when coronary arteries (CAs) that supply the heart with oxygen become diseased. Collateral arteries, vessels that can interconnect CAs independent branches, can re-supply oxygen to the deprived muscle tissue, thereby maintaining heart function. Understanding the molecular factors involved in the development of the CAs and collaterals can lead to potential treatments for CAD. The transcription factor, DACH1, is necessary for CA development. In order to evaluate the role of DACH1 in collateral artery formation, we used an inducible transgenic murine line where DACH1 has been over-expressed (OE). Mice were induced at day 5 and processed for immunostaining at day 11 and week 12. iDISCO, a whole-mount immunolabeling clearing technique, and ImageJ were used to visualize, trace, and quantify the number of collaterals. We observed a slight decline in the number of collaterals in the OE vs WT at day 11 and expect this trend to repeat in the adults. Interestingly, a preliminary investigation on post-injury collateral formation yielded higher numbers in WT mice than OE. A qualitative analysis of the hearts suggest that the OE mice have more branches at the tips of the arteries. This indicates that the OE model may have a higher supply of oxygen to the heart and is a potential reason for the lower collateral count. In conclusion, this work brings us closer to understanding DACH1’s role in collateral artery formation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Modeling the Amphiphilic Behavior of Quorum Sensing Signaling Molecules and Their Interactions with Lipid Bilayers
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Quorum sensing is a bacterial communication process used to coordinate group behavior, such as the formation of antibiotic-resistant biofilms. Quorum sensing is controlled by the secretion and sensing a group of amphiphilic quorum sensing signaling molecules (QSSMs). In general, Gram-negative bacteria mainly use N -acyl homoserine lactones (AHLs), consisting of a polar homoserine lactone head group and a nonpolar aliphatic tail, as QSSMs. The urgency and severity of antibiotic resistance has led to interest in understanding the behavior of QSSMs in order to develop strategies to regulate bacterial communication. In this work, we developed a new protocol based on the conductor-like screening model for realistic solvation (COSMO-RS), in conjunction with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and quantum chemistry calculations, to investigate the amphiphilic behavior of AHLs by studying their self-assembly and their interactions with lipid bilayers. Atomistic MD simulations can determine the aggregation free energy and free energy of partitioning an AHL into a lipid bilayer with a large computational cost, whereas the new protocol incorporating COSMO-RS theory is at least 300 times faster than the MD simulation protocol with minor error. The results from the new protocol indicate that AHL head groups containing an additional 3-oxo group inhibit aggregation compared to their counterparts with only a single 3-oxo group in the head moiety, which is in agreement with the MD simulation results. The COSMO-RS results also indicate that longer aliphatic (more hydrophobic) tails facilitates aggregation and partitioning into a lipid bilayer, again in agreement with the MD simulation results. Comparison of the free energies for aggregation and partitioning indicates that aggregation is generally preferred, suggesting that aggregation may stabilize QSSMs in solution. Our faster COMSO-RS-theory-based protocol could be used as a high-throughput screening method for QSSM amphiphilic behavior and help guide the design of new AHL delivery techniques based on their membrane transport for better controlling the bacterial communication.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Optimization of Carbon Delivery to Nannochloropsis Oceanica 849/10
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Atmospheric carbon dioxide is a major contributor to global climate change. Nannochloropsis oceanica is a marine microalgae species showing viability as a large-scale carbon dioxide conversion method. Being a marine species, N. oceanica does not compete with agriculture for freshwater resources. This species also naturally has a high percentage of its cell weight dedicated to lipids, which can be refined into biodiesel fuel, thereby providing a renewable fuel source. In sea water, carbon dioxide is equilibrated between two forms, dissolved carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and bicarbonate (HCO 3 - ). Bicarbonate has previously been determined as the primary carbon source for microalgae like N. oceanica . To maximize carbon dioxide conversion, the algae’s growth medium must have a high bicarbonate concentration, which requires a neutral to moderately basic pH. Experiments were conducted to determine the following: 1) standard growth curve of N. oceanica , 2) does N. oceanica prefer a bicarbonate source, and 3) baseline activity assays for commercially available carbonic anhydrase. Growth trials were run to determine if N. oceanica prefers either ammonium bicarbonate or sodium bicarbonate as a bicarbonate source. Sodium bicarbonate cultures had ammonium chloride added to maintain identical nitrogen concentrations. Total organic carbon (TOC) analysis showed that inorganic carbon (IC) concentrations, the combined concentration of carbonate and bicarbonate, decreased for cultures provided with ammonium bicarbonate. This decrease means N. oceanica consumed more bicarbonate. In contrast, the sodium bicarbonate/ammonium chloride cultures did not show a significant change in bicarbonate uptake. An activity assay was conducted on commercially available carbonic anhydrase for future reference on how factors such as temperature, acidity, buffered solution, and salinity affect enzymatic activity. These results are useful in determining how to improve algae-based carbon capture since carbonic anhydrase is a crucial component of the carbon concentrating mechanism in microalgae.

Purification methods will then be used to purify the biopolymers made by the yeast.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Design Principles of Microparticle Backpacks for Control of Cellular Phenotype
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: An emerging platform for immunotherapy is the use of adoptively transferred cells of the innate immune system, such as macrophages, which can affect diseased tissues in an antigen-agnostic fashion. Macrophages display the most phenotypic plasticity out of any circulatory cell, which allows them to perform several related and often opposing biological functions, including promoting and suppressing inflammation, wound healing, and participating in host defense. However, the very plasticity that makes macrophages a versatile candidate for immunotherapy also hinders their ability to perform an intended function once transferred to the patient, as they can shift their phenotype in response to conflicting signals in the surrounding microenvironment. To address this issue, we have developed a disc-shaped microparticle “backpack” that is capable of attaching to macrophages and regulating their phenotype through the release of immunomodulatory cytokines. Backpacks are fabricated via microcontact printing of multiple layers of biodegradable polymers, which include a cell-binding layer and a cytokine-encapsulating layer (e.g., interferon-gamma, IFN-g). The thickness of the cytokine-encapsulating layer was tuned to balance stability and activity of IFN-g with microcontact-printing efficiency. The stiffness and size of the backpacks were confirmed with atomic force microscopy. Once fabricated, we show that the backpacks are able bind to the surface of primary murine-derived macrophages for at least 5 days. We also show that they release IFN-g over several hours to polarize the cells to which they are bound to a desired phenotype. Overall, the ability to control cellular phenotypes may allow for new cell-based therapies for a variety of immune-regulated conditions, including atherosclerosis, wound healing, and cancer.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Metabolic and Regulatory Profiling of Caldicellulosiruptor Bescii reveals Promising Avenues for Lignocellulose Decomposition Optimization
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Lignocellulose is the most abundant terrestrial carbon source, providing an attractive alternative to petroleum-based industrial chemicals. Harnessing the native cellulolytic ability of microorganisms is a promising avenue for industrial chemical production from renewable plant biomass; however, the need for pretreatment of lignocellulose limits its use in industrial processes. Caldicellulosiruptor bescii, a Gram-positive, anaerobic hyperthermophile growing optimally at 78°C, can deconstruct unpretreated lignocellulose and ferment both C5 and C6 sugars in a single step, making it a strong candidate for biologically mediated consolidated bioprocessing (CBP). While some chemicals such as ethanol have been demonstrated in C. bescii at moderate titers 1 , a deeper understanding of the physiology and regulatory networks of C. bescii is critical for the development of a scalable industrial process. Through metabolic reconstruction, biosynthetic pathways can be validated, prioritized, and optimized to redirect lignocellulosic sugars to target products. Here, we employed continuous culturing, transcriptome analysis, and in vitro characterization of regulatory proteins to investigate fermentation profiles, sugar uptake, and metabolic regulation. Fermentation profiles from continuous cultures of C. bescii on 5 g/L glucose or xylose at a dilution rate of 0.2 hr -1 show nearly the same theoretical yield of acetate (56.1% xylose, 55.7% glucose); however, glucose fermentation produces 4-fold more lactate. Because lactate production in C. bescii fermentation is due to buildup of H 2 , we investigated the influence of agitation rate on lactate production. Increased agitation rate from 150 rpm to 400 rpm led to a 10-fold reduction in lactate, a 1.7-fold increase in acetate, and exhaustion of carbon in the medium. By tuning the reactor operation, product yield and sugar consumption can be further controlled. Preliminary transcriptomics comparing glucose and xylose fermentation reveal upregulation of genes responsible for xylose transport and metabolism representing several distinct regulons, necessitating a robust metabolic reconstruction for sugar uptake and metabolism to account for crosstalk between pathways. Through in vitro characterization of C. bescii xylose metabolism regulators, further understanding of regulator binding and affinity will be determined, which is essential for the development of efficient, biologically mediated biofuel production. References: Williams-Rhaesa et al. Engineering redox-balanced ethanol production in the cellulolytic and extremely thermophilic bacterium, Caldicellulosiruptor bescii, Metabolic Engineering Communications, Volume 7, 2018

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Engineering of glycosylation pathways in bacterial cells has become an important tool for the development of microbe glyco-factories, conjugate vaccines, glycosylated outer membrane vesicles, and analyzing other roles glycosylated proteins play in various organisms. A novel assay was developed for the high-throughput screening of N -glycosylation in Escherichia coli : GlycoSNAP ( glyco sylation of s ecreted N- linked a cceptor p roteins). O -linked glycoproteins have a much lower specificity for sugar substrates, thus facilitating a much wider range of potential application. Here, we describe the methodology of GlycoSNAP and its variable components, as well as its potential application in regards to O -glycosylation. GlycoSNAP has proven to be a successful high-throughput screening methodology, and is more affordable than its common counterpart, gel electrophoresis followed by Western blot. Its efficiency and modularity can, in principle, facilitate its application in a wide range of glyco-engineered variants.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Proteins in breast milk not only serve as nutrients for the infant, but also exert health beneficial properties that are necessary for the body’s physiological functioning. There is still little knowledge on the effect of specific bioactive peptides on the body. Therefore, the objective of our study is to analyze the transport of peptides derived from in vitro and in vivo digestion of human milk proteins across a cell model of human small intestinal epithelium layer. Once we know more about the transport of proteins through digestion, the scientific community can further the understanding of how bioactive peptides work in the body. With the results of the experiment, there can be more research in discovering specific bioactive peptide sequences that can provide immune protection and reduce the risk of chronic diseases.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Prophage are viral sequences that have integrated into bacterial genomic DNA. Our aim is to characterize the specific proteins encoded for by the prophage, specifically focusing on the Xap toxin, which could be contributing to virulence in Xanthomonas and may be related to the zonula occludens toxin (zot) commonly produced by pathogenic strains of Vibrio cholerae . Toxins frequently impair bacterial growth during characterization experiments. For this reason, we are developing a cell-free approach to toxin production. Information regarding Xap and the group of V-phage could aid in understanding the role that bacteriophages and related molecules play as reservoirs of virulence factors in both plant and mammalian pathogens. Furthermore, future work to characterize Xanthomonas gene expression and related phage could aid in the creation of target-specific antimicrobials for common plant pathogens.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Designing Flavivirus Vaccines By Glycoengineering Protein Antigens
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The goal of our work is to develop vaccines which provide broad protection against flaviviruses such as Zika and Dengue viruses. Zika outbreaks have been associated with a large increase in cases of microcephaly and Guillain-Barré syndrome. To date, there is no approved vaccine, antiviral drug, or other modality available to prevent or treat Zika – emphasizing the present need for a vaccine. Recent vaccine efforts have been focused on the Zika virus envelope protein (ZIKV E protein), which plays an important role in viral attachment and entry into host cells. The ZIKV E protein is composed of three spatially distinct structural domains (domain I (DI), domain II (DII), and domain III (DIII)). Previous research has shown that DIII is involved in receptor binding and elicits neutralizing antibodies. Researchers have recently characterized the epitopes for two distinct antibodies that target DIII: ZV-67 and ZV-2; only the epitope for ZV-67 was accessible in the context of the virion and only ZV-67 neutralized ZIKV in vivo . Thus, the goal of this study is to design an antigen that focuses the immune response on the ZV-67 epitope on DIII and effectively elicits antibodies that neutralize ZIKV. To achieve this goal, we are tuning the glycosylation of DIII. Glycans can be used as an antigen-modifier to direct the immune response away from or to a specific region of a protein. We hypothesize that shielding non-neutralizing epitopes on ZIKV DIII by glycosylation will direct the immune response towards the ZV-67 epitope to elicit more neutralizing antibodies. We also show how glycoengineering can be applied to other flaviviruses (i.e. Dengue).

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: The Effect of Milling on Protein Enrichment of Yellow Pea during Electrostatic Separation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The standardized processes implemented for the separation of agro-material components (i.e. protein, starch and dietary fibers) are wet fractionation methods that involve the use of concentrated acids and/or alkali as well as energy-intensive dehydration step. In our Bioprocess Engineering Research Laboratory at Howard University, the focus is on developing a novel tribo-electrostatic separation process to effectively produce a protein-rich fraction of an agro-material in a water- and chemical-free environment. Our custom-built tribo-electrostatic separator encompasses of a fluidized bed, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) tribo-charging tube, and a rectangular separation chamber supplied with two copper-plate electrodes. For this study, yellow pea flours milled using two different milling types (i.e. pin and Ferkar milling systems) at two different milling intensities were first fluidized under the influence of pressurized air and then traveled through PTFE tribo-charging tube where protein particles were charged positively and attracted by the negatively-charged electrode plate. Our results highlight the importance of the milling types and intensities along with the air flow rates and electric field strengths for effective enrichment of yellow pea protein particles at their native states. Using the optimal milling and operating conditions, the original yellow pea protein content is increased by about 60% in the final collected protein fractions.
