https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Analysis of Parameter Interactions with a Box-Behnken Design on the Production of Cellulose Nanocrystals through Sulfuric Acid Hydrolysis
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Cellulose is a natural, abundant, and inexpensive, high-molecular-weight polymer that has attracted attention from various industrial sectors. Cellulose Nanocrystals (CNCs) are most commonly derived from acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of cellulose and are used in a variety of applications due to their remarkable mechanical, chemical, rheological, and optical properties. One barrier to mass implementation of CNCs is the high cost associated with the manufacturing process, primarily from low overall yields. Optimization of the manufacturing process offers a potential solution to increase yield, reduce cost, and enhance potential for mass production and total market approval. The goal of this study is to explore the interaction of sulfuric acid concentration (x1), hydrolysis temperature (x2), and hydrolysis time (x3) through a Box-Behnken Design (BBD) on the overall yield of CNCs through the sulfuric acid hydrolysis process. Our prior research has explored the outer limits of the practical design space and highlighted key processing parameters through a rotatable central composite design. However, our initial experimental design consisted of conditions at axial locations that were not achievable, either because of extreme conditions that completely degraded the cellulose, or at times that are unachievable (e.g. negative time). This BBD study encompasses a down-selected design space to further analyze targeted conditions for optimization of the hydrolysis process and subsequent yield. Conductometric titration was performed to analyze sulfate group density. Further, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy was carried out to investigate the extent of CNC degradation during synthesis. The parameter ranges selected for the study were 56-63 wt% (x1), 50-80 ℃ (x2), and 30-180 min (x3), with a maximum CNC yield of 73%.

Preliminary electrochemical cycling reveals that a derivative borane cluster decorated with lithium carboxylate exhibits redox activity at 3.4 V with a high degree of reversibility while cycling lithium. We have demonstrated the reversible (de)intercalation of Li + in borane clusters cycled in the solid state, offering a promising alternative to transition metal-based electrode materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Hydrogel Network Characterization Using Low Field Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Hydrogels, defined as linked polymer chains with high water content, present a growing interest as a drug delivery system. In order to optimize their use in the field, important characteristics such as mesh size and structure need to be understood. However, challenges arise when relying on the use of traditional methods such as Small Angle X-Ray Scattering (SAXS) or BET gas adsorption, which might be either inaccessible or require time-consuming sample preparation. As a result, the use of low field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) has become an attractive alternative for hydrogel characterization. With this method, a magnetic field induces the alignment of the samples’ NMR-active nuclei, such as 1 H, followed by a radio frequency pulse which disrupts their alignment. As the magnetic field is held constant, the nuclei tend to “relax” back while the equipment collects the output signal. The relaxation time that characterizes the nuclei dephasing in the x-y axis (T 2 ) can then be used to understand the surface-solvent interactions and provide insightful information for the mesh size calculation of hydrogel samples. The present study focused on the use of LF-NMR to characterize samples made with poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA) at high (8000 Da) and low (700 Da) molecular weights using Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) pulse sequencing and CONTIN algorithm. Accuracy of LF-NMR was assessed by comparing the obtained results to SAXS results from literature for PEGDA with the same molecular weight. The same trends were observed in the mesh size calculations for both LF-NMR and SAXS, with very similar results between the two methods for similar hydrogel compositions and differences of less than three nanometers in mesh size calculations. Our results indicate that the interaction between hydrogels and water can be captured by NMR, with noticeable differences among various molecular weights and polymer concentrations. Therefore, NMR appears to be a valuable characterization method for hydrogels and similar wetted systems.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In recent years, an increasing amount of researches has been focusing on organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), which have unprecedented advancements in display and lighting technologies. Organic electronic materials generate lights through a process called electroluminescence in which singlet and triplet excitons are formed in the first step. Singlet excitons relax to ground state and produce light while the triplet excitons dissipate their energies to the surroundings as heat. Several strategies such as thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) have been proposed to convert up to 100% of the excitons in the device into the light. In this study, a type of TADF material, 4Cz-IPN is used to demonstrate the delay fluorescence property. A combination of optical, electronic and cooling systems is built to study the temperature dependence of TADF materials and to extract the rates in the TADF process. These rates can be used to calculate the energy gap between triplet and singlet excited states, and thus giving guidance of TADF material design. This system can be applied to various topics such as the influence of gold particles doped in the TADF materials, and the host-dependence of TADF materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Synthesis of Temperature Responsive Polymeric Flocculants with Cationic Moieties for Environmental Remediation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a prolific and persistant contaminant in the environment, and our group is developing a novel copolymer sorbent with 2-phase LCST behavior to aid in PFAS removal. The hypothesis in question was that the incorporation of cationic comonomers will aid capture of anionic contaminants such as types of PFAS in temperature-driven polymeric flocculation. A model anionic organic dye, indigo carmine, was used as the preliminary contaminant in the pursuit of a conclusive visual remediation effect. The copolymers are primarily n-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAAm) with low levels of cationic comonomers like dimethylaminoethyl acrylate (DMAEA) or dimethylaminopropyl acrylamide (DMAPAA). The copolymers were polymerized via a free radical polymerization, and the structure and properties were characterized by NMR, GPC/SEC, FTIR, and UV-Vis spectroscopy. Comonomer was successfully incorporated as shown qualitatively in NMR spectra and an LCST shift upwards. The molecular weights were between 2 and 4 million g/mol. FTIR data was noisy and analysis did not clearly support comonomer incorporation. LCST was obtained via UV-Vis spectroscopy. The LCST of the new copolymers ranged from 33.75 to 40.2 °C, and was shown to be dependent on wavelength, unexpectedly. This result could challenge the industry norm of reporting LCST at a single wavelength of 500 nm. LCST of the poly(NIPAAm) (PNIPAAm) synthesized were between 30.5 and 33.75 °C, depending on initiator concentration. The copolymers were brought to flocculate in the presence of indigo carmine to determine if removal could visually or quantitatively be observed, but the efforts thus far have not been successful. The hypothesis cannot yet be proved or disproved as no contaminant removal has been demonstrated, but the comonomers were successfully incorporated into the copolymers and further optimizations to the organic anionic dye buffered flocculation study have been recommended.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Optical Characterization and Purification of DNA-Wrapped Single-Wall Carbon Nanotubes at Controlled pH
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) have unique optical, electronic, and chemical properties which can be utilized for an extensive range of potential applications, including biosensing and bioimaging. The DNA wrapping of SWCNTs has been proven an efficient method for dispersing nanotubes in an aqueous medium and their subsequent purification of chirality-defined SWCNTs. By inducing DNA conformational changes on the sidewall of SWCNTs through precise control of solvent pH, stable hybrids of DNA-wrapped SWCNTs (DNA-SWCNTs) with increased photoluminescence can be obtained. In this work, we monitored the effect of pH on optical properties of DNA-SWCNTs using single-stranded DNA of (GT) n sequences with n = 6, 10, 15, 20 at a broad range of pH 1-13. It was hypothesized that the site-specific deprotonation of nucleotide bases in basic regime at pH ≈ 12 promotes hydrogen bonding between the bases in (GT) n DNA; therefore, causing conformational changes in DNA coating structures. This conformational change led to increased fluorescence emission of nanotubes up to 7 times by effectively shielding quenching species in solvent from the surface of SWCNTs. In addition, the effect of nanotube concentration and excess unbound DNA on optical properties of DNA-SWCNTs were explored. The phenomenon of a pH-induced conformational change of DNA on nanotubes was further explored for SWCNT purification using a polymer aqueous two-phase separation method. Our preliminary work showed the potential of separating single-chirality SWCNTs by precise control of pH using specific DNA sequences. Future work will focus on developing a scalable method for separating chirality-defined SWCNTs, that can be utilized for biological sensing and imaging applications.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Vapor Induced Phase Transition of Cesium Lead Halide Perovskite Thin Films for Novel Use in Solar Cells
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In recent years, perovskite solar cells have emerged as a promising new alternative to the current silicon-based panels which have dominated the market. Research was done to characterize the black to clear phase transition undergone by thin films of cesium lead halide perovskite when exposed to various solvent vapors. The thin films of a cesium lead halide perovskite were exposed to a constant partial pressure of different solvent vapors, and the kinetics of the transition from the perovskite phase to the non-perovskite δ-phase were tracked by absorption spectroscopy. We find that other common solvents, in addition to the previously known water and alcohols (MeOH and EtOH), will catalyze this phase transition. Interestingly, we find sigmoidal kinetics for this process, indicating a cooperative nature whereby the transition of one domain further catalyzes the subsequent transition of other domains. Furthermore, we find that the rate of the phase change appears to be affected but not wholly governed by molecular dipole strength. This foundational work yields deepened understanding of the mechanisms of the clear to black phase transition in halide perovskites. In future, perovskite solar cells could be designed to resist undergoing this phase transition, so that they remain black and photovoltaically active, or they could potentially be designed to exploit this transition in a product such as a dynamically switching photovoltaic window.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Here we report novel chromogenic sensors that exhibit a change of color when exposed to an external stimulus, such as heat, pressure, shear stress, acoustic waves, and exposure to various liquids or gases. By fabricating shape memory polymers (SMPs) into the structure known as a photonics crystal, we have developed SMP sensors with dual-shape capabilities. Such sensors work by changing its shape from a predetermined shape to its permanent photonic crystal shape when exposed to the appropriate stimulus. Having potential applications ranging from user-friendly environmental monitoring to specifically detecting chemicals, these sensors introduce a more efficient alternative because they are easily perceived, inexpensive, reusable, have a small footprint, and are time and energy efficient. The active components of the SMP sensors are a few μm thick macroporous photonic crystal layers, which are fabricated using self-assembled, 3-D highly ordered colloidal crystals as structural templates. Moreover, by leveraging easily perceived color changes, which is associated with the unconventional all-room-temperature shape memory cycles enabled by the recent discovery of a new series of multi-stimuli-responsive SMPs, detection of certain analyte in complex solutions, such as hydrogen peroxide in commercial products, has been demonstrated with a detection limit as low as 1%.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Multimaterial Aerosol Jet Printing of Functionally Graded Nanocomposites
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Advanced Materials Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA Aerosol jet printing offers a digital, non-contact, high-resolution direct-write capability with broad materials compatibility. In this work, a multimaterial aerosol jet printhead is designed for in-line mixing of multiple functional inks. Drawing on fluid dynamics modeling and 3D printing for custom printhead design, this enables direct patterning of compositionally-graded films. In this case, COMSOL modeling supports static mixer development tuned for relevant aerosol parameters, with geometry optimization based on mixing efficacy, mixer volume, and particle transfer efficiency. A proof-of-concept experiment using a fluorescent tracer in epoxy and acrylate matrixes validates this approach and allows straightforward visualization and characterization. In this case, composition information is obtained from fluorescence microscopy and profilometry measurements to calibrate deposition parameters and assess print quality. This materials system is then extended to incorporate ZrO 2 nanoparticles to tailor optical and dielectric properties. Overall, this multimaterial aerosol jet printing method provides a rapid, digital, and low-waste method to control print composition on the fly, establishing this nascent technology as a compelling platform for diverse applications including, but not limited to, functionally-graded electronic, optical, and magnetic materials. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Design and Application of High-Performance Ionene Composites
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Media for state-of-the-art gas separation membranes draws from material classes including ionic liquids (ILs), poly(ILs), and supported liquid membranes (SLMs) as well as more robust materials including polymers with varied functionality. Ionenes are polymers which contain ionic moieties along the main chain, rather than as pendants, which can be designed to harness the advantageous properties and structural elements typically associated with high-performance (HP) engineering polymers (i.e. aromatic character, imide or amide linkages). We have recently investigated the design, synthesis, and application of a new class of HP ionenes, which incorporate imidazolium cations (paired with Tf 2 N anions) along the main chain, alternating with diverse functional groups. The modular design of functional bis(imidazoles) and bulky dihalide monomers linked via the Menshutkin reaction, we have synthesized numerous derivatives of these ionenes which can be processed and tuned for a variety of applications. These materials exhibit intriguing self-assembly and nanostructuring, which is dictated by the complex combination of ionic and functional intermolecular interactions, leading to sophisticated materials with good thermal and mechanical stability. This structuring can be further tailored via the addition of “free” imidazolium-based ILs or functional ionic fillers, which serve as a non-covalent crosslink between polymer chains, stabilizing the polymer matrix and increasing the free volume between chains. These composites are processed into thin films (solvent-cast or melt-pressed) and the performance of these materials as membranes for light gas separations is analyzed. Due to the diverse potential structural combinations which lead to unique properties and behaviors, certain derivatives have also been investigated as functional coatings, elastomeric shape memory materials, additives, and fibers for additive manufacturing. Here, we present the development of these ionene composites resulting from complex monomer units, and the impact of design and processing on structure-property relationships and performance in the aforementioned applications.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: CFD and PBM Modeling of Particle Aggregation in Mixing Tanks
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Latex emulsions are systems containing a discrete phase of latex particles dispersed in a continuous aqueous phase and are widely used in industrial mixing processes. In the mixing of latex emulsions, small particles aggregate into larger, more uniform particles to establish a particle size distribution (PSD) required for quality standards. Particle aggregation and colloidal interactions are governed by the Derjaguin, Landau, Verwey, Overbeek (DLVO) theory. Perikinetic aggregation due to Brownian motion is the dominant form of aggregation for very small particles in latex emulsions. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Population Balance Modeling (PBM) are two techniques that are used to develop simulations and computational models of the mixing and particle aggregation involved in emulsion mixing processes. CFD is used to model the fluid and flow properties associated with the mixing, whereas PBM uses population balance equations to track the PSD of the latex particles. This project aims to understand the complexities associated with colloidal dispersions and emulsion aggregation in mixing tanks and the issues involved with scaling-up these mixing processes. By examining (1) the velocity profiles, (2) the change of PSD over time, and (3) the specific areas of the tank at which particles accumulate, two tanks of different sizes can be compared. Using ANSYS Fluent, CFD-PBM simulations of latex particle aggregation in water were run in a Pilot Plant tank and a larger Manufacturing tank using a user-defined function based in DLVO theory to calculate particle aggregation rates. The simulations illustrate a lack of mixing in areas at the top and near the wall of the tank in addition to slower and less uniform particle aggregation patterns in the Manufacturing tank compared to the Pilot Plant tank.

Electrospinning is a promising technique for fabricating scaffolds due to its ability to easily and inexpensively manipulate nanofiber morphology. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Evaluating and Modeling the Strength of 3D Printed Samples Using a Design of Experiments Framework
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Advanced technologies that precisely and rapidly convert designs into real-world products have the potential to transform industries ranging from healthcare to aerospace. Additive manufacturing offers advantages over subtractive manufacturing methods, which include such advantages as high accuracy prototyping, complex internal geometries, and less material waste. In particular, stereolithography (SLA) printing offers a reliable platform for generating mechanically isotropic parts with high feature resolution. In SLA printing, photo-sensitive liquid resin is selectively cured using UV light into solid parts in a layer-by-layer process based on specifications from a computer-aided design stereolithography file (STL). Potential challenges associated with large-scale use of SLA printing are the need for significant quantities of specialized liquid resins and long printing times. In this work, we designed and tested part geometries with varied void patterns and fractions to investigate the trade-off between reduced material use and decreased mechanical strength. To determine which patterns are most effective at maintaining the material strength per weight, we investigated three different void patterns with varying void fractions at two layer heights using a statistical design of experiments (DOE) methodology. The parts were designed and tested in accordance with ASTM standards and post-cured in a custom-built curing chamber. Tensile tests were used to measure the Young’s modulus and ultimate tensile strength for each part using an Instron testing system. Overall, circular void patterns resulted in the highest mechanical strength for a given void fraction. Moreover, finite element analysis was utilized to inform and corroborate the experimental results. This work can inform the design of parts with decreased material use, making the process more economical.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In recent years, ligand-protected Au nanoclusters (NCs) have retained tremendous interest due to their structural determination with atomic precision, unique optical and electronic properties, and great potential in diverse nanotechnological applications like catalysis, biomedicine and imaging. Since their discovery, Density Functional Theory (DFT) has been instrumental in calculating the electronic properties of NCs. Although accurate, DFT is computationally expensive, especially for NC systems consisting of a couple of hundred atoms. Thus, rapid methods that retain the accuracy of DFT are highly sought after to screen NCs exhibiting desirable electronic properties. Towards this goal, we developed a computational framework to discover structure-property relationships on ligand-protected Au NCs. Our approach connects NC descriptors based solely on experimental structural data to electronic properties calculated with DFT. Applying our framework, we developed a universal NC electronic gap model based on a sample of 22 NCs ranging from 18 to 102 Au atoms with 8 different ligand types. The model was in turn used to elucidate the structural features that dictate electronic gaps of NCs. Overall, this research accelerates materials discovery at the nanoscale by developing structure activity relationships on ligand protected NCs. These relationships elucidate how NC size (number of Au atoms) and presence of ligands (number of thiol ligands) affect the NC electronic properties and are able to identify specific NC morphologies that exhibit desired electronic properties.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Measuring the Surface Tension of Different Surfactants to Make Better Polyhipes
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Foams and emulsions are created by the combination of either two immiscible liquids or one liquid and a gas with the addition of a surfactant. Water and a hydrophobic phase, such as a monomer, are two liquids that are commonly used. As the water and monomer do not mix, a surfactant must be used. A surfactant is a molecule with hydrophilic and hydrophobic components, which allows the two immiscible materials to mix. The first step in creating a polymer foam is creating an emulsion that consists of the monomer (continuous phase), water (dispersed phase), and a surfactant. Then the emulsion is polymerized resulting in a polymer foam filled with water. These voids are often interconnected in the polymer, so liquid is able to flow in and out. The water is then dried out of the foam to result in a polymer foam with voids. These polymer foams have been proven useful in many engineering applications such as tissue engineering, cosmetics, and food science. The goal when making these emulsions is to increase the surface area of the voids in the polymer foam to enable more interaction between the surfactant and the fluid. This is a result of many smaller voids being distributed throughout the foam rather than larger voids existing in a smaller quantity. The way void size is controlled is through the manipulation of surface tension. Surface tension is a resistance force that exists on the surface of a liquid. It is important for the creation of emulsions because the lower the surface tension, the higher the emulsion surface area. After testing the surface tensions of different surfactants with other monomers, a relationship between surface tension and concentration can be quantified. As more surfactant is added, the surface tension will decrease with the goal of determining the lowest possible surface tension that can be achieved. The concentration at which this occurs is called the critical micelle concentration. As a result of how low the CMC found is, it can be determined which surfactants work best with different mixtures and better emulsions can be achieved. Using a tensiometer, concentrations of the surfactants Triton X-100, C-TAB, Kaolin, Span 80, SDS, and Hypromellose in the monomers Styrene and 2-Ethylhexyl acrylate were evaluated.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: An Assessment of the Biofilm-Prevention Efficacy of a Silver Carboxylate Eluting Titanium Dioxide and Polydimethylsiloxane Matrix on Spinal Implants
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Healthcare acquired infections (HAI) cause an increased burden and excess length of hospital stays (LOS), which accounts for approximately 90% of total costs. 1 Moreover, infection rates in biomedical implants can be as high as 4% for some devices and can cause up to $50,000 to fix. 2 These infections specifically may involve the spread of a family of gram-negative bacteria, Enterobacteriaceae (CPE), including Serratia marcescens , and is becoming a global public health problem associated with healthcare facilities. 3 Human infections by this pathogen were not recognized until the latter half of the 20th century. 4 S. marcescens is a gram-negative bacterium commonly associated with chronic orthopedic wounds, specifically in the spine. These infections may be comprised of biofilms, which are communities of microorganisms that are attached to a surface and are resistant to antibiotics, resulting in recurrent Surgical Site Infections (SSIs). 5 However, in recent years the use of silver as an antimicrobial agent has received attention for its ability to combat biofilm formation through its long-lasting release, broad antibacterial spectrum, and low incidence of antibiotic resistance. 6 In response to these concerns, we have developed a coating composed of a titanium dioxide and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix doped with silver carboxylate that allows for the controlled release of silver, acting as an antibiotic-independent antimicrobial by preventing biofilm formation. This project involved the assessment of the antimicrobial capabilities of various composition ratios of the matrix and silver carboxylate on three spinal implant materials. Stainless steel, titanium, and polyetheretherketone (PEEK) were chosen for this study due to their varying topographies, but also widespread use and effectiveness as surgical implants. The coating does not affect the mean roughness of the implant and does not interfere with osseointegration. The layering is thin, on the order of 10-100 nm, and can be applied incrementally to create a desired thickness. Multiple trials showed that microbial adherence and percent area coverage decreased with increasing silver dosage. Across all implants, the best performance was found using a 95% TiO 2 and 5% PDMS matrix, with a 10x concentration of silver carboxylate. Scanning electron microscopy and confocal microscopy analysis showed the highest CFU per area for the stainless steel, resulting in a higher adherence rate for S. marcescens on stainless steel than the other two materials. Future direction of this study will constitute of an in-depth characterization and improvement of the coating itself.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Confined Diffusion through Macroporous Structures
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Currently, confined mass transport through subsurface environments (e.g., soil, sediment, rock) is primarily investigated using computer simulations or run-off studies of core samples. Computer simulations lack empirical grounding while core studies provide little insight into the solutes’ interactions with the internal structure. We created an empirical model of these complex subsurface systems that observed individual particle trajectories. Macroporous structures (possessing a pore size greater than 50 nm) were created from silica (< 10 µm) packed on Piranha cleaned glass wafers and inside cured polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) flow channels. We employed single-particle tracking methods to visualize the path of 40 nm carboxylate-modified fluorospheres through macroporous structures. A Nikon A1R microscope capable of Laser Scanning Confocal and Total Internal Reflectance Fluorescence (TIRF) with an attached camera was used. Two kinds of tracking experiments were conducted: static diffusion and flow. During experimental runs, the capture images were acquired at a rate of 50 ms and combined in a single movie (2400 frames per movie). The movies were analyzed using in-house single-particle tracking code. Trajectory maps, tortuosity averages and diffusion coefficients were calculated for each sample. Analyzing the static diffusion experiments, tracer particles in 4.3 μm structure experienced more tortuous paths compared to the 4.3 μm + 9.2 μm and 9.2 μm structures. All packing structures yielded lower diffusion coefficients compared to unconfined diffusion. The flow experiments posed a challenge in creating a close packed porous structure that remained immobile but still allowed fluid flow. Future work will observe flow behavior through packed structures and derive mathematical relationships. The overall goal of this project is to inform mass transport through low porosity environments such as soil systems and porous rock.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Synthesis and Characterization of Multifunctional Bio-Based Polybenzoxazines and their Blends with Epoxy Resins Sarah Salazar, Amanda McCahill, Alexandra Chong, Joseph F. Stanzione III Department of Chemical Engineering, Rowan University, Glassboro, NJ 08028 Abstract The uncertainty of the petroleum industry and increase in environmental concerns has caused a growing interest in bio-based polymers. These uncured and cured resin mixtures were characterized using DSC, TGA and DMA to understand their structure-property relationships. Overall, bio-based benzoxazines with increased oxazine functionality and their epoxy blends were investigated to produce environmentally sustainable polymers with enhanced thermal and mechanical properties.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Colloidal Gelation of Silica Suspensions with Varying Salt and Surfactant Concentrations
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Colloidal gelation can be useful to prevent sedimentation of complex fluid products such as oral medicines or paints. Colloidal particles remain suspended in a liquid when interparticle repulsive forces are stronger than the attractive forces, especially at low volume fractions. When attractive forces dominate, colloidal particles may form an “attractive gel”. For aqueous suspensions of charged colloidal particles, electrostatic repulsive forces can be weakened by counterions. Similarly, agents can be added to strengthen attractive forces. For ionic surfactants at concentrations below the critical micelle concentration (CMC), there are no micelles, and they act as simple electrolytes. It is hypothesized that above the CMC of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) surfactants (CMC = 8 mM), micelles will introduce attractive depletion forces between particles, altering gelation. Consequently, when compared to the baseline system of a simple salt, one may expect colloidal suspensions to gel at lower concentrations of SDS than of NaCl. Using negatively charged silica in water as a model colloidal system, the goal is to understand how gelation phase behavior differs in the presence of increasing concentrations of simple NaCl electrolyte versus SDS. The phase behavior of Ludox colloidal silica was characterized according to transitions from a fluid to an attractive gel phase. Purified suspensions were prepared at a variety of silica concentrations. Suspensions were monitored over time to record the onset gelation time, which was characterized qualitatively based on flow characteristics of the sample. Thus far, a phase diagram mapping the effects of added salt and SDS on the silica suspensions has been prepared. The phase boundary between gel and fluid phases for SDS samples was observed at two to four times higher concentrations as compared to the phase boundary for NaCl samples for all the silica concentrations studied. In addition, gelation was faster for samples containing NaCl as compared to those containing equivalent concentrations of SDS. Whereas all NaCl added to solution contributes to screening of electrostatic repulsions, SDS micelles do not contribute to screening. Thus, only a fraction of sodium counterions for SDS added above the CMC contribute to screening. The results indicate that attractive depletion forces induced by SDS micelles were not sufficient to compensate for the weakened ionic strength enhancement caused by SDS addition compared to NaCl. The ionic strength effects dominate the gelation process.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Architected Porous Media for Metered Liquid Transfer Flexographic Printing
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The development of printed and unconventional electronic devices to meet application-specific needs requires innovation in printing technologies. Flexography (flexo), a rubber-stamping method developed in the 19th century, has proven scalable (meters per second) for graphic arts but is underdeveloped for printed electronics, particularly transistor and transparent electrode applications, due to limited feature resolution (>50 µm). Although much work has gone into understanding the structural and fluid mechanics of the ink transfer processes, little attention has been paid to the actual stamp, typically fabricated via polymer replication of a hard master. The elastomeric stamp is top-side inked and compressed on a substrate, a process that has inherent limits for materials transfer and results in uneven pixel quality (poor feature resolution) due to compression-induced spreading. However, consider a porous stamp that undergoes precise deformation such as negative Poisson’s ratio (NPR) during this process. Here, ink transfer could be a metered process with the pore-space being the reservoir and the mechanical deformation being the “metering pump”. Moreover, a stamp that exhibits a slight NPR may allow for controlled expulsion and sharper transfer foot print (minimal line-edge roughness). Only recently has it been feasible to produce such engineered structures at high resolution, for example, using multiphoton-induced, direct laser writing (DLW). Here we investigate how precisely architected (e.g., NPR and a structured pore size distribution), 3D porous media can control the fluid saturation/capillary pressure characteristics upon mechanical compression to enable high fidelity/metered material transfer for high speed printing. In this study, we systematically investigate the effects of porosity, pore size distribution and microstructure compression on flexographic ink transfer using iterative arrays of high-resolution (<1 µm feature size) DLW structures to converge on optimized forms. Fluid dynamics simulations of defined poroelastic media provide further insight into metering ink transfer during compression. Overall, this work illustrates the design flexibility and precision control of micro- features/fluid dynamics enabled using form-fabrication of flexographic forms.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Confining Electrodeposition of Metals in Structured Electrolytes
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The 2019 Chemistry Nobel Prize for Li-ion batteries substantiates the global importance of these devices in contemporary electronics. Even so, developing electrochemical systems with higher energy density than Li-ion batteries is critical for decarbonizing our society’s energy systems. One pathway towards improving Li-ion battery involves replacing the graphitic anode with Li metal. This change can increase the anodic energy capacity 10-fold and enables the use of high capacity, Li-free cathodes. However, Li metal batteries are inherently unstable because of the high reactivity of Li metal with organic electrolytes that results in the formation of a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), an insulating layer on the Li anode surface. The SEI’s inherent inhomogeneity causes some regions on the anode surface to be more conductive than others. Thus, Li ions deposit unevenly on the metal anode, leading to the formation of sharp nucleates. Continual deposition due to the high local electric field at the tip of the nucleates forms ‘needle-like’ dendrites capable of piercing through the battery separator, causing short circuits and initiating thermal runaway reactions in organic electrolytes. These catastrophic processes can result in lethal battery fires. There have been several studies dedicated to the prevention of dendrite growth and thermal runaway reactions by means of a high modulus physical barrier. One notable study concluded that a modulus at least twice that of Li (~10 GPa ) is required to achieve stable, smooth electrodeposition. However, these high strength “solid-state electrolytes” (SSEs) have low ionic conductivity, which reduces the power these batteries can produce, and therefore limits their practical use. Thus, engineering techniques and materials to break this tradeoff are critical concerns. Recent theoretical studies have reported that rough dendrite morphology can be mediated using battery separators having pore-diameter lower than the critical (smallest) size of the dendritic nucleate. To evaluate this, we synthesized cross-linked polymer composite electrolytes with tunable pore size, which host organic liquid in these pores. We systemically varied pore size within our electrolyte systems and found that the materials are resilient towards dendritic growth below a critical pore size, as predicted by the theoretical studies. Further, by the housed organic liquid solvent within the polymer network, our electrolyte system could maintain ionic conductivity at room temperature. These results show that the tendency for battery failure by dendrite-induced short-circuits can be reduced in rationally designed electrolytes, opening the gateway for future work nanoporous electrolytes.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: 3-D Printing of Energetic Materials
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: 3-D Printing of Energetic Materials Over the last decade 3-D printing has been at the forefront of materials processing. However, for energetic materials 3-D printing is in its infancy and many critical material parameters are unknown. In this work, we explore ceramic fuel based pyrotechnics, also known as pyrolants. For this study, a ceramic fuel (MgB2) and a fluoropolymer (THV) were formulated in five different ratios of 30/70, 40/60, 50/50, 60/40, and 70/30. The combustability, combustion velocities, density, thermal characteristics, and aging were all studied in the course of this project. All five ratios were printed as inks and 30/70, 50/50, and 70/30 were printed as filament for comparison. As the amount of MgB2 was increased, the combustion velocity increased significantly with the 30/70 ratio at 4.016 mm/s while the 70/30 ratio combusted at 35.197 mm/s. In addition to the combustion velocities, the density was also assessed. The printed inks had a density of 0.4-0.7 g/cc lower than the filament most likely due to the porosity from air pockets that occur during printing. This also explains why the ratio of 60/40 was lower than the 50/50 ratio, when it was expected to be higher. Using a Brookfield Rheometer, it was determined that the 60/40 ratio fell out of the expected range with an apparent viscosity of 2,000,000 cP higher than the other four samples. Over the course of eight weeks in an aging oven, the filament aged extremely well. There was no significant change in color or in burning rate leading to the conclusion that the printed pyrolant is reliable over time. Future studies should consider optimizing printing parameters to reduce porosity.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Evaluating the Sensitivity of the Momentum TM Magnetic Particle Imager for Ferucarbotran Iron Oxide Nanoparticles
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) is a promising imaging technology that enables non-invasive quantitative visualization of the distribution of biocompatible superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) tracers. MPI signal is proportional to SPIO mass, does not suffer from artifacts arising from tissue background signal, has no limitations in tissue depth penetration, and does not use ionizing radiation. These features make MPI ideal for characterizing in vivo nanoparticle biodistribution quantitatively. The objective of this study was to characterize the sensitivity of the new Momentum TM MPI imager (Magnetic Insight, Inc.) using the commercially available SPIO nanoparticle ferucarbotran. A serial dilution of ferucarbotran iron oxide particles was prepared with the iron mass determined using the 1,10-Phenanthroline colorimetric assay for iron quantification. All samples contained 1uL of solution and were measured in triplicate, in two different positions of the field of view. MPI scans were made using four imaging modes available in the Momentum: default, isotropic, high resolution and high sensitivity. Images were analyzed using VivoQuant to evaluate signal intensity in regions of interest containing the tracer samples. The limit of detection was calculated on the basis of analyzing the spontaneous background signal of empty scans and the maximum intensity signal of samples at low concentrations. It was found that ‘ high sensitivity’ scan mode (3 T/m) had a limit of detection ~38 ng Fe, whereas ‘high resolution’ scan mode (6 T/m) had a limit of detection of ~200 ng Fe. We also observed differences in signal shape and background across all different imaging modalities. Determining the MPI limit of detection and quantification of different SPIO tracers is important for the development of a variety of applications. Understanding the optimal magnetic characteristics of SPIO tracers and their behavior on the Momentum TM MPI will provide a better understanding of the capabilities of this instrument for particle characterization and biomedical application. This will ensure that reliable data can be obtained and understood. Future studies will include determining the limit of detection for in-house synthesized particles to understand the behavior and properties of particles in the MPI, facilitating optimization of tracers for MPI imaging.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Hydrogen Peroxide Releasing Biomaterials for Vascularization in Bone Tissue Regeneration
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: In the United States, 5-10% of bone fractures result in nonunion. Traditional solutions such as autografts and allografts have significant side effects, including donor site morbidity and disease transmission, respectively. Although new regenerative engineering treatments have been developed, their high cost and limited scalability have prevented their widespread clinical adoption. An additional limitation of bone tissue regeneration is inherent tissue complexity as vascular and neural networks must be regenerated in addition to osteoblasts. The Biomodulatory Materials Engineering Laboratory is working to develop a cheaper and more widely applicable option for large volume bone repair using novel biomaterials. This project focuses specifically on using the simple signaling molecule hydrogen peroxide to induce the differentiation of endothelial cells from mesenchymal stem cells for bone tissue vascularization applications. First, the therapeutic window for the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into endothelial cells using hydrogen peroxide was determined by exposing the cells to various concentrations of hydrogen peroxide for one, three, and seven days. Proliferation and differentiation of the cells was determined for each timepoint using DNA/ATP assays and fluorescent microscopy, respectively. A novel hydrogen-peroxide-releasing biomaterial was then synthesized by modifying glutamic acid with hydrogen peroxide to form a peroxy acid (i.e., perglutamic acid). Future research will focus on leveraging perglutamic acid as a monomer for various degradable polymers (e.e, polyanhydrides, polyesters, polyamides), for which cell studies can be conducted guided by the already established therapeutic window. The effects of these new biomaterials on off-target cells will also be studied. After biomaterials for osteogenesis, angiogenesis, and neurogenesis have each been synthesized, they can be integrated for large volume bone repair through tissue regeneration.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Fabrication of PbSe Quantum Dot Thin Films with an Inkjet Printer
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The fundamental processes associated with the fabrication of epitaxially-connected quantum dot solids is neither well understood nor controlled. As a result, many of their anticipated acclaimed properties have remained elusive. Inkjet printing offers rigorous process control, enhances manufacturing scalability, enables film integration into a wide range of device platforms, and allows for patterned designs without further processing. PbSe quantum dot thin films are created at the interface of two immiscible solvents. The PbSe quantum dots are in the upper solvent phase, or superphase, and become epitaxially connected when a chemical trigger binds to the ligands on the facets of the quantum dots and removes them. Then, the chemical trigger-ligand complex enters the lower solvent phase, or subphase, promoting uniform thin film formation. For such a system to work in an inkjet printer, the subphase can be initially printed onto a wafer. Then, the superphase can be printed on top of the subphase. Finally, a chemical trigger can be applied and the film formation would occur. We optimized the jetting of the superphase onto a silicon wafer substrate. We varied the jetting conditions, such as the waveform, and the composition of the superphase, such as changing the concentration of PbSe or the solvent. We balanced the constraints due to the fluid mechanics and thermodynamics involved with droplet formation and uniform thin film formation. Our optimal superphase solution was a PbSe ortho-dichlorobenzene solution. In future studies, we will optimize jetting this superphase onto subphases and then initiate film formation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Thermochromic Cholesteryl Liquid Crystals Characterization with Polarized Light Microscopy
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Cholesteric liquid crystals have temperature responsive optical properties due to anisotropic molecular orientation that is dependent on temperature. Specifically, the twisted nematic phase creates a helical structure that reflects visible light; the pitch of the helical structure and the wavelength (i.e. color) of reflected light both depend on temperature. Such liquid crystals have applications for thermal mapping by cameras. This introduces a need to evaluate the behavior of liquid crystals through visual analysis. In this work, a method to determine the thermochromic properties of liquid crystals was developed by using polarized light microscopy (PLM). To examine the liquid crystals, rectangular capillary tubes were filled with different formulations, comprised of cholesteryl benzoate, cholesteryl pelargonate, and cholesteryl oleyl carbonate, of liquid crystals. The composition of the ternary mixture was varied to tune the thermochromic properties of the liquid crystal. The rectangular capillary tubes were sealed at one end, filled with liquid crystal; a thermocouple was introduced, and the capillary was sealed at the other end. After heating to approximately 50°C, the samples were imaged using polarized light microscopy as they cooled to ambient conditions. To observe the color change due to the change in the molecular orientation of the liquid crystals, imaging was performed at 10x magnification, the minimal field diaphragm, and about 50% aperture. To avoid saturation, images were captured with auto exposure, auto white balancing at 1 frame per second. The digital images in standard red, green, blend (sRGB) were transformed to L*a*b* color space Performing frame-by-frame analysis, observed changes in color were related to quantifiable changes in CIE L*a*b* values. Depending on the composition, the blue-start to red-end varied from of 23.0 to 25.4 °C, 25.3 to 30.3 °C, and 36.9 to 42.6 °C. Specifically, color transition temperatures between 23.0 and 42.6 °C were obtained by varying the fraction of cholesteryl pelargonate in the formulation. The analysis method developed was validated with UV reflectance; the color transition temperatures measured by PLM and UV were comparable. Interestingly, the polarized light microscopy method allows for more detailed characterization of color transition temperatures than achieved by UV spectroscopy.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Graphene Nanoscrolls Induced Unique Crystallization of Poly Lactic Acid
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Poly (lactic acid) (PLA) has gained attention for its use in biomedical applications due to its biocompatibility and optical, mechanical, and barrier properties. However, it is usually found in an amorphous or semi-crystalline state, which causes it to be brittle and have poor toughness. In order to improve the mechanical properties of this polymer, extensive research has been put into effective ways to crystallize PLA. This is difficult as PLA crystallization is a slow process that does not comply with large scale crystallization measures. A way to counteract this problem is by incorporating a nucleating agent into the polymer to lower the activation energy needed to start crystallization and affect the shape of the crystals, thereby affecting the mechanical properties of the polymer. Graphene nanoscrolls (GNS) are rolled up sheets of carbon, created by overcoming an energy barrier of about 100s to 1000s J/mol applied to graphene nanoplatelets. Once this energy is added, the flat sheets roll up and do not unscroll due to π bond interactions between the carbon molecules in different layers keeping the structure strong. Graphene itself is known for its chemical functionalization capabilities and physical properties such as high mechanical strength and thermal conductivity. GNS contains these properties from its graphene source, but also differs from other carbon-based nanomaterials such as carbon nanotubes, as its unfused edged creates an open morphology. This unique shape allows for a lattice strain which can provide more mechanical strength and create new crystallization structures. In this study, graphene nanoscrolls were fabricated from graphene nanoplatelets and used in PLA crystallization to improve the mechanical and physical properties of PLA. This was done by sonicating a mixture of GNP and toluene for scrolling and then using liquid nitrogen for structural stability to create GNS. The GNS then dried at room temperature before being incorporated into a melt-mix crystallization with PLA. Different weight percentages of GNS to PLA were used to see the affect on crystallization. Samples were then characterized by SEM, TEM, FTIR, XRD, and underwent a nanoindentation test to determine how the crystal structure of PLA changed, if any chemical interactions occurred between the PLA and GNS, the crystal structure and changes in mechanical properties. Through these analyses it was determined that the addition of GNS to PLA increases the crystallinity, crystal structure, modulus and hardness without any chemical changes to the polymer.

The device is composed of D-Sorbitol because it is biodegradable due to its presence in plants during photosynthesis, which means it can be consumed naturally. The other major material used in the sensor that is environmentally friendly and biodegradable is cellulose nanofibrils (CNF). Electrodes for the sensor can be biodegradable, as well. 3D-printing—additive manufacturing—is useful when in mass production. By producing many devices in a batch or continuous process saves time, which in turn saves money for the manufacturing company. It makes this quality very valuable to potential in the market; therefore, the device could be integrated into a marketable product that can be used as a wireless, wearable temperature sensor. In order to achieve this goal, the voltage and temperature changes must be analyzed thoroughly, as well as an analysis of the materials being used. Finally, the materials must be able to be prove that additive manufacturing is a viable option for production. The purpose of this study is to determine how the voltage is produced when a temperature difference is applied and be able to predict the temperature of the heat source given the produced voltage.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The small gravitational forces characteristic in dust systems facilitate opposing dynamics: airborne suspension and adhesion to surfaces. In the case that the particle size is larger than the length scale for surface roughness, we derive an analytic model that incorporates force contributions from all asperities on the surface. Our analytic model accurately predicts the van der Waals force, in contrast to previous models which underestimate adhesion by not accounting for the effects of all surface asperities.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Eigencages: Learning a Latent Space of Porous Cage Molecules
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Porous organic cage molecules harbor nanosized cavities that can selectively adsorb gas molecules, which lends them applications in separations and sensing. The geometry of the cavity strongly influences their adsorptive selectivity. For comparing cages and predicting their adsorption properties, we embed/encode a set of 74 porous organic cage molecules into a low-dimensional, latent “cage space” on the basis of their intrinsic porosity. We first computationally scan each cage to generate a three-dimensional (3D) image of its inherent pore cavity. Leveraging the singular value decomposition, in an unsupervised manner, we then learn across all cages an approximate, lower-dimensional subspace in which the 3D porosity images cluster together. The “eigencages” are the set of orthogonal, characteristic 3D porosity images that span this lower-dimensional subspace, ordered in terms of importance. A latent representation, or encoding, of each cage follows by approximately expressing it as a combination of the eigencages. We show that the learned encoding captures salient, inherent features of the cavities of porous cages molecules and is predictive of properties of the cages that arise from cavity shape. Our methods could be applied to learn latent representations of cavities within other classes of porous materials and of shapes of molecules in general.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Self-Assembly and Solution Structure of Supramolecular Bottlebrush Polymers
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Supramolecular polymers are unique compared to traditional polymers in that they are composed of key reversible and directional secondary bonding. Secondary bonds, most notably hydrogen bonds, can be fine-tuned and can consequentially alter the polymer’s material properties. Studies on self-assembly of linear chains with sidechain pendants (approximating the structure of graft polymer) typically use short small molecules for hydrogen bonding, yet it is unclear how well short polymers (<5K Daltons) will assemble. To study the impact of how sidechain length impacts supramolecular assembly, hydroxyl terminated polystyrene (PSOH) side chains were blended on to a poly-4-vinyl pyridine (P4VP) backbone. P4VP was chosen as the backbone due to the strength of the pyridine groups as an H-bond acceptor while PSOH of varying molecular weights were used as the pendant chains. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was primarily used to investigate the hydrogen bonding occurring in the blended samples. Employing FTIR methods provides fundamental results in analyzing the amount of the pyridine groups in P4VP that are participating in supramolecular self-assembly. Small angle neutron scattering (SANS) located at the NIST Center for Neutron Research (NCNR) was also used to track the mesoscopic solution structure. Final results from the FITR showed that a single hydrogen bond (OH-P4VP) appeared to be insufficient to drive self-assembly for even oligomeric polymer chains. These findings contrast from SANS results on a lauryl gallate (surfactant) polymer blends. These findings show promise in supramolecular graft polymer being based on the multiple hydrogen bonding sites.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Asymmetric Hybrid Solid Electrolyte with High Conductivity and Low Interfacial Resistance for Lithium Batteries
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Asymmetric Hybrid Solid Electrolyte with High Conductivity and Low Interfacial Resistance for Lithium Batteries Zachary D Althouse † , Yubin He † , Haochen Yang † and Nian Liu *† † School of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA 30332-0100, USA Abstract Lithium-ion battery technology is already nearly ubiquitous in portable electronics and is increasingly being put forward as an option in electric vehicle applications. However, current Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) possess intrinsic safety hazards because of their use of flammable organic liquid as the electrolyte. This makes solid state electrolytes (SSE) a very promising area of research as they lack the volatility concerns of their liquid counterparts. There are two main categories of solid electrolytes: polymer and ceramic. Polymer electrolytes have better interfacial contact and electrochemical stability, while being less mechanically strong. Ceramic electrolytes have good conductivity and mechanical stability but have poor interfacial contact. To mitigate the inherent weaknesses of each material, combining the two technologies into a hybrid electrolyte has recently been investigated. In this work, preliminary investigation into an asymmetric solid “sandwich” electrolyte has occurred. This design uses crosslinked polyethylene oxide (CPEG) and polycarbonate (CPC) SSE on either side of a ceramic electrolyte backbone (LLZO). Preliminary results have shown that the CPEG-SSE and UVPC-SSE exhibit high conductivity (0.36 mS/cm and 0.18 mS/cm, respectively) at room temperature. A high conductivity of 0.30 mS/cm was also observed for the asymmetric SSE (CPEG/LLZO/UVPC). The Li/CPEG/Li symmetric cell shows excellent cycling stability at 0.2 mA/cm 2 for 500 hours, demonstrating that CPEG SSE possesses good stability against Li metal anode. However, CV results suggest that CPEG-SSE has low anti-oxidation ability at higher voltage (>4 V vs Li + /Li). On the other hand, UVPC SSE showed an extended electrochemical window up to 4.6 V vs Li + /Li, but poor cycling stability in a Li/UVPC/Li symmetric cell. The Li-LiFePO 4 batteries with a symmetric SSE (CPEG/LLZO/CPEG) have demonstrated low interfacial resistance (<160 ohm) as well as excellent rate performance (155 mAh/g at 0.2 C, 93 mAh/g at 1 C, and 57 mAh/g at 1.5C). Further studies will be conducted to determine the electro-chemical stability and battery performance of the hybrid membrane. This design, if effective, could lead to increased development of a modular electrolyte system, in which specific polymers would be chosen based on the cell requirements and identity of the cathode and anode materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) is a powerful tool to extract the material and optoelectronic properties of semiconductors. However, extracting relevant information from TRPL data can be challenging as many complex electron dynamics can exist in these materials. Therefore, simulating TRPL data as a function of various material properties is of interest to better understand these electron dynamics and correlate with measured data. Dedicated commercial software for simulating transient electron dynamics is, however, limited and cost-prohibitive. Here we introduce an open-source program that we have developed to simulate transient electron dynamics in semiconductors. This program uses numerical methods to solve non-linear coupled differential equations as these equations governing the transient diffusion, drift, and the decay of electrons – whose recombination is a precursor to photon emission – can generally not be solved analytically. Our Python application for generating, visualizing, and exporting electron dynamics and TRPL data will be shown. In addition, example TRPL simulations in comparison to experimental data will be shown for thin-film photovoltaic absorbers and semiconducting nanowires.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Photosynthesis is a biological process that converts energy from sunlight into chemical energy as an organic fuel. Cuprous oxide (Cu 2 O), a p-type semiconductor, was used to mimic this process as a cathode material for a photoelectrochemical (PEC) water splitting reaction. Cu 2 O can absorb energy from sunlight and convert it into a chemical form as hydrogen. The produced hydrogen can then be used as a clean fuel in devices like hydrogen fuel cells or further converted to ammonia (NH 3 ) for transport. In this study, thin layers of Cu 2 O crystals were deposited on a planar Cu substrate using chronoamperometry (CA) and characterized using scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Mott-Schottky analysis. The peak current density for the water splitting reaction was measured in a PEC cell using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV). The effect of deposition time was investigated as the Cu 2 O layer thickness has shown to affect the activity. The Cu 2 O prepared using a 5-minute deposition time showed the best performance relative to deposition times of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 minutes. The 5-minute deposition sample produced the highest peak current density of approximately -1.70 mA/cm 2 . Longer deposition times showed decreased performance.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Improved Lithium-Ion Battery Cathode Cycling Stability at Higher Cut-Off Potential Using a Novel and Scalable Dual Coating Method
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: The electrification of transportation and the need for grid energy storage to accompany renewable energy require secondary batteries with higher energy density, longer useful lifespans and lower cost. In order for lithium-ion batteries, the most developed battery technology suitable for these uses, to achieve greater energy density at the cell level, the operating voltage window tolerated over the course of long-term cycling must be increased. In this work we have demonstrated a promising dual coating system of Li 2 SrSiO 4 and Al 2 O 3 achieved via an easily scalable sol gel technique and confirmed via XRD, used on commercial LiCoO 2 cathode powder. We demonstrate our finding that the optimal thickness of each coating can lead to increased specific capacity (~185 mAh/g at 0.5C) at a cut-off potential of 4.5 V and greater stability through multiple cycles at very high C rates (up to 10 C). Cyclic voltammetry was used to demonstrate reduced polarization, and therefore increased stability, after cycling in the dual coated cathodes relative to bare or Al 2 O 3 coated material. Fluorescence mapping of elemental distribution provides evidence of mechanical property advantages of the dual coating system, and the ability of the dual coating to preserve the cathode particles despite inhomogeneous thickness. The mechanism of the superior performance relative to bare and Al 2 O 3 coated cathodes was studied using scanning and transmission electron microscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and synchrotron X-ray spectroscopy in pristine and cycled cathodes. These findings have implications for the search for still better materials for which our simple coating method could be utilized. Additionally, we aim to gain insights into the transferable nature of the mechanisms by which this coating stabilizes cathodes at high voltage between the LiCoO2 utilized in this work, and experimental, lower cobalt cathode materials such as NMC811 or lithium-excess materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Optimizing Conditions for Thermal Exfoliation of Graphite Oxide Films
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Thermal exfoliation of graphite oxide is an effective and economically feasible large-scale production method for graphene-based materials. These materials are desirable for various applications such as catalysts, selective membranes, semiconductors, batteries, and sensors. In the process of GO film synthesis, the vast graphene oxide (GO) theoretical monolayer specific surface area (2600 m 2 /g) is lost due the perfect face-to-face GO monolayer alignment. In GO synthesis, modified Hummers method was applied, and the GO suspension (2 mg/mL) was used to prepare drop-cast and wrinkled GO films of varying thicknesses. These GO films were thermally exfoliated in an instrument set low (10 K/min) and high (100<HR<1000 K/min) heating rates. At low heating rates, GO drop-cast films below thickness 36 µm exfoliated into low surface area (<37 m 2 /g) and non-porous reduced graphite oxide (rGO) films. GO drop-cast films with thickness above 36 µm subjected to low heating rates yielded rGO films with modest surface area (~171 m 2 /g). Independent of the film morphology (wrinkled/drop-cast) and thickness, at high instrument heating rates the graphite oxide films explosively exfoliated into rGO powder with fairly large surface area (~700m 2 /g) and total porosity (~1.8 cc/g). It seems there is a critical film thickness and heating rate at which mass (product gases) and heat generation rates surpass their transfer rates out of the rGO system and GO exfoliates explosively. Wrinkled GO films did not demonstrate significant differences in thermal exfoliation compared to the drop-cast GO films. These insights are valuable for researchers trying to optimize GO thermal exfoliation process to produce graphene-based materials in large scale for variety of application venues.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Development of a Rechargeable Antimicrobial Textile
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Functionalizing cotton with antimicrobial properties shows promise for applications in hospitals, for the military, and the general public. There has been a great deal of attention paid to methods of attaching n-halamine compounds to textiles for this purpose. Over time, the halogens present on these compounds dissociate into the surrounding environment and function as biocides. After dissociation, the n-halamines can be recharged by exposure to a solution containing halogen ions. One such n-halamine is 5,5-dimethylhydantoin (DMH), which is commonly brominated to a biocidal form for water purification. Previously in this project, a procedure for the synthesizing and purifying a DMH derivative, allyl-5,5-dimethylhadantion (ADMH), had been optimized. This compound retains the antimicrobial functionality of DMH, yet also can be chemically bonded to cotton. Once bonded, the strength of the antimicrobial properties was evaluated by exposing the fabric to the bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and Serratia marcescens and observing the growth inhibition in comparison to a positive and a negative control. Currently, tests have shown bacterial growth inhibition on only the fabric surface, suggesting that no chlorine is leaching into the environment surrounding the sample. This is desirable since skin irritation is noted as a possible drawback of using chlorinated n-halamines. Previous work on this project followed a “bottom-up” approach to the fabric modification; each necessary molecule is added to the fabric individually concluding with ADMH and its chlorination. This process does not allow for quantitative assessment each reaction’s efficiency. It is desired to produce the final biocide in solution so that it may be attached in a single step which is ideal for synthesis on an industrial scale. Thus far, the molecule that links ADMH to the fabric has been synthesized and precipitated out via acidification. No IR spectroscopy data exists for the linker currently, and therefore this route of analysis has been performed by matching peaks with bonds known to exist on the linker. The final goal of this project is to develop a water-soluble molecule for which the process of synthesis and fabric attachment can be easily scaled up. This allows the treated fabric to be available to a wide range of consumers and may be implemented in a variety of fields where textiles are in continual contact with skin.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: An Improved Characterization of Topological Features in Molecular Simulations Using Persistent Homology.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: We apply a mathematical method known as persistent homology to analyze the geometrical features of mesophases produced from molecular dynamics simulations. Specifically, we study ionic liquid/hydrocarbon mixtures. Ionic liquids (ILs) are salts with unique properties, which have made them ideally suited for many applications. Their ability to dissolve different, sometimes amphiphilic, compounds is likely tied to the formation of segregated nanoscale domains. These domains, or aggregates, are created due to the separation of the polar and nonpolar regions in the ionic liquid. Determining the shape of these domains is very important in understanding the behavior of the system. Persistent homology uses a process known as filtration that incorporates a geometric measurement into topological invariants. By using a filtration parameter, simplicial complexes, such as triangles, are generated. The lifespans of the invariants are then recorded in a barcode. Such barcodes can be interpreted to determine the geometry of the object. Persistent homology was tested on objects with well-defined shapes, providing an understanding of the detailed barcode resulting from the analysis, such as the interpretation of the lifetime of lines in the barcode and the different dimensions. Comparisons between the shapes of these mesophases was done via persistent homology using the bottleneck distance to determine how similar two topologies are from one another. The smaller the value of the bottleneck distance, the more similarity exists between the two shapes. Additionally, persistent homology can be used to analyze different properties, such as thickness and diameter, of 2D and 3D shapes to see how each property affects the barcode. Such tests gave an insight on how persistent homology works, allowing us to use it on systems of ionic liquids to quantitatively characterize their topology. Multiple simulations containing the mixtures of lipid-inspired ILs with either hexane or cyclohexane were conducted at various mole fractions and analyzed. The barcodes from each simulation showed that increasing the concentration of IL in the system increases the number of aggregates in both 2D and 3D. Furthermore, most holes generally appear to have the same size, suggesting a characteristic size that the IL aggregates like to adopt. Future studies will compare these simulated IL aggregates with a library of idealized shapes to identify its characteristic shape. Moreover, work will be done to extend the persistent homology code to accurately deal with topologies extending across periodic boundaries.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Synthesizing Silver Selenide Thin Films Via the Cation Exchange Process for Thermoelectric Applications.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Thermoelectric (TE) devices are unique semiconductor devices that can directly convert heat to electricity and vice versa to serve applications such as waste heat recovery and solid state cooling. Bismuth-Tellurium and other commonly used alloys have been shown to be high performance TE materials but are composed of elements that are toxic, rare and expensive to process. To accelerate the widespread adoption of TE devices, safe and abundant materials need to be integrated into TE devices at an economical cost. Prior research has involved synthesizing Ag 2 Se nanoparticles, however this is an energy-intensive and time consuming technique with poor yields. To tackle this problem, we optimize the TE performance of Ag 2 Se by producing it via a low-cost, solution-processable approach relying on the cation exchange of Cu 2-x Se to Ag 2 Se. Cation exchange has recently emerged as an extremely versatile tool that allows manufacturing of a variety of materials whilst maintaining the morphology of a known anionic structure. We report a maximum power factor (PF) of ~800 µWm −1 K −2 achieved via a simple thin film soak. This PF is the highest value reported to date for a solution-processable Ag 2 Se thin film at room temperature. This soaking technique allows for a safe, economical and scalable solution to using Ag 2 Se in a variety of TE applications.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Development of Accurate Eam Potentials of Gold with Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: One of the most critical limitations to performing successful molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of metal structures in many fields of study is the availability of suitable interatomic potentials. Embedded atom potentials (EAM) in particular provide a unique solution due to their low computational cost and ability to accurately model bulk properties of pure metals and their alloys. Many EAM potential parameters for gold have been developed to reproduce experimental and/or quantum calculations data. However, when these parameters are used to simulate systems beyond their calibrated environments, the data presented can be invalid or open to interpretation. We present accurate EAM interatomic potentials for gold that was developed to reproduce its experimental properties by integrating particle swarm optimization (PSO) with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The resulting EAM parameters of gold were validated by performing Bayesian uncertainty quantification. Overall, these new parameters of gold are robust and transferable across a range of different conditions. The interactions between these new gold parameters and water were also developed to reproduce its interfacial tension at 300 K.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.title: Additive Manufacturing with Semi-Crystalline Thermoplastics: Properties for Printability
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2019/meet.abstract: Temperature control is an integral part of success in 3D printing. Slight changes in printing conditions can drastically affect the printed part. This project is aimed to investigate the thermal properties of common semi-crystalline 3D printing thermoplastics in fused filament fabrication (FFF) with thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) and polylactic acid (PLA). Melt flow behavior of the filaments was studied by printing lines on the printer bed to determine the mass flow rate over a range of nozzle temperatures from a high temperature of 255⁰C to the values where no filament is extruded by 2⁰C increments. The time remained constant throughout the experiments for each filament. However, the mass flow rate drastically decreased as the nozzle temperature dropped below 209⁰C and 183⁰C for TPU and PLA, respectively. Filament behavior changed with nozzle temperature, so while the filaments could be extruded at lower than manufacturer suggested temperatures, the overall printability is drastically reduced below a certain threshold of nozzle temperature. This behavior is attributed to change in melting range of the polymers with the heating rate. Therefore, the data was compared to DSC measurements at different heating rates to better understand the range of melting temperatures of the semi-crystalline polymers. This data can be used to achieve more successful 3D prints and an overall better understanding of printing behaviors at various temperatures.
